# Diese helfer sind teuer helfen aber gar nicht so viel

Die Analyse zu „Diese helfer sind teuer helfen aber gar nicht so viel“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.title: Interdisciplinarity on the curriculum—teachers hold different views on what students should learn
items.subtitle: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs…
items.feedText: Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland and Aalborg University in Denmark. The paper is published in the Journal of Engineering Education.
items.articleBody: The climate transition, energy supply and technological development are just some examples of areas where knowledge from several disciplines needs to come together to find relevant solutions. Engineering students are therefore often given the opportunity to work on interdisciplinary projects. But the term "interdisciplinary" encompasses widely differing ideas about what the teaching should involve and what students are actually expected to learn. This is shown by a study in which researchers interviewed 18 teachers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden, Aalto University in Finland and Aalborg University in Denmark. The paper is published in the Journal of Engineering Education.

items.title: iPhone 18e könnte größeres Display und deutlich mehr Akkukapazität erhalten
items.subtitle: Das iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max und iPhone Duo hat Apple bereits „abgefrühstückt“.
items.feedText:
Blieben noch das iPhone 18, iPhone 18e und iPhone Air 2. Die drei zuletzt genannten Smartphones sollen im Frühjahr 2027 erscheinen. Nun gibt es frische Gerüchte zum kommenden Einsteiger-iPhone. Neue Gerüchte zum iPhone 18e

Nachdem Apple bereits vor wenigen Wochen drei neue iPhone-Modelle auf den Markt gebracht hat, arbeitet das Unternehmen hinter den Kulissen bereits an den nächsten Modellen. Glaubt man aktuellen Gerüchten, so könnte Apple dem kommenden iPhone 18e zwei größere Hardware-Verbesserungen spendieren…
items.articleBody:
Das iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max und iPhone Duo hat Apple bereits „abgefrühstückt“. Blieben noch das iPhone 18, iPhone 18e und iPhone Air 2. Die drei zuletzt genannten Smartphones sollen im Frühjahr 2027 erscheinen. Nun gibt es frische Gerüchte zum kommenden Einsteiger-iPhone.

Neue Gerüchte zum iPhone 18e

Nachdem Apple bereits vor wenigen Wochen drei neue iPhone-Modelle auf den Markt gebracht hat, arbeitet das Unternehmen hinter den Kulissen bereits an den nächsten Modellen. Glaubt man aktuellen Gerüchten, so könnte Apple dem kommenden iPhone 18e zwei größere Hardware-Verbesserungen spendieren. Ein neuer Leak deutet darauf hin, dass das günstigere Modell nicht nur einen größeren Bildschirm, sondern auch einen deutlich leistungsfähigeren Akku bekommen könnte. Damit würde es sich dem „normalen“ iPhone 18 in einigen wichtigen Bereichen annähern.

Ausgangspunkt der neuen Gerüchte ist eine auf Weibo verbreitete Grafik, die den mutmaßlichen Innenaufbau von iPhone 18 und iPhone 18e gegenüberstellt. Der chinesische Leaker Fixed Focus Digital erklärt, dass ihm die Darstellung bereits bekannt sei und sie grundsätzlich zu den Informationen seiner Quellen passe. Besonders die gemeinsame Akkukonstruktion sei ein Beispiel für die zuvor vermutete Verwendung gleicher Komponenten.

Beide Modelle mit 4.430-mAh-Akku?

Laut den Beschriftungen der Grafik sollen sowohl das iPhone 18 als auch das iPhone 18e einen Akku mit 4.430 mAh erhalten. Für das iPhone 18e wäre das ein Zuwachs von rund elf Prozent gegenüber den 4.005 mAh des iPhone 17e. Beim regulären iPhone 18 würde die Kapazität sogar um etwa 21 Prozent gegenüber dem Vorgänger steigen.

Beim Standardmodell soll der zusätzliche Platz unter anderem durch Veränderungen am unteren Lautsprecher und an der Vibrationskomponente entstehen. Die beiden Geräte könnten dadurch trotz unterschiedlicher Ausstattung auf dieselbe Akkukapazität kommen. Ob sich das tatsächlich in einer entsprechend längeren Laufzeit niederschlägt, hängt allerdings auch von Display, Prozessor und Energieverwaltung ab.

Widersprüchliche Angaben zur Displaygröße

Besonders interessant ist die mögliche Vergrößerung des Bildschirms. Die Grafik nennt für beide Modelle eine Diagonale von 6,3 Zoll. Das iPhone 17e besitzt dagegen ein 6,1-Zoll-Display. Ein solcher Schritt würde das günstigere iPhone beim Bildschirmformat näher an das reguläre iPhone 18 heranbringen.

Allerdings widerspricht diese Angabe bisherigen Informationen eines anderen Weibo-Leakers (Digital Chat Station). Dieser erwartet für das iPhone 18e weiterhin ein 6,12 Zoll großes OLED-Display mit einer Bildwiederholrate von 60Hz. Das reguläre iPhone 18 soll dagegen ein 6,3-Zoll-Display mit bis zu 120 Hz erhalten. Welche Darstellung zutrifft, lässt sich derzeit nicht beurteilen.

Bei der Kameraausstattung dürfte Apple weiterhin einen deutlichen Abstand zwischen den Modellen schaffen. Während das iPhone 18 der geleakten Grafik zufolge zwei rückseitige Kameras einschließlich Ultraweitwinkelobjektiv erhalten soll, bleibt es beim iPhone 18e offenbar bei einer einzelnen Hauptkamera.

A20-Chip und neues Mobilfunkmodem erwartet

Weitere Gerüchte betreffen den Prozessor. Das iPhone 18e soll den A20-Chip erhalten, der im moderneren 2-Nanometer-Verfahren gefertigt wird. Damit würde Apple den A19 im 3-Nanometer-Verfahren aus dem iPhone 17e ablösen. 9GB RAM statt 8GB wurden bereits in der Vergangenheit kolportiert. Auch Apples eigenes C2-Modem wird für beide Geräte erwartet. Es würde beim iPhone 18e das bisherige C1X-Modem ersetzen.

Wie immer gilt: Gerüchte sind immer mit einer Portion Skepsis zu betrachen.

items.articleBody:
We’re excited to announce that as of today, AppStories, MacStories Unwind, and NPC: Next Portable Console all support HLS video streaming. We’re also beginning a special AppStories miniseries on iPhone Duo apps beginning today.

For Apple Podcasts listeners, that means you’ll be able to switch between the video and audio-only versions of the shows on demand with the tap of a button that appears just above the app’s playback controls. The update also means you can watch the video versions of our shows in Apple Podcasts on the Apple TV. HLS also means you can lock your iPhone or iPad while watching an episode and continue listening uninterrupted, which is great when you’re on the go.

Pocket Casts, which is a favorite of many MacStories podcast listeners, supports HLS video, too. And, for podcast apps that don’t support video, you’ll still get the audio-only version as you always have. The YouTube channel isn’t going away either.

From the beginning of our shows, we’ve been committed to offering high-quality audio to our audience. HLS and a lot of work behind the scenes allow us to bring that same high-quality audio edit to video for the first time.

Because our podcasts started as audio-only, getting here required a rethinking of every part of the production process from start to finish. One result of that effort is a suite of custom internal tools that has simplified our podcast workflow, giving our audience more ways to enjoy the shows than ever before.

It’s worth noting that one limitation of Apple’s HLS implementation is that it does not currently support paid shows, which means AppStories+, MacStories Unwind+, and NPC XL don’t support HLS streaming. That’s something that we’d like to add in the future, but currently, it’s not possible.

Plus, we’re kicking off the transition to HLS with a special AppStories miniseries on iPhone Duo apps. There’s a lot of ground to cover, so we’re not sure yet how many episodes we’ll be doing. However, today’s episode features 17 Duo apps we love, which is a good start.

Every episode of our podcasts now includes a formatted and linked transcript.

Oh, and one more thing… we’ve added transcripts to the show notes for each episode. After the show notes links, you’ll find a “Show Transcript” disclosure triangle. Click it to reveal a neatly formatted transcript with timestamps for each chapter and turn in the conversation. The timestamps for the free versions of the shows are also linked to Apple Podcasts, so you can jump from an episode’s page on MacStories straight to that spot in the audio or video.

Finally, thanks to everyone who has listened, watched, and subscribed to MacStories podcasts. We’re coming up on the 10th anniversary of AppStories early next year, and we never imagined then that we’d still be doing it today, let alone with two other shows.

Bei NAM (Neural Amp Modeler) handelt es sich um eine Open-Source-Lösung, mit der sich Verstärker, Effektpedale, Outboard-Geräte und komplette Signalketten simulieren lassen.

Und auf den Heritage Audio i73 Pro können nun NAM-A2-Modelle direkt über den DSP des Interfaces benutzt werden. Die CPU des Rechners wird also nicht belastet und gleichzeitig verspricht dieser Ansatz auch kaum spürbare Latenz.

Der speziell für die Interfaces entwickelte Loader unterstützt .nam-Dateien und kann ebenso Impulsantworten (IRs) lesen. Und weil NAM eben ein offenes Format ist, gibt’s Zugriff auf riesige Bibliotheken wie zum Beispiel von TONE3000.

In jedem Slot verfügt der NAM-Loader über einen integrierten Tuner. Bis zu vier .nam-Captures und vier IRs lassen sich speichern. Auf dieser Basis kannst du dann eigene Presets erstellen und so deine bevorzugten Rig-Konfigurationen speichern.

Zusätzlich ist es auch möglich, über den DSP-Mixer des Heritage Audio i73 Pro die Plugins des Herstellers und ebenso VST3-Plugins von Drittanbietern für das Monitoring nutzen. Das ist praktisch, wenn du beispielsweise Vocals mit deinem Lieblings-Reverb-Plugin abhören willst und dabei den Prozessor schonen möchtest. Dabei kannst du dann sogar das trockene und das bearbeitete Signal gleichzeitig in deiner DAW aufnehmen.

Nach dem kostenlos erhältlichen Firmware-Update lassen sich NAM-Modelle direkt über den DSP des Interfaces nutzen · Quelle: Heritage Audio

Und auch VST3-Plugins können auf dem DSP berechnet werden · Quelle: Heritage Audio

Sehr schönes Update, das du hier kostenlos bekommst.

Und hier bei Thomann* ist das Premium-Interface Heritage Audio i73 Pro Edge erhältlich. Mehr über die Reihe liest du in der Nachfolgenden News.

[23. Januar 2024] Drei neue Audiointerfaces, die aber einiges miteinander gemeinsam haben. Heritage Audio i73 Pro One, i73 Pro 2 und i73 Pro Edge werden nämlich alle über USB-C angeschlossen und verfügen über einen eingebauten DSP für eigene Effekt-Plugins. Aber das ist noch nicht alles! Denn wie der Name schon andeutet, stecken hier Class-A Vorverstärker im „73er Stil“ der Heritage Preamps drin.

Mit den großen grünen Buttons aktivierst du den oder die Preamps, um dann Bass, Gitarre, Vocals oder einfach Line-Signale mit bis zu 70 dB Verstärkung durch den Preamp zu schicken. Beim Blick auf die drei Modelle siehst du, dass die kleine Variante Heritage Audio i73 Pro One mit einem Preamp dieses Typs ausgestattet ist, die größeren Modelle verwenden jeweils zwei davon.

Über den Marconi-Regler im typischen Look des Herstellers (angelehnt an Neve) drehst du Input-Gain auf, über die Output-Regler kannst du das Signal nachträglich wieder etwas zähmen. Buttons für das Aktivieren von Phantomspeisung und Pads, dem Umdrehen der Phase und Funktionen wie Mute, Dim und Mono sind ebenfalls an allen drei Heritage Audio i73 Pro Modellen verfügbar. Der große Dual Encoder sorgt für die Steuerung der Monitor- und Kopfhörerlautstärke.

items.articleBody:
A flock of chickens seem to be living an idyllic life in the shadow of a nuclear power plant, because they are birdbrains and have no concept of the possible danger. Then one day something goes wrong, and the farm is showered with radioactive fallout. The effects are the ridiculous extremes we saw in 1950s B-movies, like immediate mutant growth and unexplainable super powers. The chickens are still birdbrains, but they have an idea of how to stop the nuclear plant from further contaminating their environment.

Atomic Chicken is a student film from the French art school Ecole des Nouvelles, specifically the 2023 graduation film for animation students. I like the animated fabric textures, but was a little surprised at one point. "Hey, we can see this chicken's cloaca!" There's a reason for that, since a hen's main talent is laying eggs. That's important to the story, although what they do with that talent is surprising. -via Kuriositas

items.articleBody:
Lange stand beim digitalen Führerschein nur „Ende 2026“ im Kalender. Jetzt wird das Bundesverkehrsministerium konkreter: Noch im November soll die Fahrerlaubnis in die i-Kfz-App einziehen. Wir zeigen euch, was ihr dafür braucht und wo der digitale Nachweis gilt.

Start Ende November, Test läuft bereits

Gegenüber der Frankfurter Allgemeinen Sonntagszeitung nannte das Ministerium Ende November als Zeitraum für den Start. Einen festen Tag gibt es noch nicht. Das Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt testet die Funktion derzeit intern, zum Stand der Tests gibt es keine Angaben. Die rechtliche Grundlage steht bereits. Seit dem 14. Oktober 2026 regelt der neue § 2d im Straßenverkehrsgesetz den digitalen Nachweis der Fahrerlaubnis.

Eine App für Fahrzeugschein und Führerschein

Eine zusätzliche Anwendung braucht ihr nicht. Der Führerschein landet in der i-Kfz-App, die das KBA gemeinsam mit der Bundesdruckerei entwickelt hat. Dort lässt sich schon seit November 2025 der Fahrzeugschein, also die Zulassungsbescheinigung Teil I, digital hinterlegen. Ihr könnt dort mehrere Fahrzeuge verwalten und die Dokumente bei Bedarf weitergeben, etwa an die Werkstatt. Die App kommt gut an: Laut KBA war sie im August auf mehr als zwei Millionen Smartphones installiert.

Diese Voraussetzungen gelten

Zum Start ist der digitale Führerschein für Inhaber eines gültigen deutschen Kartenführerscheins gedacht, der ab dem 1. Januar 1999 ausgestellt wurde. Die Identifizierung läuft über den Personalausweis mit aktivierter Online-Ausweisfunktion. Wer die PIN vergessen hat, kann sie beim Bürgeramt neu setzen lassen. Auf dem iPhone setzt die App iOS 17 voraus, unter Android mindestens Version 12. Wie die Einrichtung des Führerscheins im Detail abläuft, hat das Ministerium noch nicht verraten.

Gültig in Deutschland, EU-Lösung folgt

Bei Kontrollen in Deutschland genügt künftig das Smartphone. Die Plastikkarte bleibt trotzdem gültig, und die Nutzung ist freiwillig. Bei einem Fahrverbot oder einer vorläufigen Entziehung der Fahrerlaubnis greift der digitale Nachweis nicht. Für Fahrten ins Ausland gehört die Karte weiterhin ins Gepäck. Europaweit soll der digitale Führerschein laut der 4. EU-Führerscheinrichtlinie bis spätestens 2030 kommen, über die sogenannte EUDI-Wallet. Die deutsche Wallet „d-you“ soll Anfang Januar 2027 starten und den Führerschein ebenfalls aufnehmen. Auch bei Carsharing und Mietwagen soll der digitale Nachweis künftig helfen. Ob die Anbieter schon zum Start mitziehen, ist noch offen. Die i-Kfz-App ist kostenlos im App Store und bei Google Play erhältlich. Wer den Führerschein direkt zum Start nutzen möchte, sollte schon jetzt prüfen, ob die Online-Ausweisfunktion aktiviert und die PIN griffbereit ist.

items.articleBody:
Map expert Matt Forrest broke down a composite map of players’ guesses from Borderline, a free game by Habibi Code where people redraw US state borders from memory. He found that deceptively simple square states, such as Colorado and North Dakota, were the least accurate, while Illinois and Indiana scored highest.

The best state is Illinois at 96.5 with Indiana right behind it at 94.1. And I think the reason for this is that Illinois is mostly made up of rivers, the Mississippi on one side and the Ohio on the other.

Players hoping to do better might take a cue from former Senator Al Franken, who once drew a map of the US from memory during a radio appearance at the Minnesota State Fair.

items.articleBody:
The future of flight meets space exploration as a futuristic electric aircraft hovers beside Blue Origin's massive New Glenn rocket stage. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd/Future)
A futuristic single-person aircraft takes to the skies at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, with the upper stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket providing a dramatic backdrop.

The unusual scene was captured during the MAX POWER event, which brought together innovators and emerging technologies at the iconic spaceflight facility.

What is it?

The photograph shows a single-person electric aircraft called Jetson ONE, developed by Jetson, a Swedish startup company working to bring personal flight to the skies.

The compact rotorcraft uses multiple propellers to climb into the air, allowing it to take off and vertically without the need for a runway.

The aircraft was performing flight demonstrations during the UP.Summit gathering, which formed part of the larger MAX POWER event at the Kennedy Space Center.

During the demonstrations, the Jetson ONE demonstrated its ability to maneuver through the air and hover in place, giving spectators a close-up look at the technology in action.

Jetson ONE demonstration at MAX POWER. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd/Future)
Why is it amazing?

The photograph offers a fascinating glimpse at two very different approaches to flight.

While Jetson is developing small electric aircraft designed for personal transportation, Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket is built to carry payloads far beyond Earth's atmosphere.

On the edge of the lowlands of Zeeland lies a village dedicated to celebrating the mussel fishing industry. A vital part of life in Bruinisse for centuries, mussel farming has long been one of the main sources of income for the local area. Bruinisse harbour is the heart of the village and is home to a large, active mussel fleet. The mussel season runs from July to April, with mussel cutters setting sail daily from the harbour to collect some of the finest mussels in the Netherlands.

Mussel Boulevard runs along the dyke which protecting the village from rising waters in the estuary. At the end of this boulevard, visible from the main road, stands a large artwork in the shape of an opened mussel shell. The giant mussel symbolises the mussel fishing industry that defines Bruinisse.

Located on the salt water lake Grevelingen, Bruinisse is ideally situated in an area where the tide, channels and shallow water are perfectly suited to the cultivation of mussels and oysters. Cultivation plots are created using mussel seed - very young mussels harvested from the wild – which are then grown in columns. These mussel columns can be seen throughout the estuary, each marked by a floating blue barrel.

The conditions in the estuary allow the mussels to grow naturally and strict regulations ensure the process remains sustainable and does not harm the surrounding environment. Mussel quality can vary greatly depending on the conditions in each cultivation area.

A whole industry has developed around the harbour, not just the fishing fleet but also the wholesalers, shops and the Mussel Guild. Historically, a large number of the population worked in the mussel sector. The Mussel Guild regulate quality and restaurants belonging to the Guild serve the best mussels. Towards the end of the 19th Century, the industry shifted from wild mussel fishing to mussel cultivation.

Each year, the village hosts Fishing Day, a three-day festival held on the third weekend of July, where the whole community honours the fishermen and celebrates mussel culture. This festival marks the official opening of the mussel season.

items.articleBody:
Hello Friends!

I need some help troubleshooting my current DIY project: “Crawler”.

@ParanormalPatroler has already teased it a little in the Pre-release Megathread, but I haven’t said much about it yet.

I wanna clarify two things before I start:

This will be an open source release, for anyone to order their own PCBs and build their own. I don’t intend on manufacturing these in bigger runs. I design&build my stuff for myself in the first place, and then put it out there for the community, in case anyone is interested.

Disclosure of LLM useage (I’m only explaining and summarizing my use, I think I’m not allowed to post any LLM-output, and I don’t intend to anyways. Spoilered for those who don’t wanna see too much of this stuff)

LLM Useage (click for more details)

I’ve just finished building a few units with this first revision of hardware, and I’m pretty happy. Everything is mostly working already, just a few software side things to polish. All core functionality is there, and it’s just as fun and useful as I was hoping for.

However, with it in the rack for the first time now, I found a weird hardware-issue: If you power-cycle the rack, the module doesn’t come back on. It boots fine if the power has been off for some time (>90s reliably, sometimes also with just 10-30s, it’s quite random). I’ve also traced this issue somewhat, and have even found a working fix, but I fail to understand the root of the problem.

This has to do with the I2C bus (connected to Teletype). Without I2C connected, the issue is gone. When using my proprietary TT-Link port (2x5 1.27mm header connecting to the Teletype-Backpack, another work in progress project of mine, it provides SDA/SCL and 5V power via one cable) it’s also working fine.

The problem only appears when I2C and power are connected, and I think it happens because the Teletype’s 3.3V supply (which feeds into the I2C bus through it’s pull-ups) comes up faster than Crawler’s own supply. With just the I2C cable connected, I measure about 0.9V on the Crawler’s MCU 3.3V pin.

I’ve now solved this, by adding two BSS138 MOSFETs on the I2C lines, which only passes signal when the modules 3.3V supply is fully there. This has fixed the issue entirely. Here is the updated schematic (the BSS138s, 2x 10k and the two SMD jumpers with 4.7k pull-ups are new additions):

I’d like some input on two things:

How can I figure out where exactly this problem is coming from, and why the off-period before a successful start varies so much (I’ve seen very few successful starts after 10s, some more after 25-30s, but reliably only after 90s+). I feel like my whole power wiring with the large regulator and all those diodes may also play a role here.

Would you say this dual-MOSFET solution is a “good” approach? From my testing here it works reliably, but I don’t wanna cause new problems in the long run.

I’d love to hear some thoughts of people more experienced with the matter than myself

Cheers,

Finn

items.title: Kristalle zeigen, warum manche Vulkane ausbrechen

items.articleBody:
Nicht jedes Magma, das sich unter einem Vulkan sammelt, erreicht die Erdoberfläche. Winzige Feldspatkristalle aus den Zentralanden zeigen nun eine auffallend einheitliche chemische Signatur in ausgebrochenen Schmelzen. Die Untersuchung deutet darauf hin, dass ein Zustrom heißen Magmas aus der Tiefe Ausbrüche häufig anstößt, während andere Magmamassen im Untergrund zurückbleiben.

St Lucia (Australien). Unter Vulkanen befindet sich kein einheitlicher See aus flüssigem Gestein. Stattdessen sammelt sich Magma in verzweigten Systemen aus Schmelze, Gasen und Kristallen, die verschiedene Tiefen der Erdkruste durchziehen können. Obwohl sich dort große Magmamengen ansammeln, erreicht oft nur ein Teil davon die Oberfläche.

Besonders häufig tritt an Vulkanbögen Andesit aus, ein Gestein mittlerer chemischer Zusammensetzung, das durch die Mischung unterschiedlicher Magmen entsteht. Die chemischen Spuren in Vulkankristallen können die Entwicklung solcher Magmasysteme sichtbar machen. Doch warum bestimmte Schmelzen ausbrechen und andere über lange Zeit in der Erdkruste verbleiben, ist noch nicht vollständig geklärt.

Ein gemeinsames Muster in 28 Proben

Forscher der University of Queensland (UQ) um Daniela Parra-Encalada haben nun Plagioklas untersucht, einen in vulkanischen Gesteinen häufig vorkommenden Feldspat. Dazu analysierte das Team insgesamt 28 Gesteinsproben aus sieben Vulkansystemen der Zentralanden entlang einer rund 230 Kilometer langen Strecke in Chile und Argentinien. Darunter waren auch zwei Proben eines älteren Ignimbrits, einer Ablagerung aus einem besonders großen explosiven Ausbruch.

Die Wissenschaftler unterschieden kleine, erst kurz vor dem Ausbruch entstandene Kristalle von größeren Kristallen, die schon längere Zeit in Magmareservoiren gewachsen waren. Mithilfe von Elektronenmikrosonden und Laseranalysen ermittelten sie die Konzentrationen verschiedener Elemente sowie die Strontium-Isotopenverhältnisse in den Kristallen. So ließen sich die chemischen Spuren unterschiedlicher Phasen der Magmaentwicklung miteinander vergleichen.

Dabei zeigte sich ein auffallend einheitlicher Wert in den jüngsten Kristallen aus den ausgebrochenen Andesit-Schmelzen. Ihr durchschnittlicher Anorthitanteil, ein Maß für den calciumreichen Bestandteil des Plagioklases, lag bei rund 61 Molprozent mit einer Standardabweichung von sieben Prozentpunkten. Dieses Muster trat bei Vulkanen unterschiedlichen Alters und Ausbruchstyps auf.

Heißer Nachschub verändert das Magma

Im Inneren älterer, größerer Kristalle fand sich dagegen meist eine andere chemische Zusammensetzung. Ihre calciumärmeren Bereiche weisen auf die längere Kristallisation in stärker kieselsäurereichen Magmen hin, die unter den Vulkanen gespeichert blieben. Unterschiede in den Spurenelementen und Strontium-Isotopen zeigen zugleich, dass sich die Magmaspeicher über längere Zeit veränderten.

Die calciumreicheren Ränder der großen Kristalle und die jüngsten Kleinkristalle deuten hingegen auf den Zustrom heißeren, magnesiumreicheren Magmas aus tieferen Bereichen hin. Durch diesen Nachschub können ältere Schmelzen erneut erwärmt und vermischt werden, wodurch ein Teil des Magmas aufstiegsfähig wird. Das beobachtete Muster bezeichnet die Studie als Plagioklas-Eruptionsfeld.

Thermodynamische Modellrechnungen ordnen die Bildung der jüngsten Kristalle Temperaturen von etwa 900 bis 975 Grad Celsius und Tiefen von ungefähr elf bis 19 Kilometern zu. Die Werte sind modellierte Bedingungen und keine unmittelbar gemessenen Temperaturen oder Tiefen vor einzelnen Eruptionen. Sie stützen die Deutung, dass heißer Magmanachschub häufig einen entscheidenden Anstoß für Andesit-Ausbrüche gibt.

Große Eruptionen folgen nicht immer demselben Muster

Anders sieht das Bild bei Gesteinen aus, die von früheren besonders voluminösen explosiven Eruptionen stammen. Deren Plagioklase zeigen überwiegend Merkmale einer längeren Kristallisation in vergleichsweise kühlen, kieselsäurereichen Magmen. Die charakteristischen Veränderungen an den Kristallrändern fehlen dort weitgehend, sodass heißer Magmanachschub nicht der wichtigste Auslöser gewesen sein muss.

Ein Abgleich mit Mineralanalysen aus 26 Vulkanbögen weltweit ergab zwar ähnliche chemische Verteilungen wie in den Zentralanden. Ihre Streuung war aber größer, weil in den Vergleichsdaten verschiedene Kristalltypen häufig nicht getrennt erfasst waren. Wie weit sich das Plagioklas-Eruptionsfeld auf andere Vulkanregionen übertragen lässt, muss deshalb noch genauer untersucht werden.

Die Ergebnisse machen deutlich, dass ausgestoßene Lava nicht den gesamten Magmavorrat eines Vulkans widerspiegelt. Ein großer Teil kann als kristallreicher Magmabrei im Untergrund verbleiben und später zu festem Tiefengestein erstarren. Die Kristallsignatur hilft zunächst, vergangene Eruptionsprozesse zu rekonstruieren, erlaubt aber noch keine Vorhersage des Zeitpunkts eines künftigen Ausbruchs.

Quellen:

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin Nature Communications, doi: 10.1038/s41467-026-78932-9

items.articleBody:
The Department of Justice’s birthday was not in 1776, when America first declared independence as a nation, or 1788, when the U.S. Constitution was ratified. It was in 1870, when the law creating the department was signed. The Department of Justice is not a creature of the U.S. Constitution; it is a creature of Congress.

Before America had a Department of Justice, the attorney general was a sort of general counsel for the president and his administration. After the Civil War, it was Congress that gave the attorney general a whole new department of government, the U.S. Justice Department, so he would have the means and the manpower to serve a broader clientele, and a broader remit.

The Reconstruction Amendments, ratified in the years before the department was established, abolished slavery, gave Black men the right to vote, and prohibited any state from denying equal protection of the laws to all Americans. Properly conceived, the new Justice Department was to make sure that the promise of the newly amended Constitution extended to real life: “One of the most powerful peace-time forces known to our country,” as Attorney General Robert Jackson memorably put it in a speech. “This authority has been granted by people who really wanted the right thing done,” and who “wanted the best in our American traditions preserved.”

And indeed, when the Justice Department has inserted itself between citizens denied their equal rights and the forces denying those rights, it has been a potent use of the U.S. government. Equally, though, when the Justice Department has inserted itself on the side of those denying others their rights, it has been a force multiplier for powerful interests. Short of the U.S. military, there is no greater coercive power that is brought to bear by the government against its citizens.

[Quinta Jurecic: DOJ’s try-anything approach]

How DOJ has used its power has been the great shaper of America’s character as a nation. It determined the shape of the peace following the Civil War, and the shape of the economic system as the country industrialized. It shaped the perimeter of acceptable political expression and association as Americans settled, uneasily, into a competitive two-party democratic system, and it shaped how first- and second-tier citizenship were allocated so strictly by race.

With DOJ on the case, wholly and without reservation, almost anything is possible. Without it, almost nothing is. When the Department of Justice neglects its unique responsibility and unique capacity to ensure that Americans are equally protected by the law, no substitute force can make up the difference.

Over the course of its century and a half of existence, the Justice Department has been noble; it has been feckless; it has been corrupt. But now, in the midst of a full-fledged authoritarian challenge to the constitutional republic, the Justice Department has entered a whole new phase it has not been through before. It’s a phase you might call “gone”: missing, presumed dead.

In Donald Trump’s second term, the federal agents shooting protesters, tear-gassing nonviolent crowds and whole neighborhoods, breaking down doors without judicial warrants, grabbing people in courthouse hallways, and even menacing election officials are, for the most part, agents of the sprawling Department of Homeland Security, not the Department of Justice. Homeland Security’s various three- and four-letter agencies have essentially dissolved into an amorphous, masked, pro-Trump secret police force with as little connection to the Article III legal system as they can get away with. DOJ, meanwhile, is now mostly irrelevant. Broken as it is, Trump’s threats that he would use the department to destroy his enemies have been (mostly) just menacing hot air.

Staffed by C-list podcasters, QAnon-adjacent influencers, weirdo cable-news gadflies, and the kinds of friendless indoor boys who try to choose their own nicknames (see Trump’s first acting U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, a man no one ever called “Eagle Ed”), the Justice Department has at last been emptied out and deconsecrated. Trump’s efforts to prosecute people for political advantage have largely failed. Trump has been able to use DOJ to harass his opponents, and to cost them money in legal fees, but—with a few notable exceptions—not to convict them. Judges, and even grand juries, have laughed the Trump-era DOJ’s amateur legal filings out of courts of every level.

For his first attorney general in his second term, Trump installed Pam Bondi, a former Florida official with whom he had history—he had sent a political committee supporting her campaign a $25,000 check before she punted a fraud investigation into his fake Trump University. Under Bondi, senior career DOJ lawyers with decades of experience in national security, immigration, espionage, antitrust, and other complex areas of law were fired wholesale or busted down to entry-level jobs to demoralize them.

[Read: Inside the plan to send 1,000 DOJ monitors to the polls]

This article has been adapted from Rachel Maddow’s new book, Department of Fate: The Promise, the Power, and the Collapse of America’s Most Consequential Institution.

Those who chose to remain soon found that they were required to make a show of their willingness to submit. Assistant U.S. attorneys were told not just to drop a corruption prosecution against one of the president’s allies, but to submit a written admission of wrongdoing for having brought the (well-predicated) case in the first place. The U.S. pardon attorney was ordered to give her blessing for restoring the gun rights of a right-wing actor—a supporter of the president—who had been convicted of a domestic-violence offense. The president’s pardon and commutation powers are absolute under the Constitution; there is no need for a pardon attorney to paper a decision like that, in either direction—that is, unless it’s important to make clear to everyone, including the pardon attorney, that she’s on board with the new regime. Trump and his enforcers have not just torn down the department; they have salted the earth to be sure there will be no uncorrupted survivors.

Even as he has failed to do much of consequence with his warped DOJ, Trump has used the pardon power enthusiastically, and for the most corrupt possible purposes. Despite the existence of a pardon attorney at DOJ to advise the White House, the pardon power is not technically a use of the Justice Department; it’s more a means of negating the department’s past work. And the negation of the Justice Department overall appears to be the larger political project that Trump, and the Trumpist movement, have set as their course.

If the Justice Department, for all of its flaws and failures, is the means by which Americans effectuate the protections of the U.S. Constitution, then a revolutionary effort to end those constitutional protections must also end the Justice Department, or at least render it comically inept. But that doesn’t make it inert. The DOJ is dangerous now in the way a defective firework or a broken gun is. It can still kill, just not in the manner or at the time you might intend.

The great political freedoms enshrined in America’s founding documents—the freedom of speech, the freedom of assembly, the right to petition the government for redress of grievances, the right to vote—perhaps inevitably lead to the rise of political movements seeking to end those freedoms for others. But here, too, the Justice Department retains a singular purpose: With its unmatched power and unique remit, it can ensure either that the Constitution protects all Americans or that some are excluded from this protection.

Against a determined enemy, DOJ can wield hard power, as its first attorney general, Amos T. Akerman, was unafraid to do against the Ku Klux Klan and its protectors, and as Assistant Attorney General John Doar carefully but forcefully ensured in the 1960s during the civil-rights movement. Against a determined enemy, DOJ can also fail. It can fail, as the robber-baron-era attorney general, Richard Olney, did in the 1890s, to find the right side at all. Or it can simply fail to deliver, as it did in its aborted efforts to prosecute American fascists before World War II, or as the interregnum Justice Department did between Trump’s two terms, bringing low-level prosecutions of the January 6 rioters (which were all overturned by pardon on his first day back in office) and failing to proceed to federal trial at all for the ringleader himself.

[Read: DOJ’s collapsing probe into a supposed anti-Trump conspiracy ]

The special counsel assigned to investigate Trump’s role in the insurrection plot, Jack Smith, spoke in April about the concerted attack against DOJ and its career personnel in Trump’s second term. “To erode the rule of law in our country, you need to attack these people, and that is what we have seen since January of 2025,” Smith said. “And let me be clear: This attack on public servants—it’s not a byproduct of the attack on the rule of law. It is a central component of it.” In so many words, if what you’re planning is a crime spree, it’s not an irrational strategy to try first to disable the cops.

Many career Justice Department personnel—fired and forced out by the thousands in Trump’s second term—have found new careers, and new patriotic purpose, in helping defend the protesters, political opponents, and immigrants against whom Trump has sicced their former department. It says something important about DOJ’s promise and prospects for reinvention that so many of its attorneys who were ousted when Trump set fire to the department nevertheless found ways to remain at the job of ensuring that justice will be done.

Trump’s return to office offers nothing so much as clarity. He seeks, bluntly and inarguably, to rule indefinitely and by fiat, and to end all barriers to him doing so. The Constitution, of course, aims to protect citizens from rule by fiat, and more broadly from the whims of a tyrant. The Justice Department is how the country makes those protections real. In the fight of despotism versus democracy, small-d democrats must wage an asymmetrical war, using democratic means to fight off their opponents, while authoritarians don’t have to be so picky. In America, however, would-be tyrants also know that when they commit crimes, they may be pursued by the component of government that is responsible for policing and prosecuting violations of the Constitution. It should not surprise us that the first shots fired in this authoritarian revolution were intended not merely to degrade or corrupt the U.S. Justice Department, but to end it.

For that reason, when Trump’s reign ends, the first order of business in the country will be to found a new Department of Justice. And properly this time. For good.

This article has been adapted from Rachel Maddow’s new book, Department of Fate: The Promise, the Power, and the Collapse of America’s Most Consequential Institution.

items.articleBody:
David Lyons, emeritus professor of philosophy and law at Boston University, has died.

The following memorial notice is by Aaron Garret (Boston University).

David Lyons

David Lyons passed away at his home on October 24th at the age of 91. He had an extremely distinguished philosophical and legal academic career.

David was John Rawls’ first doctoral student and his thesis became the groundbreaking book Forms and Limits of Utilitarianism. After a year at Oxford under the supervision of H. L. A. Hart, he taught at Cornell for over thirty years in the philosophy department (from 1964) and for over fifteen years as a professor of law (from 1979). Upon retiring from Cornell, he joined the Boston University law faculty in 1995 and later joined the Philosophy department. David retired from full-time teaching at Boston University in 2015 but continued teaching as an adjunct until Spring 2022, organizing and unionizing adjunct and part-time faculty, and helping to negotiate collective bargaining agreements.

Throughout his long and extremely fruitful academic life David’s political and moral commitments were at least as central to him as his philosophical work—in fact his political commitments preceded his academic ones.

Among the many philosophical and legal topics he made major contributions to were the study of  Bentham, Mill and the utilitarian tradition, the understanding of rights, the rule of law, legal formalism and legal theory, reparations, and the history and law connected with the creation and maintenance of the color line in the U.S. He is survived by Sandra Lyons, his wife and partner of 70 years, his three children Matthew, Emily, and Jeremy, his grandchildren, and the many friends, students, and colleagues who loved and admired him.

You can learn more about David Lyons’ writings here.

The post David Lyons (1935-2026) appeared first on Daily Nous.

items.articleBody:
Wer Wert auf die Aufzeichnung von Gesundheits- und Fitnessdaten legt, hat mit einer klassischen Armbanduhr schlechte Karten. Mit dem Azume One soll sich das ändern. Der kompakte Sensor wird auf der Rückseite einer vorhandenen Armbanduhr befestigt und soll diese um zahlreiche Gesundheitsfunktionen ergänzen.

Azume One klebt magnetisch auf der Rückseite der Uhr

Die kleine Scheibe misst 30 Millimeter im Durchmesser, ist 2,8 Millimeter dick und wiegt fünf Gramm. Damit soll sie sich unauffällig zwischen dem Gehäuseboden der Uhr und dem Handgelenk tragen lassen. Ein eigenes Display oder Bedienelemente sind nicht vorhanden. Die Daten werden direkt an das Smartphone übertragen. Die Akkulaufzeit wird mit bis zu 48 Stunden angegeben.

Befestigung ohne Klebstoff oder Magnete

Für die Befestigung verwendet Azume eine Technik namens Nano-Suction. Der Sensor soll ohne Klebstoff oder Magnete an der Unterseite einer Armbanduhr haften und sich rückstandsfrei entfernen und an einer anderen Uhr befestigen lassen. Nach Angaben des Herstellers soll dies mit nahezu allen herkömmlichen Armbanduhren funktionieren.

Alternativ kann der Azume One mit einem speziellen Textilarmband getragen werden. Dieses sogenannte FitBand gehört zum Lieferumfang und ist insbesondere für die Nutzung beim Sport oder während des Schlafens gedacht.

Gesundheitsdaten ohne zusätzliches Display

Der Azume One soll unter anderem die Herzfrequenz, die Herzfrequenzvariabilität und die Sauerstoffsättigung des Blutes erfassen. Hinzu kommen Informationen zu Bewegung, Kalorienverbrauch und sportlichen Aktivitäten. Auch die Schlafdauer und verschiedene Schlafphasen sollen erfasst werden

Unterschiedliche Tracking-Funktionen

Die gesammelten Daten werden per Bluetooth an eine zugehörige App übertragen. Dort sollen Nutzer unter anderem Auswertungen zu ihrer täglichen Belastung, ihrem Schlaf und ihrer körperlichen Erholung abrufen können. Die Anwendung soll zudem persönliche Vergleichswerte ermitteln und dafür die Daten der ersten beiden Nutzungswochen auswerten.

Vorbestellung für 119 Euro möglich

Der Azume One kann derzeit zum Einführungspreis von 119 Euro vorbestellt werden. Der reguläre Verkaufspreis wird mit 149 Euro angegeben. Die Auslieferung soll noch in diesem Jahr beginnen. Ein kostenpflichtiges Abonnement ist laut Anbieter nicht erforderlich.

★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★

Der Beitrag Azume One macht klassische Armbanduhren zum Fitness-Tracker Wurde zuerst auf iphone-ticker.de veröffentlicht.

items.articleBody:
On 4 November 2026, ten days after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth presidential term, the Brazilian COP30 Presidency published two roadmaps: one on transitioning away from fossil fuels and one on halting and reversing deforestation by 2030. Brazil had promised them at the close of COP30 in Belém, after efforts to include a reference to a fossil fuel roadmap in the negotiated outcome failed. Both documents are voluntary and sit outside the formal UN process. Yet they also set a benchmark against which Brazil’s own record can be read.

These two roadmaps correspond to two very different domestic stories with legal angles that we highlight here. On forests, Brazil can point to a sharp fall in deforestation, sustained in part by litigation before the Supreme Federal Court (STF) that kept enforcement policies alive and supervised their implementation. On fossil fuels, there is no equivalent record, and courts are poorly placed to produce one: the choice to keep expanding oil production rests with the executive. Lula’s new mandate is therefore an opportunity to preserve what has worked on forests and to bring Brazil’s domestic energy policy closer to its international climate diplomacy.

Two Roadmaps and a Domestic Test

The fossil fuel roadmap creates no new commitments and is not a negotiated outcome. Its core is the “Belém Readiness Approach”, which asks how exposed each country is to the transition and how much capacity it has to manage it, across three pillars: energy demand, energy supply and the wider economy. Countries are grouped into archetypes, each with suggested levers and sequencing. On supply, the document warns that expanding fossil fuel production as demand declines deepens lock-in and stranded-asset risks, but also that premature supply cuts can cause price shocks that fall hardest on vulnerable households. It invites governments to carry out a readiness self-assessment “as soon as possible”.

The roadmap arrives at a time of visible retreat. A new study by the TPI Global Climate Transition Centre at LSE finds that only five of 71 assessed countries still have an active pledge to phase out fossil fuel subsidies, and that just seven of 75 countries with a quantified 2030 target are on an emissions trend consistent with 1.5°C.

The forest roadmap identifies five complementary areas of action, from conservation to restoration, and asks countries to diagnose the drivers of forest loss, align policies and finance, set targets, deliver, and then evaluate and adjust. It names finance as one of the largest gaps: annual forest finance would need to rise from US$84.5 billion in 2023 to more than US$300 billion by 2030. It draws on Brazil’s own experience, citing estimates that the policies introduced under the Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Deforestation in the Legal Amazon (PPCDAm) avoided around 73,000 km² of deforestation between 2005 and 2009, and that satellite monitoring combined with targeted enforcement prevented the clearing of more than 59,500 km² between 2007 and 2011.

The two roadmaps also contrast in their level of specificity, revealing different degrees of domestic credibility. On forests, the roadmap builds on policies and institutions that already exist and whose implementation courts have helped to sustain. On fossil fuels, it asks governments to consider a transition that Brazil itself has yet to translate into a clear domestic policy.

Forests and the Courts

That record has not been linear. According to Brazil’s official monitoring system (PRODES/INPE), Amazon deforestation reached 13,038 km² in 2021, the highest figure since 2006. During President Jair Bolsonaro’s government (2019-2022), the Amazon lost 45,586 km² of forest, 55% more than in the previous four years. From 2023, with the start of President Lula’s third administration, deforestation fell year on year, and in 2026 it reached its lowest level in 41 years. The 2026 Presidential election made the stakes explicit. Flávio Bolsonaro’s programme promised that the environment would no longer be “an obstacle to development”, while Lula’s programme committed to “zero net deforestation”.

A change of government explains much of this turnaround, but not all of it. A less visible factor is litigation. During the Bolsonaro years, political parties and civil society organisations brought a series of constitutional actions before the STF challenging the dismantling of environmental policy. Seven of them were listed for joint judgment in 2022 as the so-called Green Package. The most relevant here, ADPF 760, challenged the federal government’s abandonment of the PPCDAm – the same policy that the forest roadmap now presents as a model. When the judgment began in 2022, the rapporteur, Justice Cármen Lúcia, described the government’s approach as a “termite-like” destruction of environmental governance. The Court concluded the case only in 2024. It acknowledged the progress made under the new government but still required substantial commitments from it. Later implementation decisions required a plan to rebuild the workforce of environmental and Indigenous affairs agencies, authorised extraordinary budget appropriations and barred spending freezes on environmental budget lines.

While litigation alone did not produce the observed decline in deforestation, it helped preserve the legal and institutional infrastructure through which a more committed executive could act, and it made the rebuilding of that infrastructure subject to continuing judicial oversight.

Forests: Closing the Implementation Gap

ADPF 743, on fires in the Pantanal and the Amazon, shows why the design of implementation matters. After the 2024 judgment, the Court issued 55 implementation orders, bringing the federal government and the states of both regions together in joint action against forest fires. Two specialised STF units support this work, one assessing compliance in structural cases (NUPEC) and one facilitating consensual solutions (NUSOL). In public, televised hearings, the parties and amici curiae work through outstanding issues with Justice Flávio Dino, who oversees implementation, from the integration of land registry databases to an inter-federative plan for fire prevention and response.

The fossil fuel roadmap could contribute to this picture of more effective implementation. It distinguishes a policy gap, where a measure has yet to be adopted, from an implementation gap, where a measure exists but fails to deliver because capacity, financing, enforcement or coordination fall short. Structural litigation in Brazil has worked mainly on the second. The STF did not design deforestation policy; it required the government to apply the policies it had and monitored whether it did so.

The STF’s expansive role in Brazilian politics and continuous judicial supervision of public policy may raise questions about the separation of powers and institutional capacity. But the Court has relied largely on dialogue and coordination, giving effect to the duty to protect the environment that Article 225 of the Constitution imposes on public authorities. By recognising rights and monitoring compliance, it can support government action as much as constrain it.

However, the implementation of climate policies and decisions will remain challenging. More than half of the newly elected members of Congress have previously acted against Indigenous rights or Amazon conservation, and governors aligned with Bolsonaro will lead seven of the nine Amazonian states. Courts can contain some setbacks, and structural cases offer a forum for coordinating federal and state action, but neither substitutes for political commitment and engagement.

Fossil Fuel: Confronting the Policy Gap

On fossil fuels, Brazil’s record is perhaps even more complex. Lula’s government has combined lower deforestation with support for oil expansion and exploration. Shortly before the roadmaps were published, the state-controlled company Petrobras announced its third oil discovery in Block FZA-M-59, offshore near the mouth of the Amazon. If Brazil applied the Belém Readiness Approach to itself, as the Presidency invites all countries to do, it would find that the roadmap points large producers with substantial transition capacity towards diversifying their supply mix and redirecting infrastructure and industrial capabilities – priorities that sit uneasily with opening new oil frontiers. Brazil’s own NDC, which commits to cutting net emissions by 59–67% by 2035 relative to 2005, and its Climate Plan 2024–2035 set the domestic benchmark.

This is where the limits of litigation become clear. Courts can protect institutions, budgets and procedures, and they can hold governments to the commitments they have made. They can review licensing, environmental impact assessments, and consistency with climate targets, but they cannot design a country’s energy pathway. International law adds pressure: the International Court of Justice has observed that fossil fuel production, the granting of exploration licences and fossil fuel subsidies may constitute internationally wrongful acts, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires heightened due diligence in the face of the climate emergency. Translating these standards into decisions about particular licences can be a legal task, but deciding whether and how Brazil should open new oil frontiers remains, first and foremost, a political choice.

The roadmaps’ own advice is to “start now, from where you are”. On forests, Brazil starts from a stronger position, with rebuilt institutions, courts that supervise implementation and new finance initiatives such as the Tropical Forests Forever Facility, to which the Netherlands pledged a further US$500 million after the election. On fossil fuels, it starts from a government that is still expanding production. Lula’s fourth term offers a renewed opportunity to continue the first trajectory and to change the second, beginning with the readiness assessment that Brazil is now asking other countries to undertake.

The election also gave that task a renewed democratic mandate.  An army of 11 million citizens mobilized in an extremely close contest, in which environmental protection was explicitly at stake. Many, including older voters and Indigenous communities, are among those most exposed to environmental degradation and climate change. Responding to them requires Brazil not only to lead through international proposals, but also to confront the contradictions in its own development model.

items.articleBody:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made

—By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm

This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action.

But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story.

Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests

Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction.

The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree.

For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide.

Learn more about Dent, her work, and her impact on how we understand the role rainforests play in regulating our climate.

—Matthew Ponsford

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia is investigating its own boss
Jensen Huang has admitted to intimacy with a suspected Chinese spy. (NYT $)
+ Shares in Nvidia were down 5% in pre-market trading. (CNBC)
+ Huang’s children are also employed by Nvidia. (WSJ $)

2 Democrats are planning a blitz of investigations into Big Tech
Reportedly starting with Apple, Meta, and Musk’s companies. (WP $)
+ They’re hoping to harness the data center backlash to rein in the AI sector. (Vox $)
+ Here’s why the midterms sparked an AI stock selloff. (BBC)

3 The UN annual climate meeting starts today
It’s the first to be held after confirmation the planet will exceed 1.5 °C warming. (Nature)
+ How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Connecting fridges to the internet looks like a bad move now
We still don’t know who is behind recent hacks, or even if they’re connected. (The Atlantic $)
+ Experts say they should be a “wake up call” for the industry. (NPR)
+ Are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic? (The Guardian)
+ AI is already making online crimes easier. It could get much worse. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Tesla is axing the Cybertruck
RIP, we hardly knew ye. (Wired $)
+ The Cybertruck was on our “worst tech flops of 2025” list. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Iran might attack subsea cables if the US escalates again
That’s the message it’s sending via several loitering tankers. (FT $)

7 Chinese AI labs are struggling to poach Silicon Valley workers
Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot have an uphill battle as they try to fill new US offices. (Rest of World)
+ China’s AI models have Trump’s AI world at war with itself. (MIT Technology Review)

8 Online piracy is back
But this time, archivist zeal is at least as big a draw as accessing content for free. (The Verge)
+ Inside the race to save our online lives from a digital dark age. (MIT Technology Review)

9 How do you land on a moon with almost no gravity?
It’s a huge challenge to land on Martian moon Phobos—here’s how Japan’s going to attempt it. (IEEE Spectrum)

10 Meet Philadelphia’s delivery robot saboteur
Carolyn Marvin is going to court for blocking them, and it’s turning her into a local hero. (The Guardian)

Quote of the day

“Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.”

—Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia employees for his affair with a suspected Chinese spy in a mass email sent yesterday, the Washington Post reports.

One more thing

STUART BRADFORD

AI is coming for music, too

AI models are marching into a creative field that is uniquely vulnerable to disruption: music.

AI-generated creative works—from orchestra performances to heavy metal—are poised to suffuse our lives more thoroughly than any other product of AI has done yet.

The songs are likely to blend into our streaming platforms, party and wedding playlists, soundtracks, and more, whether or not we notice who (or what) made them.

Here’s why AI is set to forever change how we make music.

—James O’Donnell

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ French bardcore band Corseval has given ABBA a medieval makeover.
+ A stunning collection of prehistoric engravings has been found in a Spanish cave.
+ This browser game flips a retro classic on its head: you control the asteroids, not the spaceship.
+ From a caiman in a wig to a leopard doing a handstand, the Comedy Wildlife Awards shortlist is a delight.

items.articleBody:
It’s one of the peculiarities of American regulatory history that a natural gas pipeline can cross state lines with a single federal permit, but oil and electricity must run a gauntlet of state approvals. When a power line crosses one state to reach another, for example, the intervening state often imposes exorbitant tolls or, worse, vetoes the project entirely. It’s the holdout problem played out among the states.

In a new paper, Liscow, Shapiro and Williams show that after Congress ended the states’ veto over interstate gas pipelines in 1947, miles built per year rose nearly sixfold. Oil pipelines, which still had to run the state gauntlet, held steady. Lower transaction costs let natural gas flow to where it was most valued, creating a national market.

Today, as Liscow and Shapiro write in the Washington Post, the issue is electricity:

An interstate power line, however, typically needs approval from every state it crosses. That gives each state a veto over projects in which the benefits often flow mostly to its neighbors.

New England has experienced the consequences. In 2016, Massachusetts attempted to import Canadian hydropower. New Hampshire, which would have hosted the power lines without getting the same influx of cheap energy, rejected it. A second route through Maine was blocked in a referendum and didn’t deliver power until January. Meanwhile, Massachusetts households paid some of the highest electricity prices in the country.

As with natural gas, electricity is cheapest to produce far from where it is most valued, so to get the most from our national resources we need to transmit electricity across the country.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which faces a Senate cloture vote on Monday, would let FERC approve an interstate line that a state has blocked or stalled for a year, a big step toward a national market in electricity.

Let the power flow!

items.articleBody:
U2 kehren 2027 mit einer großen Welttournee auf die Stadionbühnen zurück. Doch der Ticketvorverkauf sorgt bei vielen Fans für Frust. Karten für mehrere Hundert Euro und umstrittene Platin-Tickets bei Ticketmaster werfen erneut Fragen zum Dynamic Pricing auf. Auch Frontmann Bono gerät wegen seiner Haltung zu hohen Konzertpreisen in die Kritik.

Remy, CC BY

U2-Tickets 2027: Mehr als 500 Euro für einen Konzertbesuch

Mit ihrer „The Greatest Show On Earth World Tour“ kehren U2 2027 auf die großen Stadionbühnen zurück und machen dabei auch in Deutschland Halt. Am 30. Juni und 1. Juli wird die irische Rockband zwei Konzerte im Berliner Olympiastadion spielen. Musikalisch begleitet wird das Comeback vom neuen Album „Carnaval De Luz“, das bereits am 13. November 2026 erscheint.

Die Vorfreude auf die Rückkehr von Bono und seinen Bandkollegen ist groß. Doch beim offiziellen Vorverkaufsstart am 6. November folgte für viele Fans die Ernüchterung. Während günstigere Tickets schnell vergriffen waren, wurden bei Ticketmaster deutlich teurere Karten angeboten. Die regulären Ticketpreise für Berlin beginnen bei 93,75 Euro für Sitzplätze. In der höchsten regulären Sitzplatzkategorie werden 266,25 Euro fällig. Ein Stehplatz kostet rund 191,50 Euro. Wie der ROLLING STONE berichtete, waren kurz nach Verkaufsbeginn allerdings auch sogenannte Platin-Tickets für bis zu 526,25 Euro erhältlich.

Besonders bitter: Bei diesen hochpreisigen Karten handelt es sich um gewöhnliche Konzerttickets. Zusätzliche VIP-Leistungen sind darin nicht enthalten. Wer mehr bezahlt, erhält also keineswegs automatisch ein besonderes Erlebnis.

Dynamic Pricing bei Ticketmaster: Warum sind U2-Tickets so teuer?

Im Mittelpunkt der Kritik steht das sogenannte Dynamic Pricing. Bei diesem Preismodell orientieren sich die Kosten an Angebot und Nachfrage. Stark gefragte Tickets können dadurch deutlich teurer ausfallen. Ticketmaster bietet mit seinen Platin-Tickets entsprechende nachfrageorientierte Angebote an. Laut Unternehmen werden die Preise von den Veranstaltern beziehungsweise den jeweiligen Künstlerteams festgelegt. Die Karten sollen zu ihrem Marktwert verkauft werden.

Allerdings bestreitet Ticketmaster, dass ein Algorithmus die Preise während des Verkaufs automatisch in Echtzeit erhöht. Unterschiedliche Beträge können laut Anbieter auch dadurch entstehen, dass günstigere Kategorien bereits ausverkauft sind. Ob bei U2 tatsächlich einzelne Ticketpreise während des Vorverkaufs automatisch angehoben wurden, ist bislang nicht unabhängig belegt.

Für viele Fans bleibt die Preisgestaltung dennoch ein Ärgernis. Wer nach langer Wartezeit endlich zum Ticketkauf gelangt, muss unter Umständen deutlich mehr bezahlen als ursprünglich geplant. Dass die Kritik über Deutschland hinausgeht, zeigt sich auch in London: Dort berichteten Konzertbesucher von Stehplatzkarten für mehr als 400 Pfund. Der Besuch eines U2-Konzerts wird damit zunehmend zu einer Frage des Budgets.

Bono verteidigt hohe Ticketpreise und weckt Erinnerungen an Oasis

Für zusätzlichen Gesprächsstoff sorgte U2-Frontmann Bono mit seinen Aussagen im Podcast „The Interview“ der „New York Times“. Wie das Wirtschaftsmagazin Fortune berichtete, hat der Sänger grundsätzlich nichts dagegen, wenn wohlhabende Fans für ein Konzertticket tief in die Tasche greifen. Gleichzeitig wolle die Band dafür sorgen, dass auch begehrte Plätze zu bezahlbaren Preisen erhältlich bleiben. Wie viel Einfluss U2 selbst auf die Ticketpreise haben, scheint allerdings eine andere Frage zu sein. Laut Bono habe die Band bei der Preisgestaltung nur wenig mitzureden.

Ganz neu ist der Ärger um teure Konzerttickets allerdings nicht. Schon beim Vorverkauf für die Oasis-Reunion 2024 gab es heftige Kritik, nachdem Fans über hohe Preise und mangelnde Transparenz beim Ticketkauf geklagt hatten. Die britische Wettbewerbsbehörde Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) nahm den Verkauf daraufhin genauer unter die Lupe. Dabei zeigte sich, dass die verschiedenen Preisstufen für Stehplätze nicht ausreichend klar kommuniziert worden waren. Belege dafür, dass ein Algorithmus die Ticketpreise automatisch in die Höhe getrieben hatte, fand die Behörde jedoch nicht.

Im September 2025 verpflichtete sich Ticketmaster schließlich zu Änderungen, um Käufer künftig früher und verständlicher über die verfügbaren Preiskategorien zu informieren. Dass die Kritik nun auch die U2-Tour 2027 begleitet, zeigt jedoch, wie umstritten die Preisgestaltung bei großen Konzertveranstaltungen weiterhin ist. Besonders die erheblichen Preisunterschiede zwischen vergleichbaren Plätzen sorgen bei vielen Fans für Unverständnis.

U2 Tour 2027: Wird die große Show zum Luxus für Fans?

Die Ticketpreise der U2-Tour 2027 stehen beispielhaft für eine Entwicklung, die die Live-Musikbranche seit Jahren beschäftigt. Große Stadionkonzerte werden zunehmend teurer und stellen viele Fans vor finanzielle Herausforderungen. Wer zwei Karten für jeweils 500 Euro kauft, gibt bereits 1.000 Euro aus, ohne mögliche Kosten für Anreise oder Übernachtung einzurechnen. Für Menschen mit durchschnittlichem Einkommen kann der Besuch ihrer Lieblingsband damit schnell zur finanziellen Belastung werden.

Die Ticketbranche rechtfertigt nachfrageorientierte Preise häufig mit dem Argument, den Schwarzmarkt eindämmen zu wollen. Statt professionellen Wiederverkäufern sollen die höheren Einnahmen den offiziellen Veranstaltern zugutekommen. Für Fans, die sich die Karten ohnehin kaum leisten können, dürfte diese Unterscheidung allerdings wenig ändern.

Dabei zählt die Rückkehr von U2 zweifellos zu den mit Spannung erwarteten Live-Ereignissen des kommenden Jahres. Mit ihren aufwendigen Stadionproduktionen hat die Band in der Vergangenheit immer wieder Maßstäbe gesetzt. Auch die „The Greatest Show On Earth World Tour“ verspricht ein spektakuläres Konzerterlebnis, doch der Ärger über die Ticketpreise überschattet bereits jetzt die Vorfreude. Ob die große Show ihren hohen Preis am Ende wert ist, werden die Besucher selbst beurteilen müssen. Fest steht jedoch, dass sich längst nicht alle langjährigen Anhänger einen Konzertbesuch leisten können. Und so bleibt die Frage, für wen die größte Show der Welt eigentlich noch bezahlbar ist.

items.articleBody:
Two of the top lawmakers backing the Pentagon's Golden Dome missile defense shield are among the wave of Republicans leaving Congress in the coming Democratic takeover, raising questions about the future of President Donald Trump's signature second-term defense initiative.

The shakeup on Capitol Hill comes after military officials signaled in recent months that they might backpedal from one element Trump asked for in Golden Dome: the capability to shoot down missiles in their initial boost phase shortly after launch.

The Golden Dome has escaped serious congressional scrutiny since Trump announced the program in January 2025, one week into his second term in the White House. That lack of scrutiny will change as Democrats take responsibility for writing the Pentagon's budget, introduce limits on funding, and put forth bills to strip out Golden Dome's most controversial component and give the program a new name.

items.articleBody:
philippe jarrigeon finds a surreal world in nature

French photographer Philippe Jarrigeon looks to the contorted beech trees of Champagne for Le Vrai du Faux, his series presented at Paris Photo 2026, where he is also the recipient of the eighth Prix Maison Ruinart.

The project follows Rocher Fatal, his second book published by RVB Books, which brings together two years of photographs made in the Forest of Fontainebleau. Moving from the woodland landscapes of Fontainebleau to the Champagne region, Jarrigeon finds inspiration in unusual natural forms, including the contorted beech trees known as the Faux de Verzy. Their twisting branches seem almost impossible to have occurred naturally, making them fitting subjects for his playful approach to photography.

Jarrigeon takes this strangeness as a starting point, bringing the trees into conversation with shells, flowers, animals, and objects. His photographs play with the idea of what nature can be, and with the curious possibility that the world might contain forms of life and ways of being that sit outside our usual understanding.

all photography by Philippe Jarrigeon

a photographic language between fashion and fantasy

Jarrigeon’s approach to photography has developed over nearly two decades, moving between editorial commissions, commercial work, and personal projects. After graduating from ECAL (École cantonale d’art de Lausanne) in 2006, he began building a practice shaped by the visual languages of fashion, design, advertising, and popular culture.

His photographs often borrow from the polished aesthetics of fashion campaigns and the saturated imagery of 1980s and 1990s popular culture. Vivid colors and elaborate compositions give his images an immediately recognizable visual character. Yet Jarrigeon rarely uses these references straightforwardly. Humor, irony, and unexpected details introduce a sense of play and disrupt the apparent perfection of the scenes.

Le Vrai du Faux, Prix Maison Ruinart 2026

entering the forest with ‘Rocher Fatal’

In Rocher Fatal, Philippe Jarrigeon spends two years photographing the Forest of Fontainebleau, approaching it as a setting for a series of curious episodes. Published by RVB Books with a text by Laura Vazquez, his second book brings together abandoned castles, dormant quarries, hikers, deer, and a fallen knight. A smiling flower and a seemingly ordinary rock also find their way into the story, alongside appearances by artists Nina Childress, Théo Mercier, Vimala Pons, Laura Vazquez, and Rebeka Warrior.

The photographs have a cinematic quality, but Jarrigeon’s sense of humor keeps the scenes from becoming too serious. The forest is at once recognizable and strangely theatrical, with its trees and inhabitants becoming part of the same narrative. In the years following the photographs, fires damaged parts of the Fontainebleau forest, affecting its trees, habitats, and well-used paths. The book also recalls a landscape that has since undergone significant damage.

the photographs in Rocher Fatal have a cinematic quality

imagining other forms of life

In Le Vrai du Faux, Jarrigeon continues this exploration in the Champagne region, where geological history and living forms become material for an imaginative photographic project. The Faux de Verzy, with their unusually twisted trunks and branches, are among its central subjects. Their shapes give the trees a supernatural presence, and Jarrigeon photographs them as though they were characters.

Other images introduce shells, remnants of a sea that once covered the region, alongside bouquets, luminous forms, and ambiguous figures. In The Harvest, Poppy, and The Surprise, familiar natural elements take on an unfamiliar character through composition and staging. The presence of animals and human figures complicates the distinction between observer and subject, while objects appear to belong as naturally to the landscape as the plants and creatures around them.

Jarrigeon describes the project as an invitation to look beyond nature as scenery. ‘With Le Vrai du Faux, nature is never treated as a mere backdrop; it becomes a source of inspiration and a space for imagination. My experience of Champagne has shaped a vision of landscapes inhabited by presences, spirits, remnants of the past, and fictions,’ the photographer notes.

Les Fleurs III

imagining life beyond familiar boundaries

Jarrigeon avoids the usual solemn approach to nature, creating images in which trees, flowers, shells, animals, and man-made objects appear side by side. The combinations are often unexpected, giving familiar elements a different character.

The photographs also move away from a human-centered view of the natural world. People are only one presence among many, sharing the scenes with plants, animals, and objects. Jarrigeon leaves the relationships between them open, allowing the images to move between the recognizable and the absurd.

Le Vrai du Faux is presented by WOMANRAY in the Émergence section of Paris Photo, taking place at the Grand Palais from November 12 to 15, 2026. The project also marks Jarrigeon’s selection for the Prix Maison Ruinart. Meanwhile, his solo exhibition Rocher Fatal is on view at WOMANRAY in Paris through December 24, bringing together work from his recent exploration of the Forest of Fontainebleau.

items.articleBody:
London studio EBBA Architects has updated and extended a house within a converted barn in Cornwall, stripping away previous alterations to create open, pared-back interiors.

Topped by a distinctive gambrel roof, the former agricultural barn had already been converted into a dwelling, but also undergone years of incremental, ill-suited adaptations and extensions.

Drawings and photos

Previous

Next

Drawings and photos

Close

EBBA Architects looked to restore the Dutch barn's original, open spatial character, expanding its area by almost a third with the addition of a pavilion-like extension that is framed by columns of white stone.

"The overall concept was about finding clarity in the form of the building and finding ways to add in a way that didn't take away from the original character," EBBA's founding director, Benni Allan told Dezeen.

"Over the years the barn had gathered a series of piecemeal alterations that took away from the original simplicity. Our process involved removing later additions and then adding where felt most appropriate," he added.

"The house is a place that will act as a place to enjoy the vast contrast of weather throughout the year, while also providing a calm sanctuary and background for family life."

The ground-floor plan of Dutch Barn is based on the central position of an existing stair, around which a bathroom and storage core has been built to separate the more open kitchen and living spaces.

A row of full-height openings links the existing barn to its extension, where a long, uninterrupted space containing a skylit dining area and lounge opens out onto a covered colonnade via sliding doors.

"The intention is for the house to be used by the large family, and for there to be a blend between spaces," Allan explained.

"We are always interested in making flexible arrangements in planform, to accommodate different ways of living."

The home's interior finishes were also guided by ideas of simplification, with plaster walls, concrete floors and gridded white-painted timber ceilings.

EBBA Architects wanted to emphasise material junctions, as seen in a new oak column in the kitchen, which has been rotated to highlight where it meets the flitch plates that connect it to the exposed ceiling beams.

Externally, this theme was extended into the design of the extension's roof, which stops short of the edge of the stone columns to emphasise the point where the two meet.

The existing barn was clad in reused cedar shingles that were replaced where necessary, while the extension was built using white stone masonry that references the walls on the adjacent street.

"At first glance the house presents itself as a simple barn, but we like that a series of quite serious architectural moves have been complemented with some playful elements, such as the exaggeration of the junctions and the contrast between textured columns and clear, almost gallery-like floors," explained Allan.

Read:

Studio Weave designs kitchen as "piece of public realm" at South Barn in England

"We wanted the projecting roof and new columns to read as an independent object that reaches out into the garden and takes up the change in level, rather than as a continuation of the barn," he added.

EBBA Architects has previously completed a cafe in Marylebone with clay plaster walls and an illuminated glass ceiling, and an apartment in London for its founder that is lined with Douglas fir.

items.title: Tons of “Bunker-Buster” Bomb Parts for Israel Go Through JFK Airport
