Challenge Airlines, a cargo hauler based in Israel, made three flights this spring carrying the bomb casings for BLU-109s — a 2,000-pound munition that has been tied to numerous mass-casualty attacks on civilian neighborhoods in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and Iran in recent years — according to open-source data obtained by the Movement Research Unit and r…
items.articleBody:
An Israeli airline shipped thousands of pounds worth of parts for controversial “bunker-buster” bombs through John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York during the height of the Israeli–U.S. war against Iran, according to a new investigation by a left-wing research group.

Challenge Airlines, a cargo hauler based in Israel, made three flights this spring carrying the bomb casings for BLU-109s — a 2,000-pound munition that has been tied to numerous mass-casualty attacks on civilian neighborhoods in the Gaza Strip, Lebanon, and Iran in recent years — according to open-source data obtained by the Movement Research Unit and reviewed by The Intercept.

The airline also made more than 100 shipments of guidance kits known as joint direct attack munitions, or JDAMs — which are used to convert so-called “dumb bombs” into GPS-guided munitions capable of striking a specific target — according to data shared with The Intercept. Many of the guidance kits were marked for use on the MK-84, another 2,000-pound bomb Israel used in its campaign to level Gaza, where fragments of JDAMs have repeatedly been found at the site of airstrikes.

The 2,000-pound bombs present a serious risk of civilian casualties, according to Josh Paul, a former State Department official who resigned at the outset of the war in Gaza to protest the Biden administration’s sale of weapons to Israel.

“If you look at historic U.S. use of 2,000-pound bombs, in the entire counter-ISIS campaign, there were just two that were dropped in the vicinity of the city of Mosul precisely because there is no way to use a 2,000-pound bomb discriminately in an urban environment,” Paul said, referring to an American air war during the final years of the Obama administration to end the Islamic State’s control of the Iraqi city of Mosul.

Israel hasn’t shared the United States’s reservations. The country made extensive use of the weapons to attack targets in Gaza and Lebanon, including a deadly strike on Gaza’s Jabaliya refugee camp that killed dozens of civilians, according to an analysis by the New York Times.

“If you look at a picture of Gaza right now, I would say Israel’s use of these weapons is functionally indistinguishable from indiscriminate bombing,” Paul said.

“There is no way to use a 2,000-pound bomb discriminately in an urban environment.”

Challenge Airlines, and the Israeli military did not respond to request for comment.

“We work closely with all airport partners to ensure the safety of public, neighboring communities, and airport personnel,” said a spokesperson for the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK Airport. “The federal government and commercial airlines have primary responsibility as to what is allowed to be shipped on aircraft. We are pre-empted under federal law from interfering with these activities.”

While the shipments of JDAMs and bomb bodies for BLU-109s did not include active munitions, previous shipments of weapons through JFK have included explosives, including 14 tons of nitrocellulose bound for Israel in May 2025.

Related

Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point

The Intercept verified the data showing all three shipments of bunker-buster bomb bodies, and verified a portion of the data showing shipments of JDAM kits. Movement Research Unit, an investigative outlet whose prior work has uncovered shipments of drone tech to Israel and the transport of fighter jet parts by United Airlines onboard civilian passenger flights, shared the data on the condition that some specifics of its methods be withheld to prevent a crackdown on the availability of such data.

In response to the flow of weapons and materiel through JFK, the New York City chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America has been organizing a campaign to stop the flow of weapons to Israel through the airport.

“This is another example of a growing body of reporting that shows how civilian infrastructure is used for the genocide in Gaza,” said a DSA member named Henry, who asked to be identified without his last name in order prevent retaliation from his employer. “Civilian air travel should prioritize passengers, travelers, and the international community — not weapons — and no worker should be forced to serve the militarized supply chain.”

Tons of Pressure

Challenge Airlines shipped the bunker-buster bomb bodies on flights leaving JFK for Tel Aviv on March 12, April 30, and May 6, according to the data shared with The Intercept.

They shipped the guidance kits far more frequently, with 109 shipments leaving JFK for Tel Aviv between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026. Cargo documents indicate that most of the shipments were of JDAM kits designed for 2,000-pound MK-84 bombs but also included at least one shipment of kits for bunker-buster bombs.

Related

Congress Is Trying to Permanently Integrate U.S. and Israeli Defense Tech

In total, the airline shipped 175,884 pounds of BLU-109 casings and more than 5 million pounds of JDAM kits between December 22, 2024, and June 7, 2026, according to the data obtained by Movement Research Unit.

JFK Airport is the main export hub for such munitions flying by air to Israel, according to federal data: More than half of all Israel-bound air shipments of weapons that fit the government export category for bombs and missiles was sent abroad from JFK.

It was not immediately clear where the bunker buster and JDAM shipments originated, but sales of military hardware to Israel typically either come from deals between the Israeli and U.S. governments or direct commercial purchases under a special export license made by the Israeli military from private companies.

In the first two years of Israel’s war on Gaza, the U.S. spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel, according to a study by analyst William Hartung. That has included multiple shipments of 2,000-pound bombs like the BLU-109 and the MK-84, as well as JDAM kits to equip the weapons with GPS guidance.

The Biden administration in May 2024 halted the shipment of MK-84 2,000-pound bombs to Israel, citing the potential harm to civilians, but President Donald Trump resumed shipments of the heavy munitions within weeks of retaking the White House.

News of the shipments comes just over a month after the Associated Press revealed plans in the works for the U.S. to ink a vast $2.8 billion arms sale to Israel that would include thousands of 2,000-pound bombs.

The ongoing sale of such heavy weapons to Israel underscores the need for a federal solution, according to Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., who sponsored last year legislation dubbed the “Block the Bombs Act,” that would bar the U.S. from selling BLU-109s, JDAMs, and other munitions central to Israel’s war effort.

“It’s good that people are putting pressure locally, but ultimately it is Congress’s responsibility to make that happen.”

“It’s the only bill that prohibits these weapons transfers from happening, and the only bill that creates a comprehensive process of oversight,” Ramirez told The Intercept. “There’s been a big push, particularly in New York and around JFK, to block these transfers and it’s good that people are putting pressure locally, but ultimately it is Congress’s responsibility to make that happen.”

First introduced in May 2025, the bill has gathered more than 80 co-sponsors but has thus far languished in legislative limbo. With the House of Representatives soon to be under Democratic control, Ramirez said she plans to bring the bill to the floor next session.

items.articleBody:
The biggest collective brain fart by the Democratic Party over the course of my career was almost certainly convincing itself that America’s rising Hispanic population share guaranteed a progressive hammerlock on American electoral politics.

This 2013 take from Ron Brownstein — that Barack Obama’s re-election proved culturally conservative white people had become irrelevant — had an unusually blunt headline but was typical of the spirit of the era.

This analysis never made a ton of sense, even on its own terms. In 2012, Obama won Iowa and Ohio and Michigan and Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, none of which had a particularly large Hispanic population share. This basic math was known and knowable at the time, but it was ignored amid emerging Democratic majority hype and a focus on non-pivotal states like Nevada.

But the notion that demographic changes meant Democrats didn’t have to do politics was misguided in deeper ways, and it helped set the party up for some serious tactical and strategic errors. Those mistakes led to blowing off not only the actual views of the kind of secular white working-class Midwesterners who were important to Obama’s wins but also to blowing off the actual views of most American Hispanics.

In 2020, Donald Trump shocked many liberals by making meaningful gains with Latino voters even while doing quite poorly overall. Then in 2024, with the national trends at his back, he did even better.

A huge part of the 2026 story is Hispanic voters coming back to Democrats. Trump’s own choices are the largest factor, but an important secondary one is Democrats developing a more sophisticated understanding of the Hispanic electorate. And part of that, I think, has been cultivating a larger crop of moderate Latino politicians. Slow Boring’s 2026 candidate slate featured three different Latino guys who wear cowboy hats. And if Democrats want to continue to win, politicians like that — people who actually represent their voters and know what they’re like — have to control the narrative and not let it be seized again by unaccountable NGO types spinning wildly unrealistic dreams of endless progressive dominance.

The false dawn

One serious problem with post-2012 hubris about Hispanic voters is that it kind of understandably radicalized Republican opinion against immigration.

People have a range of concerns about immigration, some more fact-based than others. But people also have lots of opinions about topics that aren’t immigration. The thrust of Brownstein’s argument was that catering to people with culturally conservative views on non-immigration topics was now unnecessary thanks to the rising Hispanic tide. This notion got rephrased by conservatives as an alarming and possibly potent narrative that immigration debates should be understood not as economic policy but as a progressive effort to perpetrate a “great replacement” of the existing electorate.

And at the same time, it generated a breakdown of ideological discipline in the Democratic Party.

items.title: Living While Mourning Those Impermanence Will One Day Take

items.articleBody:
Boom, boom, boom, boom. Lying in my husband’s arms, close to his chest, I feel anxiety rise in my body, growing with every beat of his heart. I resist the urge to move away for a few seconds, then hurriedly shift to lie beside him, sad that I can no longer rest in the silent communion this closeness once invited.

His steady heartbeat, a sound that once soothed me, now sounds like a ticking clock—one that could stop without warning at any moment. The first time I abruptly pulled away like this, he was taken aback. Now, he simply reaches for my hand and holds it tight, knowing why I have moved away. In his own way, he knows this fear too.

At times like this, part of me wishes I could go back to not being so deeply aware of impermanence—to forget, if even briefly, what I know to be true.

I was surprised to find this same impulse reflected back to me in an unlikely place. In the 2026 comedy-mystery film The Sheep Detectives, some of the titular sheep choose not to carry the memories of painful losses because remembering hurts too much. The film even makes the bargain visible: If they erase the grief, they also erase the one they once loved. That stayed with me, because I recognized a quieter version of the same impulse in myself. I was not trying to forget the people I loved; I was trying to forget that they could be taken from me.

I hadn’t realized how much I had been trying to keep impermanence—and my own mortality—at the edges of my day-to-day awareness until I visited Varanasi in 2013. It is believed those who are cremated in this sacred town gain instant liberation from the cycle of birth and death. At my spiritual teacher’s suggestion, I asked a boatman to take me near Manikarnika Ghat, one of the eighty-four ghats of Varanasi and widely known as Varanasi’s principal cremation ground. As our boat approached the blackened primeval cremation site and came to rest, I gazed somberly at the holy orange flames devouring the wooden funeral pyres. A body wrapped in glittering cloth arrived on a stretcher and was laid down to await its turn. So this is how it all ends. One day, that will be me—the realization hit me with a jolt.

I was overcome by deep sorrow. It was the beginning of a long and difficult reckoning with impermanence—and with how to keep living while grieving what I knew it would take: those I hold most dear.

For years, the awareness of impermanence frightened me terribly. If nothing could be held on to, if everyone I loved would one day be gone, what was the point of any of it? Often, the thought opened into a kind of despair in which life felt dark, fragile, and almost meaningless, and I was left with the terrifying image of myself utterly alone and bereft. There were periods of deep anxiety and depression, and days when, once I had done what needed to be done, I would retreat to bed for hours.

And yet I did not want to turn away from the truth. I wanted to learn how to live with impermanence and gently prepare for the losses it would bring, without being entirely undone by them when the time came to let go.

Over the years, I have been learning that there is no neat way through this. I have searched online, listened to dhamma talks, and returned again and again to spiritual teachings. The guidance is often to accept impermanence, and though I understand the wisdom of it, I am still learning what acceptance looks like when dread grips my body and my mind races ahead to loss. Over time, the question has shifted for me from how to stop fearing loss to how to keep living fully while knowing that loss will come.

Over time, the question has shifted for me from how to stop fearing loss to how to keep living fully while knowing that loss will come.

Perhaps there is no single map for that. Mine is still taking shape, slowly, as I meet the fear and grief again and again. And yet, over time, a few guideposts have emerged along the way, pointing to steps one can take in learning how to keep living and making the most of life while grieving what impermanence will take.

The first step has been to stop fighting grief simply because the loss has not yet happened. I used to get annoyed with myself: Don’t get carried away into a future that has not yet happened. Come back to this moment—he is right here with you. Initially, I thought mindfulness of the present meant pushing the grief of the future aside. But I have come to see that the grief about losing him is also part of what is here now, and forcing it away does not make me more present.

In fact, at times, it helps me cherish the life I still have with him more fully—when my husband leaves for work and we kiss goodbye at the door, the knowledge that I may not see him again adds a sweet poignancy and tenderness to the moment. The same awareness also softens me after a disagreement. I may still be hurt, but knowing that our time together is finite makes me less willing to let resentment harden into distance.

The second step has been learning to discern when to lean into grief and when to set its burden down. When it feels overwhelming, I choose to lie down and allow sorrow to take over. As its force softens, I may choose to sit up, breathe with it, and look more closely at what hurts. What am I afraid of right now? Growing old alone? No longer having him beside me to share the small joys and sorrows of an ordinary day? Naming the fear helps me mourn what I stand to lose rather than remaining engulfed by an unnamed dread.

At other times, I realize I have reached my limit. I check what I have the energy and inclination for and may try to do some art, knit, or disappear into a period drama. I used to feel guilty about such choices, but I have come to understand that distraction is not always avoidance. Some guilt still arises—especially when I am binge-watching a show—but I am learning to honor the changing rhythm of grief: to lean in when I have the capacity and to rest from its weight when I do not.

Naming the fear helps me mourn what I stand to lose rather than remaining engulfed by an unnamed dread.

Along the way, it has been reassuring to discover that I do not have to force my own way back out of grief. Whenever the dishwasher beeps, my dog waits for his walk, it is time to prepare for an online therapy session, or I hear my husband’s key in the door—I come back to the present. I have begun to trust the movement of grief: to let it carry me out for a while, knowing that, in its own time, the same tide will return me to the shore of the present moment.

The third step has been to notice what awakens curiosity, wonder, or joy, and then to deliberately nourish that. It may be the tiny Indian silverbills at the bird feeder outside my room, or the wispy clouds floating across a pink-purple evening sky. When something holds my interest, I try to linger in it, practice gratitude, and remember Thich Nhat Hanh’s teaching—present moment, wonderful moment. One moment of aliveness often opens into another—I may open my sketchbook to draw the birds or play with the pinks and purples of the sky, or simply make myself a cup of tea and sit on the balcony to share the passing hour with my plants, the birds, and the sunset.

Sometimes, the very knowledge that something will not last deepens this sense of aliveness. Each morning, I pluck the small, fragrant flowers of my parijat, or night-flowering jasmine, and carry them to my altar. With one hand, I remove yesterday’s flowers, now dry and shriveled; with the other, I place the fresh ones down, their white petals and bright orange centers still vivid and alive. The faded flowers remind me what will become of the ones I am holding now, and somehow that knowledge makes me more grateful for them. Perhaps this is part of what I am learning about the people I love too: that their fragility does not have to diminish my joy in them; it can make their presence matter even more while they are still here.

Image courtesy Tara Anand

The fourth step has been to try to become more of a refuge to myself. “Be an island unto yourself,” the Buddha taught. Part of my fear of losing my husband comes from knowing how much of my emotional life I have built around his presence—he is the person I instinctively turn to—to share what has moved me, seek comfort, feel understood, have fun.

So I have been trying, gently, to build more of a life within myself too. I travel on my own sometimes, allowing some experiences to belong just to me, and practice staying with loneliness rather than immediately reaching for him.

The more I discover that I can be at home in my own company, the more I trust that the future-me will in time find her way through loss when it comes.

And yet, after all these years of contemplating impermanence, I still catch myself reaching for certainty. Recently, Joey, my seven-and-a-half-year-old Shih Apso, had a sudden bout of seizures, and we have since learned that there may be a problem with his heart.

Up until then, he had been in robust health, and without quite realizing it, I had been living with the expectation that losing him was something I wouldn’t have to face until five or six years down the line. I realized that while I had not erased the possibility of loss, I had placed it far enough into the future to feel a false sense of security.

Perhaps the practice is neither to brace for loss nor to tuck it safely away in some distant future but to let hope remain hope—without mistaking it for a promise.

Now, when Joey settles into my lap, I stroke his back and take comfort in his familiar weight. My husband’s hand comes to rest on him, too, and for a while we sit there together—not knowing how many more ordinary evenings there will be.

For now, Joey is warm and solid in my arms, and the three of us are here together. I let myself feel both the grief of knowing this will end and the precious tenderness of being inside it while it is still here.

Rise ’n shine! No sooner had the last Whitney Biennial closed than we got news about the next one — or its curators, at least. Staff Writer Anna Lee has the details on the appointment of Meg Onli, co-curator of the 2024 edition, and Zack Winokur, opera director and producer, for the blockbuster American art exhibition’s 2028 iteration.

Speaking of museums of American art, we caught up with pathbreaking Kiowa and Tongan curator Jordan Poorman Cocker, who just organized a major reinstallation of contemporary Indigenous art at Crystal Bridges. She talks with Petala Ironcloud about approaching Indigeneity as a global framework and telling a “more honest story of American art” through her community-driven work.

items.articleBody:
6 Min Read

CHAPEA Mission 2 Crew Reflects After 378 Days on Simulated Mars

The CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog) Mission 2 crew egress from their simulated Mars habitat, completing their mission on Oct. 31, 2026, at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.

After 378 days without windows, the sounds of the outside world, or real-time calls with family and friends, four research volunteers stepped out of NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, completing the agency’s second yearlong Mars surface simulation.

Ross Elder, Ellen Ellis, James Spicer, and Matthew Montgomery entered the roughly 1,700-square-foot, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston on Oct. 19, 2025, for CHAPEA (Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog) Mission 2.

The crew participated in simulated Marswalks, robotic operations, habitat maintenance, exercise, and crop cultivation.

“Their work means more than completing a mission,” said Johnson Director Vanessa Wyche. “It is about preparing for the challenges of human exploration beyond Earth, gathering the knowledge we need to protect crew health and performance, and paving the way for future missions to the Moon and, one day, Mars.”

Family, friends, and colleagues welcome the CHAPEA Mission 2 crew as they exit the building housing the Mars Dune Alpha habitat on Oct. 31, 2026.

NASA/James Blair

NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway put the crew’s time in isolation into perspective: While they were inside the habitat, he completed a 237-day mission aboard the space station and returned to Earth.

During that same period, the Artemis II astronauts traveled around the Moon and set the record for the farthest humans have traveled from Earth. NASA also celebrated 25 years of continuous human presence aboard the International Space Station on Nov. 2, 2025.

“The reality of what you guys did here required immense physiological and psychological strength, teamwork, and human grit,” Hathaway said.

Supported by researchers and ground teams across the agency, the CHAPEA crew collected health and performance data while navigating limited resources and communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way.

Ross Elder: Commander and Test Pilot

Ross Elder, CHAPEA Mission 2 commander, prepares for a simulated Marswalk in the habitat’s airlock.

Elder brought a U.S. Air Force experimental test pilot’s approach to leading the crew. He found simulated Marswalks and robotic exploration “uncannily similar” to operating as part of a flight. From inside the habitat, crew members remotely operated a drone and a rover to survey terrain and identify or collect rock samples.

The demanding Marswalk schedule also sharpened his understanding of the physical preparation future explorers will need. Preparing suits, completing airlock procedures, and making long traverses took time and stamina. He emphasized nutrition, exercise, and rest as essential to sustaining that pace.

His steadfast leadership and mission focus drew praise at egress for keeping the team motivated and improving. For Elder, seeing his crewmates combine their strengths was a highlight of the mission.

“The real magic has been the privilege and pleasure of seeing everyone come together, with the makings of one of the finest teams I’ve ever been a part of,” Elder said.

Ellen Ellis: Medical Officer and Tactical Thinker

Ellen Ellis, CHAPEA Mission 2 medical officer, exercises on a stationary bike inside the habitat.

Ellis, a U.S. Space Force officer with experience at the National Reconnaissance Office, brought a background in military operations and systems engineering. As medical officer, she helped organize biological sample collections and prepare supplies for the crew’s health research.

As procedures became familiar, she emphasized the discipline needed to follow every step carefully. She also enjoyed solving problems with the tools available. “There is a kind of tactical creativity that I find energizing,” she said.

Contributing to human spaceflight research helped sustain her motivation. So did the relationships with her crewmates. “It would be difficult to convince someone who has never lived in isolation that most days, I don’t feel isolated. I have three teammates that I rely on every day to get through the mission.”

She also credited exercise, behavioral health, nutrition, and medical specialists for their coordinated support throughout the mission.

“When I look back on the mission, the most salient point I’ve learned is that a future Mars crew requires a highly integrated ground team,” Ellis said.

James Spicer: Flight Engineer and Systems Specialist

James Spicer, CHAPEA Mission 2 flight engineer, conducts a maintenance activity outside the habitat during a simulated Marswalk.

Spicer brought experience in satellite communications and spacecraft development to the habitat’s maintenance work. At egress, he was thanked for keeping its systems running smoothly and described as the “flight engineer extraordinaire and resident data scientist.”

He compared the year to living aboard a submarine or boat, where limited supplies and space shaped daily decisions. The crew tracked consumables from dish soap to respirator filters and carefully managed food and water.

The crew had access to resources that provided news, and Spicer was surprised by how little he missed constant news and social media updates. The break from distractions helped him focus on the mission.

Inside the habitat, stories and jokes around the kitchen table brought laughter to demanding days. He told his crewmates they had made the year “not a chore, but a joy.”

“We’re inspired every day knowing that the data we’re generating is informing Martian mission planning and increasing the safety, health, performance, and comfort of future Martian crews,” he said.

Matthew Montgomery: Science Officer and Versatile Engineer

Matthew Montgomery, CHAPEA Mission 2 science officer, displays vegetables harvested from the habitat’s hydroponic crop system.

Montgomery brought experience in hardware engineering, robotics, technology startups, and independent films. At egress, he was described as the “Swiss Army knife of crewmates” for his technical knowledge and problem-solving skills.

He helped crewmates identify rock samples collected during simulated Marswalks and set up the habitat’s 3D printing capabilities. His background in indoor agriculture also carried into a seed-germination experiment that used a control and simulated Martian soil.

Maintaining a consistent data set remained a priority. Montgomery learned to investigate anything that gave him pause, describing instances when speaking up helped identify concerns with equipment, safety, and data quality.

He also learned to give himself more grace when an outcome fell short.

At egress, he credited the crew’s different perspectives with producing solutions stronger than any member could have developed alone.

“It’s really the people that make exploration possible,” he said.

Looking Toward Mars

The CHAPEA Mission 2 crew celebrates after stepping outdoors for the first time in 378 days on Oct. 31, 2026, at NASA’s Johnson Space Center.

NASA/James Blair

Two weeks of post-mission evaluations and debriefs will help researchers interpret the crew’s data alongside their experiences. The study builds on the first CHAPEA mission, which concluded July 6, 2024.

Grace Douglas, CHAPEA’s principal investigator, said the research will help NASA weigh human health and performance risks against resources, including crew time, communication capacity, and food and water system designs. She also noted that many resource challenges facing space explorers mirror problems on Earth.

Sara Whiting, CHAPEA project scientist, said the data comes as NASA plans how astronauts will live and work at the Moon Base, humanity’s first lunar outpost near the Moon’s South Pole.

“This is really the now moment for this kind of data,” she said.

items.articleBody:
Donald Trump Jr., left, and Eric Trump, right, watch as their father, Donald Trump, center, speaks to members of the media in 2024. Justin Lane/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The Trump administration awarded a small biosecurity company nearly $40 million to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases just months after a firm linked to President Donald Trump’s elder sons invested in its parent company, according to records and interviews.

The contracts, one to screen for Ebola in several U.S. airports and the other to respond to disease outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo, are seven times the total value of government contracts the company had directly received before.

The company, XpresTest, has years of experience monitoring for COVID-19 and other diseases for the government at U.S. airports. That makes its parent, XWELL, an unusual hybrid, selling both spa treatments and biosecurity services. Last year, it made most of its money from waxing salons and airport spas that offer manicures, massages and “chakra beds.”

The contracts are the latest example of the president’s family benefiting financially from his administration’s actions. And the stakes for these deals are particularly high. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, an Ebola outbreak has killed more than 5,000 people this year, and the federal government is trying to stop the pathogen from coming to the U.S.

XpresTest has never worked with Ebola or provided biosecurity services abroad, let alone in the kind of volatile locales it’s now expected to work in. The CEO of its parent company, Ezra Ernst, said XpresTest won both contracts in a competitive bidding process and pointed to its years of experience doing screening for COVID-19 and other pathogens at American airports. But even he acknowledged that working internationally is “a new thing for us” and expressed uncertainty about being able to complete the work in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“This is a risky contract. I’m not sure we can do it,” Ernst said in an interview.

Jeremy Konyndyk, who helped oversee the U.S. government’s response to a 2014 Ebola outbreak in West Africa, said there are some parallels between monitoring for COVID-19 and Ebola at airports, but he said it’s concerning that the government would award such a lucrative contract to a company that has no experience in Africa.

“There are countless organizations in the world that have decades of experience doing this work,” Konyndyk said. “I have to wonder why the hell they’re not going with someone who has actually done this before.”

Under previous administrations, the U.S. government addressed international disease outbreaks in partnership with the World Health Organization. But Trump withdrew from the group last year, dismantled the U.S. Agency for International Development, which handled much of this work, and dramatically scaled back the global presence of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At the same time, the State Department launched the America First Global Health Strategy, which calls for the U.S. to use aid to foreign countries to “promote American companies and American innovations abroad.” This March, the State Department announced it would be giving up to $4.5 billion in funding for various purposes, including responding to infectious disease outbreaks.

Under that program, XPresTest was awarded $20 million. Other funding went to better-known global aid nonprofits, including International Medical Corps, Save the Children and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, whose awards ranged from $25 million to $35 million.

The CDC also awarded XPresTest a contract, for $18.8 million.

In response to questions from ProPublica about XPresTest and its parent company, XWELL, the State Department noted the firm’s previous work screening for diseases at airports under a contract with the CDC and said its own award was made “through a competitive process that builds on this successful model.”

The CDC did not respond to a request for comment.

A spokesperson for the president’s sons Donald Jr. and Eric Trump said that they are “merely passive, minority investors in a fund that invested in this company,” and that they had no “involvement in or knowledge regarding the negotiation or procurement of any of its contracts, including any government contracts.”

“Both are private citizens who hold no government positions, broken no laws and who have every right to pursue lawful business and investment opportunities,” the spokesperson said.

The Trump sons’ connection to XWELL was established in February, when a fund called American Ventures invested in the company. The fund was launched by Dominari Holdings, a small financial firm with offices inside Trump Tower in New York. The leaders of Dominari hired the Trump sons as advisers after their father was elected to a second term and granted them a stake of more than 10% in Dominari.

Anthony Hayes, the CEO of Dominari Holdings, told ProPublica, “We have never seen or even heard of Don or Eric using their family name to influence the granting of a government contract.”

American Ventures has taken stakes in other companies that have benefited from Trump administration actions. The Florida-based drone company Powerus got a contract worth up to $90 million from the U.S. Air Force five months after the Trumps’ involvement was announced. Through American Ventures, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump also are acquiring a stake in a critical minerals group that has received U.S. government support to mine for tungsten in Kazakhstan. The Trumps have described themselves as passive investors who do not advocate for the companies they have stakes in before their father’s government.

XWELL was founded in 2006 as a line of airport-based spas that provided massages and facials. During the pandemic, the company, then known as XpresSpa Group, got $5.5 million from the CDC to offer travelers COVID-19 testing. It also collected waste from airplane toilets to check for new viral strains. It has done similar work for at least one other company that has received government contracts.

In January, XWELL announced that it was hiring a former senior adviser at the CDC who created and led the agency’s traveler surveillance program. The firm said the move was part of a plan to expand “its traveler-based pathogen surveillance capabilities to support international travel hubs and large-scale mass gathering events worldwide.”

The following month, American Ventures invested about $30 million in XWELL. The company had lost money the previous year. “We were so cash-strapped, close to bankrupt,” its CEO said.

Its valuation before the cash infusion was just $3 million. In exchange, American Ventures got a roughly 10% stake in the company to start, with an option to essentially print and sell millions of shares in the future.

Why American Ventures would invest so much in XWELL is unclear. In other cases, when the fund has invested in similar tiny publicly traded companies, some of those firms have moved into hot new sectors and drawn publicity for their connection to the Trumps, then Dominari has offloaded shares. In this case, there is no indication it has sold any of its stake yet.

In June, XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract for what a public notice about the grant said was “Ebola entry screening services.”

XpresTest then received the State Department grant for “rapid, effective, and coordinated outbreak response” to infectious disease threats in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which began in September, according to a government database. The company is also planning to work in Kenya and Morocco. XWELL’s website shows it is now hiring specialists in Ebola response training and biosecurity in the U.S.

An XpresSpa at Miami International Airport Karston Tannis/Monmouth Media House

In July, after XpresTest was awarded the CDC contract, XWELL announced plans to sell the subsidiary along with its line of spas to a private facial spa company. Ernst, the CEO, said the government contracts played a role in the $13 million sale price and will follow XpresTest to the new company.

That means XWELL, the company that the Trump-linked investment fund took a stake in, will benefit financially from the Trump administration contracts if the sale closes, even though it won’t be involved in doing the work for the government.

XWELL said in a public filing that the sale was part of an effort “to pursue a new direction in the national security sector.” Ernst said he didn’t know the exact plans but thought the parent company might be looking to work with the Department of Defense.

XWELL did not announce either of XpresTest’s biosecurity contracts, which recently became public in federal contracting disclosures. Public companies like XWELL are required to report so-called material events, developments that could affect their share price, such as a large government contract. XWELL has publicized previous work for the federal government, including a $2 million, eight-week pilot program for testing COVID-19 in 2021.

When asked why his firm didn’t announce the awards, Ernst gave various reasons, including the possibility that XPresTest might wind up not being able to do the work — either because of its own inexperience working internationally or because the Trump administration might suddenly shift priorities and only pay for a fraction of the contract.

“None of these contracts are guaranteed,” he said.

The biosecurity awards add to the questions about the Trump family’s enrichment during his second term. The Trump family’s business activities extend far beyond Dominari and American Ventures. The president himself has made more than $1 billion from cryptocurrency ventures whose value has ballooned as his administration has taken a friendly stance to the industry. And other companies backed by his sons Donald Jr. and Eric have received billions of dollars in federal deals. Earlier this year, ProPublica reported that the Pentagon granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. The Pentagon denied preferential treatment, and a spokesperson for Trump Jr. said he played no role.

The Trumps’ financial ties to government deals and actions are expected to be a primary focus of Congress in the coming months after Democrats won control of both the Senate and the House in last week’s midterm elections.

“When the government is corrupted for personal gain over the public interest, Americans lose trust and taxpayer dollars are wasted,” Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a letter to colleagues last week.

The post Firm Linked to Trump’s Sons Got Nearly $40 Million in Federal Contracts to Screen for Ebola and Other Diseases appeared first on ProPublica.

items.articleBody:
Der Berliner Verhaltensscanner wird mit KI-Videos trainiert. Für die Qualität der Software ist das eine Herausforderung. Um sie zu verbessern, werden zusätzlich Daten von überwachten Menschen genutzt.

Anhand von solchen Bildern soll die Überwachungssoftware lernen, wie Gewalt aussieht. – Gemeinfrei: KI-generiert, Screenshot von staige.com
Das Kottbusser Tor an einem Nachmittag unter der Woche: Menschen begutachten die Auslagen des Gemüsestandes. Aus dem Rewe kommt vorsichtig eine Frau gewackelt, sie trägt zwei Einkaufstüten in jeder Hand. Eine kleine Gruppe diskutiert erhitzt, während einer mit einem beschrifteten Papier wedelt. Polizist*innen in stichsicheren Westen patroullieren über den Platz.

Alle diese Menschen werden gerade von einer Software analysiert. 30 Kameras filmen das Geschehen auf der Nordhälfte des Platzes und sogenannte KI prüft, wer was tut und ob das Geschehen Hinweise auf eine Straftat gibt. Die automatisierte Dauerüberwachung soll Kontrolle auf einem bis dahin unbekannten Effizienz-Niveau ermöglichen.

Damit die Software erkennt, bei welcher Art von Szenen sie Alarm schlagen soll, wurden zuvor viele Clips eingespeist. In diesem Trainingsmaterial muss jeweils markiert sein, ob die Szene ein Beispiel für zu tolerierendes Verhalten sein soll oder für einen auszulösenden Alarm.

Nicht genug Gewalt

Die Menge und Qualität der Trainingsdaten hat große Auswirkungen darauf, wie gut das System am Ende funktioniert. Das zentrale Problem an dieser Stelle: Wie es aussieht, wenn ein Mensch geht, kann die Verhaltenserkennung anhand von Bildern aus dem öffentlichen Raum sehr gut lernen – da gibt es viel Anschauungsmaterial. Aber an welchen Faktoren sich ein Kampf erkennen lässt, ist anhand des Geschehens vor Ort schwierig zu kategorisieren. Aus Sicht von KI-Trainer*innen gibt es einfach nicht genug Gewalt im öffentlichen Raum. „Wie sich im Verlauf des Projektes zeigte, stehen leider nur sehr begrenzt öffentliche Daten zur Verfügung“, schrieb die Mannheimer Polizei.

Deshalb arbeiten die KI-Entwickler*innen mit Bildmaterial von nicht-authentischen körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen. In Mannheim etwa haben Polizist*innen bereits 2.000 Show-Kämpfe für das KI-Training veranstaltet, die Mannheimer Polizei geht davon aus, dass noch weitere 8.000 Kämpfe nötig sind, bis die Software praxistauglich ist.

Die Mannheimer Trainingsvideos sind als „Verschlusssachen“ eingestuft und unterliegen zudem persönlichkeitsrechtlichen Bestimmungen, deshalb will die Mannheimer Polizei diese nicht herausgeben. Ein Clip ist jedoch öffentlich, er wird im Mannheimer Technoseum als Beispiel für die Trainingsvideos gezeigt. Wir haben ihn dort abgefilmt.

Die andere Fehlerart ist das false positive. „Die Software erkennt eine Szene mit einer dunkelhäutigen Person im Kapuzenpulli als problematisch, auch wenn diese Person sich nicht problematisch verhält, sondern zum Beispiel nur durchs Bild joggt.“

Berliner*innen liefern gratis Trainingsdaten

Ein PR-Mensch, der für Staige arbeitet, nennt uns noch weitere Details zum Training der Überwachungssoftware. „Das Trainingsmaterial umfasst Szenen zu Schlagabtauschen, Tritten, gewaltsamen Schub- oder Zerrbewegungen mit Bodenkontakt sowie Rangelei auf Bodenebene“, schreibt er zum Beispiel. Dafür seien zum Teil die Bewegungen tatsächlicher Menschen mit der Motion-Capture-Technik aufgenommen worden. Der Videogenerator habe aus dem abstrahierten Geschehen anschließend eine Vielzahl von Clips erstellt, die den Vorgang mit unterschiedlichen Personen zu unterschiedlichen Tageszeiten zeigen. Dem Staige-Sprecher zufolge werden die KI-Clips „am Einsatzort“ erstellt, also in einer Liegenschaft der Berliner Polizei.

Zudem wird das Berliner Modell mit den Bewegungsdaten der Menschen, die sich am Kottbusser Tor aufhalten, „weiter optimiert“, so der PR-Mensch. Die Polizist*innen, die die Videos beobachten, vermerken dann jeweils, ob ein Alarm der Überwachungs-KI gerechtfertigt war oder nicht. Und die Software nimmt auch diese Szene dann als Beispiel für „ignore“ oder „alarm“.

Die Software wird also mit den Bewegungen von Menschen am Kottbusser Tor gefüttert. Dabei sind die Bewegungen – zum Beispiel der Gang – ja ein unique identifier, so einmalig wie ein Fingerabdruck. Doch mit der Verhaltensanalyse hat die scheidende schwarz-rote Berliner Landesregierung im vergangenen Dezember auch erlaubt, Überwachungs-KI mit personenbezogenen Daten zu trainieren – und diese Daten auch an die Software-Hersteller weiterzugeben.

items.title: Explore the Reading List for Harvard’s Humanities 10: The “Brutal” Humanities Class That’s Suddenly in High Demand
items.subtitle: There are plenty of good reasons a student might want to go to Harvard.

items.articleBody:
There are plenty of good reasons a student might want to go to Harvard. One is its long history, at least by American standards; another is the formidable accomplishments of the professors hired to teach there. But on some level, a teenager looking to come up in the world — or, in many cases, parents looking to put their teenager up in the world — understands full well that much of what an institution like Harvard offers comes down to its selectivity. Considering how few get in versus how many apply, it would be easy to believe that most of a student’s battle is won at the point of acceptance. Imagine the despair, then, of a newly arrived Harvardian facing another entrance exam and written application just to get a seat in Humanities 10.

Its unintimidating name notwithstanding, Humanities 10 is the opposite of one of those introductory courses through which a vast, darkened lecture hall full of freshmen can doze. “Students read a hefty book a week and write regular essays,” reports Pamela Paul in a recent Wall Street Journal article. “There is no pass/fail option. Digital devices are verboten, and attendance is taken in every lecture.” This year’s syllabus, which the WSJ has also published (also find it below), “begins with The Odyssey, travels forward in time to James Joyce’s Ulysses and then backward to end with The Iliad. In between are assignments on Montaigne, Shakespeare, Spinoza, Baldwin, Dante and Plato.” Amid these great books of the Western world appear works by Lady Murasaki, Sor Juana, and Cao Xueqin.

With certain exceptions — Baldwin’s essays, three installments of Krzysztof Kieslowski’s Dekalog — this curriculum could be a century old. In fact, Humanities 10 dates back only to 2008, when the English professors (and acclaimed writers) Stephen Greenblatt and Louis Menand put it together “as a Harvard twist on a famed Columbia senior seminar and Yale’s Directed Studies program, and a way to combat plummeting student interest in the humanities.” But in a way, its roots run back to 1945, when the university published the report “General Education in a Free Society,” which made the case for providing all students with the same non-professional, non-specialized intellectual foundation. Around the same time, it introduced Humanities 2: The Epic and the Novel, a demanding two-semester course that nevertheless drew 850 students a year at its peak.

Its successor Humanities 10 accepts only 90 freshmen, and the resulting competition has drawn public attention. So has the admitted students’ willingness to actually do the reading — and their apparent disdain for peers who would look over a few AI summaries and call it an education. In the video above, Deep Work author Cal Newport discusses the truth this reveals, one that recent technological developments have occluded. Relying on shortcuts to feelings of reward — cultivating social media instead of a social life, watching a travel video instead of making a journey, prompting an LLM instead of actually writing — strips our activities of not just their friction, but also their context, and ultimately their meaning. Like any worthwhile human experience, these books don’t hide their value under layers of difficulty; their difficulty is their value.

# Rentenreform eine hoehere kapitalmarktrendite gibt es nicht geschenkt 52445

Die Analyse zu „Rentenreform eine hoehere kapitalmarktrendite gibt es nicht geschenkt 52445“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
Aatish Bhatia and Arkarup Banerjee use a visual explainer for how a few neurons can orchestrate seemingly complex and surprising behaviors.

If you squint very hard at this, you might be able to see the rudiments of how our brains encode preferences, such as a love for spicy food or an aversion to smelly cheese.

Of course, biology is far more complex than these simplified sparks. We intentionally gave them very simple brains, so that we can understand how every part works.

Their brains are also frozen in time. In reality, brains can learn: They alter their wiring to gain new skills such as learning to walk, ride a bicycle, or play a piano.

This is the first part in a series they call Myriad.

I like the spark characters with different wirings. I got lost in joy for a second making them chase the light.

America cannot undo Trumpism (permalink)

True Carneyism has never been tried. When Canadian PM Mark Carney traveled to Davos to declare a "rupture" in the old order (and admit that this old order was never that great to begin with) he told us that there was no going back from Trumpism. The only way out of Trumpism was through:

https://www.weforum.org/stories/forum-institutional/davos-2026-special-address-by-mark-carney-prime-minister-of-canada/

This is easy to say, but hard to do. If the old order is over, then we will never again be able to trust America to serve as the world's cop, banker, ISP, IT department and consumer of first resort.

We can't trust Americans to buy the things we make:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/16/k-shaped-recovery/#disenshittification-nations

We can't trust them not to interfere with the interconnections between fiber lines that slither out of the oceans and onto the US landmass:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/26/difficult-multipolarism/#eurostack

We can't trust them not to weaponize the US dollar to undermine sovereign nations' legitimate activities:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/26/i-dont-want/#your-greenback-dollar

And we absolutely can't trust them not to spy on, steal from, and shut down governments, firms and households around the world by cutting off access to US software and cloud services, and by bricking the world's devices, from tractors to smartphones:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition

Despite Carney's assertion that this rupture represents a welcome (if too cruel, sudden and painful) departure of the old (never very good) system, no one (not even Carney) is acting like the world has truly changed. Take Carney's answer to the Trump tariffs: retaliatory tariffs. Tariffs have a place in sheltering a nascent domestic industry from better-developed, deeper-pocketed foreign competitors, so a tariff wall between Canada and the US could make sense, if it was paired with the massive domestic investment we'd need to rebuild the manufacturing industry that Brian Mulroney sold out with the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement (and later NAFTA).

But Carney is no Carneyist. When it comes to massive domestic spending, Carney is a bog-standard, austerity-addled Reaganomics guy; a central banker and technocrat whose idea of "industrial policy" is firing tens of thousands of skilled civil servants who thwart his agenda and replacing them with defective (but obedient) chatbots running on US hardware:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/13/vibe-governance/#k-hole

Carney's retaliatory tariffs aren't what you'd do if the old order had "ruptured." They're what you'd do if you hoped that your American cousins would come to their senses, evict their mad king from the White House, tear down the Epstein Memorial Ballroom, and roll back the clock to 2016. Like a lot of liberals, Carney just wants to go back to brunch.

But as any true Carneyist knows, brunch is canceled forever. Brunch ruptured. There's no going back to the old America, and there's no going back to the old American order that had dominated the world since the end of WWII. As November Kelly says, "Trump inherited a poker game rigged in his favor, but he flipped the table over anyway because he resented having to pretend to play."

This is something we're all struggling with, including Americans. The Republicans' midterm wipeout has corporate Democrats hoping that after a few years' tinkering, they can elect a Newsomdroid or give Harris a do-over and win back the trust and reliance of the world and the American people. Even for a true Carneyist who never liked the old order very much (like me), this is a comforting prospect. No one knows what the next world will look like, and no matter how screwed up the old world was, I knew how it worked and how to make it work for me (more or less).

But there is no going back. Trump I didn't have a plan, it only had Trump, whose One Big Idea was issuing Executive Orders. Many of these were meaningless bloviating. Some were illegal and were swiftly suspended or never went into effect. Biden overturned nearly all the remaining EOs (that were both substantive and not totally illegal).

But Trump II had Project 2025. The point of Project 2025 and the ambition of the wreckers who wrote it was to push America through a series of one-way transformations that cannot be undone, and that's what's happened, over two short years. That's the bad news. The good news is that it's much easier to destroy than to build, so Project 2025 hasn't led to the creation of permanent, load-bearing fascist institutions that cannot be shuttered without bringing down large parts of the USA.

Start with values. Trumpism is a denial of democracy and the rule of law. Tens of millions of Americans have been marinated in a belief system that says that the way to win power is to claim all the elections you lose are rigged and that these "stolen elections" are best addressed by staging a coup. These people are in a cult that embraces its leader's naked corruption. They're in a cult whose doctrine treats political triumph of as divine direction to embark on looting sprees. It's a cult whose members mutilate their faces so that they can't ever leave, and the reward for this permanent disfigurement is endless influence-peddling:

https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6136101-ambassador-guilfoyle-wire-request/

Even without ritual scarification to mark them out forever, millions of these people will never come back from this cult indoctrination. They will forever be democracy's enemies, treating the idea of laws, rules and honest service as shucks for the rubes. What's more, these people's neighbors, family members and co-workers will never be able to fully trust them.

Unfortunately, those values aren't just diffused through the population: they are concentrated in the organs of state. DOGE and Federalist Society judicial appointments have created a stay-behind cadre of life-tenured fascists who now dominate America's federal judiciary and permanent civil service, including and especially the nation's law enforcement and national security agencies, from the FBI to the FDA, the NSA to the Bureau of Prisons.

Worse: DOGE also chased away hundreds of thousands of skilled, principled public servants. Those people have retired, retrained, emigrated or exited the workforce. They can't simply be re-hired and restored to their old roles. From finance regulation to the national education system, America has lobotomized itself, swapping people who understand how things work and use that understanding to enforce the laws and safeguard the American people for end-times fascists, caliper-wielding eugenicists, and Ayn Rand LARPers.

Much of the work DOGE's victims did is also gone forever. When DOGE's muskrats killed long-running NIH research projects, they pulled the plug on studies, some of which had run for decades. Many of these experiments are unsalvageable. DOGE didn't just throw away the contributions that cancer patients, people with genetic disorders and other volunteer research subjects gave to science: in halting these research projects, DOGE shredded this selfless sacrifice. Why not? When one NIH official begged his DOGE invaders not to kill long-running, valuable cancer research, the DOGE child laughed and said it didn't matter, because AI was going to cure cancer.

Then there's the NIH's research partners: the elite institutions who buckled so quickly in the face of Trump's antisemitism/DEI witch-hunts. These universities now face the same crisis as the DOGE-gutted civil service, with their best and brightest gone, grad students chased back to their home countries, and the trust of their students and faculty permanently squandered.

It's not just grad students who got chased out of America. Immigrants – documented and undocumented alike – have been terrorized for two years and many of them have fled. ICE got what it wanted: they robbed aging, stagnant America of the dynamism, aspiration and youthful vigor of the most ambitious people from every corner of the globe, people who proved their resourcefulness and bravery by making dangerous crossings. Then they navigated the US immigration system's impenetrable bureaucracy, often working without legal representation, in a language they were just learning, and still managing to clear every bureaucratic hurdle. This alone is a breathtaking demonstration of intelligence, resourcefulness and diligence. Those brilliant, hardworking people aren't coming back: some other country will get the benefit of their life's work and care. Their children will become citizens of other nations.

Now think of the hundreds of billions of dollars that have been transferred from ordinary working people who are still here, to America's oligarchs. Trump's tax cuts, corrupt policy subsidies and no-bid pork contracts have supercharged the wealth (and thus the power) of America's most corrupt elite. It will be the work of a generation to tax away their stolen loot, and much of it may never be recovered. These people will spend that time working to transform their wealth into permanent power, buying and installing politicians at every level of office.

Trumpland is a coalition of wreckers of every kind. Think of how MAHA undermined the nation's herd immunity to a host of communicable diseases, many of which can result in permanent disability. Long after MAHA is forgotten even as a punchline, the people whose health they destroyed forever will still be struggling. After a century of painstaking work to corral measles and other killer diseases, MAHA immunocompromised America itself, in just two short years. Any attempt to bring back evidence-based preventative medicine must now overcome the deep mistrust of medical science that an army of supplement-peddling quacks has sunk deep into Americans' psyche.

Speaking of mistrust: Americans must now and forever live with the knowledge that tens of thousands of their neighbors joined ICE, an armed, masked kidnapping squad that occupied US cities, murdering US citizens and noncitizens alike in the streets with impunity. Even if we try and imprison every one of those war criminals, it will take years and will shatter families and communities.

ICE proved that America is awash in small arms, but it's a different story when it comes to significant warfighting materiel. Trump's Iranian disaster used up the largest part of Pax Americana's arsenal of missiles and anti-missile interceptors. Putin doesn't need to convince Trump to cut off Ukraine's access to America's long-range arsenal. Trump shot his wad, and re-arming America is the work of decades, and it will cost billions, and it will require access to things America no longer knows how to make. Worse: the places where they do know how to make those things are no longer America's allies.

Can they be America's allies again? Well, sure, but only in a limited, Carneyist, "minilateral" way, in which countries form temporary alliances to accomplish specific goals. Biden spoke of "friendshoring" production of key goods and services. Friendshoring implies a reliable form of friendship, the sort that is built on decades of trust and interdependence. Friendshoring only works if the friends you friendshore to can be relied upon to stay your friends. Do we really think that if Venezuela deposes the puppet regime Trump installed after kidnapping the country's leader that it will remain America's "friend?"

That's the problem with weaponized interdependence: it only works for so long as the country America is screwing remains dependent on America, and now every country in the world is moving heaven and earth to break their dependencies on America, its institutions and products:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

As Nate Bethea says on this week's Trashfuture podcast, airports outside of the USA are now filled with large, splashy ads urging businesses to move their IT out of America's cloud and off of American apps:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/10/10/weaponized-interdependence/#the-other-swifties

After Microsoft obliged the Trump regime by taking away the online accounts of foreign officials who made Trump angry, will any other country ever voluntarily trust them with their industrial capacity, let alone their government?

https://www.forbes.com/sites/emmawoollacott/2025/07/22/microsoft-cant-keep-eu-data-safe-from-us-authorities/

I'm not saying America is a write-off: I'm saying that it has been sabotaged down to the foundation slab and structural members by a psychotic cadre of skilled arsonists, who were abetted by mad bombers who drove themselves even crazier by racking up life-altering debts in rigged "prediction markets" that serve as a vehicle for bankrupting yourself by wishcasting away your life's savings by betting on every aspect of a Permanent Chud Reich, as corrupt officials make out like bandits by trading on insider information.

When America comes back (if America comes back), it will not be as the organizing platform for the world's finance, military, technology and commerce. In years or perhaps decades, America may find a new stable place in the international community. But in the meantime, it cannot be relied upon to serve as the world's hyperpower. Trump forever disqualified America from enjoying that privileged place – and just to be sure, he destroyed its capacity to even try.

# Agent feedback

Die Analyse zu „Agent feedback“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

items.articleBody:
Many longtime fans of my Hexapodia podcast with Brad DeLong have been begging us to bring it back. Well, here it is! Hexapodia will now be a series of Substack Live conversations that you can tune in to, and which will be recorded as podcasts and sent out as emails.

Our first episode was a little rocky, as I got the time wrong and ended up arriving 20 minutes late. But Dan and Brad are both brilliant people, so you can watch them talk for a while before I show up! The topic of our discussion was the Anthropic IPO, inspired by my post about it last week:

I give the bull case for Anthropic, while Dan and Brad are both more skeptical. I think this quote sums up my side of the argument:

My bull case [for Anthropic] is not envisioning a world where Anthropic rules all businesses, rules 100% of every industry, or close to it. I’m also not envisioning a case where AI replaces human beings in their jobs.

I’m envisioning a change in the capital structure of the efficiently producing economy. I’m envisioning…a world where in order to succeed in any industry, you must create a tie-up with a frontier AI company that offers you access to an internal proprietary frontier model that will be months ahead of any model distilled from it. And…that doing this will require not purchasing services…at arm’s length from that company, but tying up your capital structure with that company so that you become in some sense a subsidiary of that company. I am envisioning that.

So I’m saying that instead of something where…AI is like oil and everyone has to buy oil or the things made downstream from oil…instead of that sort of arm of length world, I’m envisioning a world in which every company in order to succeed must become a subsidiary of Anthropic, OpenAI, [or] Google…and Anthropic is simply the biggest of those fish in a oligopolistic ecosystem of a few conglomerates competing against each other via their little subsidiaries in every single industry at the same time.

Interestingly, some economists at Google Deepmind just released a paper with a model in which this sort of thing happens. From the abstract of Imas, Koh, and Legg (2026):

When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a model of how intelligence…matters for organizations….AI expertise is reproducible while humans’ are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same human limits on coordination….When AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordination improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated AI-heavy firms. [emphasis mine]

I was envisioning a slightly more complex version, in which humans and AI are complements, where humans have private data that AI is better at using, and where one big conglomerate enters every industry but retains human workers. But I think Imas et al.’s model gets at some of the basic dynamics here.

Financial disclosure: I have no current position in Anthropic, but unless something major changes, I will probably buy Anthropic stock when it IPOs. I own stock in TypeSafe, an Anthropic competitor.

Subscribe now

items.articleBody:
Für ihre These, dass Künstliche Intelligenz zu einer neuen Gottheit wird, erhält die Philosophin Claudia Paganini sogar Todesdrohungen. Warum der Vergleich zwischen KI und Religion so viele Menschen provoziert und was das alles mit unserem Bedürfnis nach Sinn zu tun hat.

Frau Paganini, glauben Sie an KI?

Im Sinn von KI als Gottheit? Nein. Ich bin überhaupt kein spiritueller Mensch und ich mache die Erfahrung, dass KI ein Tool ist, das man einsetzen kann – oder eben auch nicht.

Claudia Paganini forscht und lehrt als Philosophin und Theologin an der Universität Innsbruck. In ihrem Sachbuch „Der neue Gott. Künstliche Intelligenz und die menschliche Sinnsuche“ untersucht Paganini, inwiefern Künstliche Intelligenz in der modernen Gesellschaft die Funktionen einer neuen Gottheit übernimmt. Bild: STUDIO MATPHOTO

Ihr Buch trägt den Titel „Der neue Gott“. Was macht generative Software in den Augen vieler Menschen zu einer neuen Gottheit? Wo liegen die Parallelen zu religiösen Überzeugungen?

Diese Technologie präsentiert sich uns auf eine Art und Weise, die es uns leicht macht, ihr zu viel Sinn und Bedeutung zuzuschreiben. Das ist auch der Prozess, der Religionen zugrunde liegt.

Beispielsweise boomen Prompting-Kurse und jede*r denkt, man müsse besser prompten lernen. Dem liegt die Idee zugrunde, dass die Technologie das ganze Wissen hat und ich mit diesem Orakel nur richtig umgehen muss, um daran zu kommen. Ich könnte ja auch einfach sagen: Die Antwort war unbefriedigend, das System kann es nicht besser. Stattdessen sagen Menschen aber: Ich habe einen schlechten Prompt gewählt, ich muss besser werden.

So funktioniert auch Religion. Ich beobachte ein banales Phänomen und entscheide mich dann für eine Erklärung, die weit darüber hinausgeht und irgendwie magisch aufgeladen ist.

Im Unterschied zu anderen höher entwickelten Tieren, die zufrieden sind, auf einer Wiese zu stehen, Gras zu fressen und sich die Sonne aufs Fell scheinen zu lassen, muss der Mensch immer eine Bedeutung finden. Das macht ihn prädestiniert für solche Zuschreibungsprozesse.

Viele Diskurse über KI beschäftigen sich mit der Frage, wie menschenähnlich diese Technologie ist. Sie gehen einen Schritt weiter und fragen: wie gottähnlich wird diese Technologie gesehen?

Indem man den Systemen viel mehr zutraut als anderen Menschen, würde ich eher von einem Vergöttlichungsprozess sprechen. Denn wenn es ein Vermenschlichungsprozess wäre, wäre die Begrenztheit sehr viel klarer.

Ich war selbst überrascht, wie viele Ähnlichkeiten ich zwischen KI-Vorstellungen und Gottesbildern entdeckt habe. In meinem Buch gehe ich klassische göttliche Eigenschaften durch, zum Beispiel „Allwissen“. Ich hatte erwartet, dass es bei manchen Eigenschaften schwieriger werden würde. Aber ich habe diese Zuschreibungsprozesse tatsächlich überall gefunden.

„Natürlich ist es gefährlich, KI als Gott zu betrachten, aber Religion ist per se gefährlich.“

Claudia Paganini

Möchten Sie vor einer Vergöttlichung der Technologie warnen?

Natürlich ist es gefährlich, KI als Gott zu betrachten, aber Religion ist per se gefährlich. Das gilt auch für die traditionellen Religionen. Wenn mich beispielsweise meine Religion aufgrund meiner konservativen Bibelauslegung vermeintlich dazu berechtigt, gleichgeschlechtlich liebende Menschen zu verachten.

Und natürlich macht es auch KI gefährlich, wenn sie wie ein Gott behandelt wird. Aber auch, weil diese Technologie sehr gut von Menschen instrumentalisiert werden kann, die damit Profit machen wollen. Das heißt, dass man nicht nur in Kauf nimmt, dass Menschen ihr eigenständiges Denken aufgeben, sondern das auch bewusst und manipulativ herbeiführt. Menschen werden in eine quasi selbstgewählte Unmündigkeit geführt. So wie den Lehren populärer Christfluencer*innen gefolgt wird, wird man mithilfe von Chatbots davon abgehalten, selbst zu denken und sich Urteile zu bilden.

Wir werden uns fragen müssen: Soll das die Art und Weise sein, wie wir das gesellschaftliche Zusammenleben in Zukunft organisieren wollen? Mit einer unmündigen, leicht manipulierbaren Masse, die ein paar Meinungsmacher*innen nachläuft? Oder haben wir andere Visionen von Weiterentwicklung, von Kultur und Demokratie?

Das Fresko von Michelangelo hält den Moment fest, in dem Gott die Hand ausstreckt, um Adam Bewusstsein zu verleihen. Heute wird häufig medial auf das Bild angespielt, wobei oft Adam – oder Gott – durch eine Roboterhand ersetzt wird. Bild: Michelangelo, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Tech-Unternehmen versprechen mit KI nicht weniger als die Lösung einiger der größten Probleme der Menschheit. Sind sie die Prophet*innen dieser neuen Religion?

Das kann man durchaus so sehen. Religionen haben den Menschen immer versprochen, dass sie ihre Probleme lösen, wenn sie sich nur ihnen anschließen, bereit sind, ihre Dogmen zu teilen und entsprechend zu leben. Religionen haben immer religiöse Eliten produziert. Menschen haben religiöse Bedürfnisse nach Orientierung, nach Sinn, nach Bindung. Und die werden über religiöse Vorstellungen befriedigt, weil man ihnen sagt: Da ist ein Gott, der dich gewollt hat, der dir eine Orientierung vorgibt.

Damit sie sich in der Nähe zu dieser Gottheit wähnen dürfen, müssen die „einfachen“ Menschen aber die religiösen Eliten akzeptieren, die letztlich die eigentlichen Nutznießer*innen des Volksglaubens sind, weil sie auf diese Weise Macht und Geld ansammeln können.

„Diese Warnungen vor der Zerstörungskraft der KI, die in periodischen Abständen auftauchen, ist ein Zeichen für einen Vergöttlichungsprozess.“

Claudia Paganini

Diverse Stimmen warnen vor einer KI, die eines Tages die Menschheit vernichten könnte. Sehen Sie in diesen Untergangsszenarien ebenfalls religiöse Denkmuster?

Diese Untergangsszenarien sind typisch für neue Götter. Wenn neue Gottheiten aufkommen und erstarken, dann traut man ihnen in der Regel Zerstörungsmacht zu. Es ist nämlich so, dass die Vorstellung von einem lieben Gott, der nur tröstet und versöhnt, eher typisch für den Niedergang von Religionen ist. In dem Moment, wo Religionen an Bedeutung verlieren, werden ihre Götter in der Regel freundlicher.

Das passt sehr gut zu meiner These. Diese Warnungen vor der Zerstörungskraft der KI, die in periodischen Abständen auftauchen, ist ein Zeichen für einen Vergöttlichungsprozess. Nebenbei dürfte es auch eine Marketingstrategie sein, weil das regelmäßig die Aktien der Tech-Konzerne hochtreibt. Aber trotzdem muss es in der Bevölkerung ja eine Bereitschaft geben, das Narrativ anzunehmen.

Der Widerstand gegen künstlich generierte Inhalte wächst. Was steckt aus Ihrer Sicht dahinter?

Ich sehe darin eine Kränkung. Mit der Robotik hatte man kein großes Problem, da sie nur diese dreckigen, gefährlichen und langweiligen – „dirty, dull and dangerous” – Tätigkeiten wegrationalisieren sollte. Ich fühle mich nicht in meinem Selbstwert angegriffen, wenn mein Geschirrspüler das Geschirr besser spült als ich. Unter Umständen fühle ich mich aber in meinem Selbstwert angegriffen, wenn ChatGPT die besseren Artikel schreiben kann.

Die Frage ist dann: Wie gehe ich mit dieser Kränkung um? Muss ich sie ständig abwehren, indem ich zum Beispiel sage: „Das ist viel mehr wert, weil ich es selbst gemacht habe“? Das sind meiner Meinung nach kindliche Bewältigungsschemata. Oder kann ich es akzeptieren und sagen: „Ja, okay, die KI schreibt die besseren Texte als ich. Aber das heißt nicht, dass ich aufhören sollte, Texte zu schreiben.“ Ich kann Texte nämlich auch schreiben, weil ich das gerne mache.

Ihre These der KI als neue Gottheit ist durchaus provokant. Welche Kritik haben Sie erhalten?

Meine These ruft sehr viele Emotionen bei religiösen Menschen hervor. Religion ist ein Bereich, in dem Menschen sehr verletzlich sind. Gerade weil viel auf dem Spiel steht: Ist mit dem Tod alles vorbei oder gibt es ein Jenseits, ein ewiges Leben? Deswegen entsteht auch so viel Aggression. Ich habe durch mein Buch definitiv Hater*innen gewonnen und bekomme deswegen sogar Todesdrohungen.

„Meine These ruft sehr viele Emotionen bei religiösen Menschen hervor.“

Claudia Paganini

Was sagen Sie zu diesen Reaktionen?

Ich denke, dass Glaube eine Entwicklungsdimension beinhalten sollte. Dazu gehören Krisen des Glaubens, die im Theologiestudium übrigens einen sehr wichtigen Stellenwert im Lehrplan haben. Ich finde es persönlich schade, dass sich manche Menschen darauf gar nicht einlassen können.

Viele der negativen Reaktionen, die ich erhalte, hängen damit zusammen, dass Menschen sofort bewerten und sich fragen: Was würde das für unseren Glauben bedeuten? Vielleicht, dass es gar keinen Gott gibt. Das wäre schrecklich. Ich würde also meinen, dass dieses Bedürfnis, sofort Schlüsse zu ziehen, sie daran hindert, spielerisch – und sogar freudvoll – nachzudenken und sich darauf einzulassen, bereits Bekanntes einmal anders zu sehen.

Was für eine Kritik gab es von Ihren Fachkolleg*innen?

Da gibt es teilweise Dissens zu meinem funktionalen Religionsverständnis. Ich sage, Menschen haben Gottesbilder, weil sie einen Nutzen davon haben. So können wir nachvollziehen, warum Götter über die Jahrtausende diese oder jene Eigenschaften hatten, indem wir auf den Nutzen und die Bedürfnisse der Menschen schauen.

Das ist eine bewusste Wahl, die ich treffe. Man könnte auch ontologisch herangehen und sagen, dass die Tatsache, dass Menschen über die Jahrtausende hinweg immer ähnliche Gottesbilder hatten, ein Beweis dafür ist, dass es einen Gott gibt, der genauso ist. So könnte man natürlich auch argumentieren.

Was möchten Sie mit dieser These in den Leuten auslösen – in Bezug auf unsere Vorstellung von KI?

Meiner Meinung nach ist es immer gut, einen kritischen Blick auf die eigene Religiosität und Spiritualität zu werfen, egal, ob sie sich an den klassischen abrahamitischen Gott oder eine KI-Gottheit richtet. Es gibt viele Aspekte, die wir kritisch reflektieren sollten.

Künstliche Intelligenz

Alle Beiträge zum Thema

So könnte ich beispielsweise meinen eigenen Umgang mit KI reflektieren und mich fragen, ob ich ihr einen so hohen Stellenwert in meinem Leben einräumen will. Will ich einer Technologie wirklich so viel zutrauen? Und will ich den Personen, die von diesen Zuschreibungen profitieren, wirklich so viel Macht über mein Leben und meine Realität geben?

Was mir an meiner These und der Arbeit an dem Buch Freude gemacht hat, ist, dass mir dieser ungewöhnliche Blick auf die KI selbst Dinge erschlossen und Erkenntnis ermöglicht hat. Ich möchte Leser*innen einladen, sich auf einen spielerischen Zugang einzulassen. Auf diese Weise eröffnen sich mir Möglichkeit, Aspekte oder Facetten zu sehen, die ich vorher noch nicht gesehen habe.
items.body: Warum der Vergleich zwischen KI und Religion so viele Menschen provoziert und was das alles mit unserem Bedürfnis nach Sinn zu tun hat. Frau Paganini, glauben Sie an KI? Im Sinn von KI als Gottheit? Nein. Ich bin überhaupt kein spiritueller Mensch und ich mache die Erfahrung, dass KI ein Tool ist, das man einsetzen kann – oder eben auch nicht. Claudia Paganini forscht und lehrt als Philosophin und Theologin an der Universität Innsbruck. In ihrem Sachbuch „Der neue Gott. Künstliche Intelligenz und die menschliche…
