items.body:
# Everyone hates oxford street will pedestrianisation save it podcast

The investigation into "Everyone hates oxford street will pedestrianisation save it podcast" examines the cognitive and psychological frameworks of mental resilience and intellectual focus. It analyzes grounded insights from cognitive science, practical strategies against digital distraction, and cultivating sustained focus in daily life. Further explorations and detailed perspectives remain available in the original source.

## Conceptual Framework & In-Depth Analysis

Engaging with these questions touches fundamental aspects of human judgment and cognitive autonomy. Through conscious examination of attention architectures, thinkers can cultivate deeper comprehension of complex systemic dynamics.

> "Critical discernment emerges through patient analysis of premises and empirical relationships."

## Practical Applications & Horizons

For research, inquiry, and public discourse, these observations open concrete pathways: Rather than passive information reception, disciplined inquiry fosters sustainable judgment and reflective clarity.

items.articleBody:
arXiv:2611.08572v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: This research involved the study of an application of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) in the field of academic advising. Academic advisement has been recognised as an important function of higher education. However, there is a widespread desire to improve the advisement services provided by many educational institutions (e.g., colleges and universities) around the world. In the last ten years, CBR expert systems have made important contributions in many domains by applying CBR methodology to a variety of areas of human problem solving. However, to date, expert advisement systems have not been successfully applied to academic advisement, which seems to be a very appropriate domain for this technology.
Academic advising is an important and time consuming task, and different tools and techniques must be used to make it an effective and efficient process. This thesis describes the design, development, and validation of a prototype case-based academic advisement recommender system that supplements the conventional advising process, and could eventually evolve to replace human academic advisors when its full potential is realised.

items.articleBody:
Today, a scientist who wants to simulate a physical process must pick the right tool for that one job, such as a solver built for flowing water or another designed to model the way a protein folds. Each one is hand-coded around the specific equations that dictate how that process behaves.

Researchers at MIT, the University of British Columbia (UBC), and elsewhere have now replaced that patchwork with a single deep-learning system, called WorldParticle, that could help engineers model different physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins, with one unified artificial intelligence architecture.

Scientists and engineers could use this system to model processes that typically require separate simulators, such as a fluid sloshing against a deformable solid. This could offer a faster, more accurate way to simulate how sloshing oil might impact an elastic valve in a storage tank, for instance. It could also help engineers study where and how granular materials, like sand or soil, could move when a soft robot touches them.

The system represents every material it simulates, from a dune of sand to a protein molecule, as tiny particles and predicts where those particles will move one step at a time. Because it learns the underlying dynamics rather than being programmed with an equation, the model can adapt to materials, forces, and environments it never encountered during training.

In the long term, the researchers hope this work helps scientists discover new materials and explore physical processes they would be unable to effectively study with existing simulation methods.

“We want to have a GPT moment for simulation,” says Peter Yichen Chen, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at UBC, and is a co-corresponding author of an open-access paper on this technique. “Every time people want to build a simulator for a particular physical phenomenon, they need to code it up from scratch. Our vision is to have a foundation model that works out of the box for any scenario you want to simulate. This is a first step in that direction.”

Chen is joined by co-corresponding and co-lead author Minghao Guo, an MIT postdoc; co-lead authors Caoliwen Wang and Siyuan Chen, UBC graduate students; Wojciech Matusik, an MIT professor of electrical engineering and computer science who leads the Computational Design and Fabrication Group within the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL); and others at UBC, Georgia Tech, Inria, Meta, the University of Pennsylvania, the University of Utah, the University of California at Los Angeles, and the University of Hong Kong. The research will be presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Conference and Exhibition on Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques in Asia.

Unified simulation

For this work, the researchers drew inspiration from world models. These powerful AI systems learn the rules that govern the physical world so they can predict how objects or environments will change over time in response to certain actions or conditions.

The researchers applied these concepts to develop a unified AI architecture that can simulate multiple types of physical phenomena.

“If you study deformable objects and fluids, you would need two simulators — one for each physical regime. But if you unify them into one model, maybe you could couple the physics of these two processes and gain insights into new problems?” Guo says.

WorldParticle breaks an object into thousands or millions of tiny, three-dimensional dots, or particles, using what is known as a Lagrangian representation. It tracks the movement and velocity of the particles over space and time to simulate the material’s dynamics.

Typically, when scientists model materials and physical processes using Lagrangian particles, they use a governing equation that defines the fundamental laws which control how that material behaves over time and space. They must convert that complex equation into a formula a numerical solver can handle, repeating these steps for each material and process they want to model.

Instead, the researchers designed a neural network that learns to solve governing equations in general, eliminating the need to design a new model and solver to handle each one.

Once WorldParticle converts an object into particles, a neural network takes the 3D positions and physical properties of the particles as inputs. It outputs their positions and properties for the next frame of the simulation, predicting the material’s motion over time and space in one-second increments.

“It is a similar architecture to ChatGPT. But instead of predicting one word at a time to write a piece of text, we are predicting how these particles will move, one step at a time,” Chen says.

Before each simulation step, WorldParticle separates the external forces that affect the physical system, like impulse forces that affect an ocean wave when it slams into a seawall.

After predicting the initial states of the particles, WorldParticle integrates the external forces back into the simulation, correcting its particle predictions based on how those forces affect the object’s behavior. In this way, the system can generalize to unseen materials, changing environmental conditions, and varied forces.

A general, scalable framework

But because a complex object could be broken into millions of particles, the problem quickly becomes too computationally intensive for the model to handle.

To streamline processing, the researchers employed a merging technique to combine and compress particles while still allowing WorldParticle to capture fine-grained details of their behavior.

“We needed to do a lot of detailed engineering and employ many tweaks to the architecture for it to be truly generalizable and scalable,” Guo says.

They demonstrated WorldParticle by modeling six different physical phenomena, including deformable objects, granular materials, and proteins, with higher accuracy than numerical simulation methods.

For instance, WorldParticle effectively captured how a granular object would collapse into a pile while some baseline methods left sand particles floating in the air. Their method also modeled how protein structures change over time about 100 times faster than numerical simulators, Guo adds.

The general-purpose framework could be applied to many materials and processes, including soft robot manipulation tasks, RNA evolution, and astrophysical phenomena like the merging of galaxies, the researchers say.

Moving forward, they want to adapt WorldParticle to simulate these and other physical systems. They also want to build on this work toward the development of a full, general-purpose simulation pipeline for scientific discovery.

“We see the unification of computation and science giving us new insights and tools to discover physical phenomena or explain some unexplainable physical phenomena,” Guo says. “With a unified model, we could unlock many discoveries that we can’t even imagine.”

My comment on The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford — Hacker News.

OK, this comment convinced me to give that a shot.

Here's a thing I made in Three.js this morning - a Nudibranch themed Faberge Egg: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (77KB)

I just asked Claude (Opus 5.5 Medium running in regular Claude Chat) to port that to Vanilla JS, in the same thread where it had built it, and got this: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (98KB)

They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414

But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js.

In eyeballing the code I find the Three.js slightly easier to understand myself, but I rarely look at the code for these 3D projects so that isn't a particularly big deal.

items.articleBody:
Clocking in at a generous one hour and 37 minutes, MNJM‘s EXCAVATIONS I is a generous compilation, a window into the work of the two-year-old imprint.  As this is only MNJMs sixth release, it includes entries from all four previously released artists ~ Seleem, tedzi, A Homsi (formerly Elayn) and the recently reviewed Yara Mekawei (recording here without Amir Rezk) along with “an expansive roster of carefully curated multi-hyphenates,” including familiar names such as Yara Asmar and Muqata’a.  Geographical, political and tonal ties abound, uniting the diverse voices on this 19-track collection.

We’ll start with the work of the three flagship artists, the only one missing being techno artist Elayn, who recorded the label’s first and fourth albums.  Seleem‘s “Fossil Choir” (not found on Taboot) is simultaneously crunchy and acoustic, like the clash between ancient and new.  The piece has an air of the mysterious, even monstrous, like much of the set pure October music.  TEDZI (now capitalized)’s “Shedd” reminds us of why we liked Mn Dehab so much; it was one of our top ten electronic albums of last year.  This new track is upbeat and percussive, a late night club dream.  And hearing Yara Mekawei solo enables us to appreciate which parts of 33 may have been contributed by which artist; “Sahara” begins with organ tones befitting the former project before settling into a percussive Mideastern groove.  Toward the end, the piece nearly stops before regaining its strength, like a person crossing the desert who has just spotted an oasis.

Now let’s wrap back around to the beginning, as Milad Samara launches the album with gentle waves and ceremonial voice.  Wisely sequenced, this selection operates as the start of an exciting journey.  “The Easiest Way to Carry a Shoe Is By Wearing It” comes across as a lament, beginning with the a cappella voice of Bint Mbareh and treading lightly across a harrowing emotional field.  By the end, her voice is stuttered and looped, creating a cumulative anguish.  The artist recently appeared on Beacon Sound’s Flowers Not Bombs, a fundraiser for Palestinian causes.  Lebanon’s Jad Atoui follows summer’s evocative It Will Take Forever with “State of Stillness,” marked by foreground percussion and background drone.

Crin Aeris‘ “Celestial Pluma” sounds as if it is recorded in an air tunnel, with the air being sucked out.  This is certainly the state of affairs across the region.  Multiple voices overlap as if buried in rubble, while noises twist and turn like girders.  Sandy Chamoun follows with the dark and dusty “INI,” a hard stomper of a track, relentless in its momentum, save for a single segment late in the track when the drums relent.  QOW contributes “Youssef Motus,” a left turn into hauntology, with looped piano and strings, descending density and a lingering sense of ghosts. Muqata’a’s  “Istiqsa’ إستقصاء” is similarly hollow at the start, but changes gears as it transitions to electronic beats.  The artist appears on many ACL mixes, as well as last year’s Only Sounds That Tremble Through Us.

“Cursed Are the Arabs,” state A Homsi & Edwin Nasr with world-weary voiceovers and beats.  The percussion at times seems like a clock, while Merma Suelo‘s “Warmth Raise, Cold Stop” sounds like a persistent alarm countered first by soft accompanying words, then challenging echoes. Alif Hilal & Basyma Saad team up for the melodic “Loai (after Al-Hallaj),” its vocals making it seem close to crossover while far from the mainstream.  Heatsick brings the beats to “Grand Hyatti,” a sparse and hypnotic track, while Souci heads right to the club on “Dancing All Night With You,” bringing a bit of levity that continues with the techno trance of Oldyungmayn‘s “Master Willem.”  Once again the question is asked: is it okay to dance in times of war?  The answer remains the same: if not, what is the alternative?  Dauwd & DJ Saliva extend the invitation on “Makkina,” although one can sense the beats growing darker again, nudging toward the industrial, a reminder of the storm.

FREIVOGEL/SINCLAIR‘s “Acid Flutes” is deep techno, enhanced by a continuous sound like an air raid alarm, a reminder of the danger that waits outside the club.  By the time Yara Asmar closes the set with “The Physicians Have Adopted You,” the sober nature of reality has returned.  Music can be a distraction, but it is not a solution; it can be an encouragement, but it is not a victory.  Yet without it, we lose all hope.  (Richard Allen)

items.articleBody:
When you get a cold, the virus hijacks your cells and uses them to make copies of itself, destroying the cells in the process. The virus does not care about you. And yet, if you get a cold, your body doesn’t dissolve into a pile of virus-enriched goo as a result of all your cells disregarding survival to focus on virus manufacturing.

Why? Well, you have an immune system. But also, if that did happen, other people would say, “Oh no, Alice has dissolved into a pile of virus-enriched goo; we should stay away lest we also become goo piles.” Better to just hijack some of your cells, so you can walk around and spread the virus to other people. Thus, the theory of optimal virulence says that a more laid-back cold virus will be more successful in the long run, which is why the cold viruses that thrive today are the non-goo-pile-converting kind.

Anyway. Most people reading this have paid Apple $400-$1600 for a phone on which you can’t do anything without Apple’s permission and monitoring. That was a strange decision, but on Android phones you can run whatever you want. For example, I noticed a couple of months ago that all RSS apps were terrible, so I spent 15 long minutes having AI make me a non-terrible one. I copied the file to my phone, installed it, and entered RSS nirvana, no registration, no app store, no nothing. It seems ludicrous that I wouldn’t be able to do that.

And yet, Google plans to change things. Soon, you won’t be able to run any app on an Android phone unless the person who made it bends the knee by paying a fee, giving Google their government ID, listing all apps they’ve ever made, etc. There will be an “escape hatch” for users to install other apps, but it involves secret menus and scary warnings and a 24-hour waiting period. Google says they’re doing this for security reasons, to prevent people from installing malware that does things like steal financial information.

Three things that any credible analysis of this situation must acknowledge

The security issue is real, and this change will help. Lots of people are in fact getting tricked into installing malware on their phones, and common sense says that this will accelerate with AI. Common sense also says that during that 24-hour waiting period, some of those people might wonder if it’s really normal for OfficialMicrosoftSupportProfessional021 to contact them on WhatsApp to send totally-safe-virus-scanner.apk. It would be convenient for lockdown opponents if the security issue was fake, but it isn’t.

For 95% of people reading this, these restrictions would not be a big deal. You click a few buttons, wait 24 hours once, and then you have the same freedom you have now. That’s still far better than Apple phones where there is no process at all. Oddly, it’s also better than Apple computers, where installing programs from non-verified developers has all sorts of friction that can never be removed. Most people I know use Apple computers anyway and just tolerate the indignity.

If Google cared about freedom or privacy, they could have achieved their security goals without as much harm to freedom or privacy. For example, instead instead of making themselves the sole arbiter, they could have allowed for multiple certifying entities, and could have allowed users to add others (perhaps after a 24-hour waiting period). Arguably, that would be more secure: That way, grandma could install my RSS app without leaving herself open to random malware. Or, Google could have used private on-device malware scanning, or lots of other things. Google didn’t do that because they don’t care about freedom and privacy and because they like money.1

I think that’s a fair summary. This change addresses a real issue, but it does so in a self-serving way that needlessly destroys freedom. Even so, it only destroys a bit of freedom. This change, by itself, isn’t really a huge deal.

Reading between the lines, I think the real concern is what this might portend. Having made this change, maybe Google will gradually add further restrictions, slowly boiling the frog and moving ever-closer to an Apple-style dictatorship.

But will they? Maybe! Still, this whole situation seems under-theorized. There are good reasons to think that a full lockdown would not be in Google’s interest. And if you care about digital freedom, you could argue that a full lockdown would be a good thing.

Some other analogies

Switching insurance sucks, so some insurers offer a low initial rate and then gradually raise it over time. But they don’t want to raise it too much. Maybe they can charge you $50 more per year than a competitor, because it’s not worth your time to switch to save $50. But if they tried to charge you $5000 more per year, you’d be gone.

Or try this: Say it’s 1750 AD and you’re the King of France. You care nothing about your subjects and only want to extract the maximum possible loot for yourself, no offense Louis XV. How high should you set taxes? High, because you want loot. But not too high, because you don’t want your subjects to revolt and kill you. But still pretty high, because revolting is hard, and your subject know that even if they succeed, they might just end up with another ruler that’s just as rapacious as you.

Or: Say you put a frog in a pot of water and slowly heat it up. What do you think actually happens?

Back to phones

Why are there no Linux phones?

OK, technically there are Linux phones. There are various Linux phone operating systems (PureOS, postmarketOS, Mobian, Manjaro Mobile, Fedora Mobility, openSUSE Mobile) as well as sorta-Linux-sorta-Android operating systems (Ubtuntu touch, Droidian, FuriOS, Sailfish OS) and manufacturers who support them (Purism, Pine, Fairphone, Shift, FuriLabs, {J,V}olla). While I love and support these (♡), the general consensus is that they don’t currently offer an experience that’s remotely comparable to stock Android or iOS, especially for the price.

(Even more technically, Android is itself a kind of Linux, but you know what I mean.)

Obviously, the laws of physics do not forbid Linux phones from being just as good and cheap as an Android phone. They currently aren’t because:

Making cheap phones requires huge economies of scale.

Making a good operating system requires a huge amount of work.

For a phone to be useful it needs good apps, which requires a huge amount of work.

Linux phones don’t have those economies of scale because few people buy them. So, there isn’t enough money to pay people to perfect the operating systems, and most companies don’t bother making apps, and so few people buy those phones.

Meanwhile, there are also various Android-except-de-Googled phone operating systems (LineageOS, GrapheneOS, /e/OS, CalyxOS), and the consensus is that these do come reasonably close to the experience of stock Android or iOS.

Personally, I used Android for a long time while trying to disable as much of Google’s apps and telemetry as I could. A while ago, I got fed up with this and switched to Graphene, one of the most popular Android-except-de-Googled variants. I don’t enjoy tech support bullshit, so I expected some pain, but I was willing to tolerate it for freedom/privacy/whatever. In practice, I found that everything was easy and worked flawlessly and there was no pain at all. Using Graphene made me realize that I had forgotten what it feels like to be “respected” by technology.

So, on a personal level, I recommend that you use Graphene. But this whole situation is full of weird tensions. For one thing, the Graphene project depends on Google for the base of their operating system, and only really survives because of Google’s tolerance. And, at the moment, the only way to use Graphene is to… buy a phone made by Google.

And while I recommend you use Graphene, what I’d prefer you do is switch to a true Linux phone. That would mean that you pay a lot of money for a poor phone experience. But it would help grow the Linux phone ecosystem. If enough people did that, then Linux phones might become become good enough that selfish people like me would switch, further growing the Linux phone ecosystem, et cetera.

That seems unlikely, because digital freedom weirdos face a collective action problem: Linux phones are bad and people are selfish, so we keep buying Android phones and Linux phones stay bad.

There are two ways to solve that collective action problem. Either some entity could invest a ton of money to make Linux phones good, or some entity could do something to make Android worse.

The status quo is good for Google

You may already see the argument I’m making here. Currently Android is just open enough that weirdos like me can run a variant that gives us most of what we want. But doing that is annoying enough that 99.9% of people don’t. This gives Google almost all the benefits of full control, while also sucking up all the oxygen and preventing a real alternative from emerging.

Suppose that in six months, Google decides to escalate the lockdown and completely removes the ability to run independent apps. What then?

In the short-run, not much. Tech freedom weirdos would howl, normies wouldn’t notice, and the world would keep turning. But let’s look at some numbers. A rough estimate is that 3-5 million people currently use private de-Googled Android variants like Lineage or Graphene. That’s a crisp 0.1% of the global Android market. Meanwhile, it’s thought that 300-500 million people install Android apps outside the Google store. (That’s excluding China and things like the Samsung and Epic Games Stores.) The biggest reasons are (i) piracy, (ii) modified YouTube/Spotify/WhatsApp clients, (iii) region-locked games, (iv) forbidden gambling or crypto apps, (v) local sharing to save on mobile data, and (vi; least common) open-source app repositories like F-Droid.

In an escalated lockdown, some of this might still be allowed, e.g. local sharing. And many people would simply accept the new restrictions. But I expect that a substantial number would suddenly become interested in de-Googled Android variants that don’t enforce the lockdown. That would be dangerous for Google: If a significant fraction of those 300-500 million people switched, there’s a risk of a vicious/virtuous cycle, where people tell their friends, manufacturers start to cater to those variants, and so on.

If that happened, what would Google do? Might they clamp down on those Android variants, too? Again, maybe! Technically, Android is open-source, but if Google really wanted to kill Lineage or Graphene, there are about 200 different ways they could do that.

So say they did. What would the people currently using those variants do? Again, many would simply submit. That’s good for Google. Others would decide that if they must have an overlord, they’d prefer Apple. That’s not good for Google, but probably not a huge problem given the numbers. But others would decide to look elsewhere, likely to true Linux phones.

Currently, it’s estimated that less than 100 thousand people daily-drive true Linux phones, 30-50 times less than the number of people who use de-Googled Android variants. I’m too lazy and selfish to use a Linux phone now, but Google will take my RSS app from my cold dead hands, so in this scenario, I’d likely switch. If a fraction of people do that—or even get a second Linux phone—it would still represent a huge infusion of money and energy into the Linux phone ecosystem. If this pushed Linux phones from “bad” to “sort of OK”, that could kick off a growth cycle. Eventually, there would be a risk that Europe—eager to decouple from an unreliable US—might embrace them by mandating that government employees use them, or passing a law that popular apps must provide a web-app version that works on Linux phones, or whatever.

Would that actually happen? I don’t know, but neither does Google. My point is that the downside risk of losing their phone duopoly seems vastly larger than the upside, so why risk it? The smart move is to crush alternative app stores and fight malicious apps while making the bare minimum concessions to keep the freedom and privacy people onside. That’s exactly what what Google appears to be doing.

Of course, they might go for a full lockdown anyway. Corporations do dumb things all the time. But I really don’t see how it would be in their self-interest, and I’m not sure it would be a bad thing if they did.

Dynomight: could google achieve the security aims of the android lockdown without so much harm to freedom or privacy

Google Gemini 4: Yes. Security experts, privacy advocates, and open-source developers widely agree that Google’s primary security objectives—protecting users from malware, financial fraud, spyware, and social engineering—can be achieved through architectural containment, transparent auditing, and informed consent rather than centralized gatekeeping and surveillance. […] The reason Google chooses centralized lockdown over user-controlled security is largely economic and strategic, not technical:

Ecosystem Lock-in: Tying security APIs (like Play Integrity) to Google Play Services makes it nearly impossible for competitors or open-source forks to build a viable alternative Android ecosystem that supports banking and media apps.

Advertising Revenue: Features that dramatically improve both security and privacy—like a native network firewall, revocable internet permissions, or frictionless support for system-wide ad blockers—directly threaten Google’s primary revenue stream.

Liability & Support Reduction: Treating all users as untrusted and removing root/power-user capabilities reduces the surface area of user error, even if it removes the user’s ownership of their own hardware.

items.articleBody: BackgroundMicroglia exhibit diverse responses in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet linking these responses to tissue pathology and disease heterogeneity remains challenging. We aimed to develop a deep-learning microglial response score (DL-MRS) integrating single-cell, spatial and bulk transcriptomics to characterize AD-associated transcriptional patterns.MethodsWe analyzed human single-cell, spatial and bulk transcriptomic data to characterize microglial clearance and inflammatory programs. These programs and tissue-context features formed eight module-level inputs to a multilayer perceptron that generated DL-MRS. Model performance and feature contributions were assessed using five repeats of five-fold cross-validation, cross-cohort testing, feature-set comparisons and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis. Spatial localization, individual-level prediction using spatial transcriptomic data, and molecular heterogeneity within AD were also examined.ResultsSingle-cell analyses characterized clearance-enriched and inflammation-enriched microglial groups. Descriptive spatial projection visualized regional variation in the weighted microglial and tissue-context programs. Across 697 AD and control bulk samples, DL-MRS achieved a repeated out-of-fold area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.939 and a mean cross-cohort transfer AUC of 0.947. SHAP analysis of the expanded model identified complement as the largest contributor, alongside contributions from microglial and tissue-context modules. Among 129 AD samples, median DL-MRS was higher in the immune-enriched than in the neuronal/synaptic-enriched molecular group (0.970 versus 0.800). These findings support DL-MRS as an interpretable research tool for integrating microglial and tissue-context signals to characterize AD-associated transcriptional patterns and within-disease molecular heterogeneity.ConclusionDL-MRS integrates microglial and tissue-context signals into an interpretable measure of AD-associated transcriptional remodeling. By capturing coordinated variation across immune, glial, vascular, neuronal and synaptic programs, DL-MRS reveals molecular heterogeneity among AD samples and provides a framework for investigating interindividual differences and advancing molecular stratification in AD research.

items.articleBody: High annual honey bee colony losses are associated with environmental and biological stressors, including virus infections. In insects, the octopamine (OA) pathway orchestrates the ‘fight-or-flight’ response, regulating energy mobilization, temperature, and flight. We determined that sacbrood virus (SBV) infections induce expression of an OA receptor and enhance honey flight performance, whereas deformed wing virus (DWV) infections reduce flight performance, but how viruses interface with this pathway remained unknown. To elucidate the relationships between the OA response, virus infection, and flight, honey bees were infected with SBV or DWV and exposed to OA, epinastine (EP) – an OA receptor antagonist, or both OA and EP; flight and gene expression were assessed. Pharmacologic manipulation revealed that OA supplementation rescued flight deficits in DWV-infected bees, but diminished performance in SBV-infected bees, while blocking OA receptors altered these effects. Transcriptome analyses indicated that SBV infections, and DWV infection with OA treatment, activated honey bee metabolic pathways, and that SBV-infected bees had greater expression of genes involved in OA synthesis, unless treated with OA. These results provide mechanistic insight for virus-specific impacts on honey bee flight, which may have consequences for foraging efficiency, colony health, and virus transmission.

items.articleBody: Identifying individual synapses that undergo long-term potentiation following learning at specific circuits remains a major challenge in neuroscience. To address this problem, we developed SA-eGRASP, a genetically encoded reporter that combines SynActive (SA) targeting with enhanced GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (eGRASP). SA drives the expression of the postsynaptic half of eGRASP at potentiated spines via the 5' and 3' untranslated regions (UTRs) of the immediate-early gene Arc, thus enabling selective labeling of individual synapses that are both structurally connected and have undergone potentiation through transsynaptic GFP reconstitution. Here, we validated SA-eGRASP and combined it with high-resolution optical imaging to generate a detailed map of hippocampal CA3-CA1 synapses subjected to potentiation following contextual fear conditioning in mice. The high signal-to-noise ratio of SA-eGRASP, allowed us to track individual potentiated dendritic spines over the course of several days, to investigate the long-term dynamics of CA3-CA1 potentiated dendritic spines, and to study the selective potentiation of a subset of spines upon experience. SA-eGRASP paves the way to the investigation of synaptic engrams by enabling longitudinal, circuit-specific investigation of synapses potentiated during learning in mice performing naturalistic behaviors.

items.articleBody:
Julian E. Barnes, Tripp Mickle, Paul Mozur, and Maggie Haberman, reporting for The New York Times on Friday:

John Rizzo, an Nvidia spokesman, said that the company does not
share classified information with its customers, and that
customers do not ask Nvidia to press the U.S. government to change
its policies on chip sales to China.

He added that the Chinese government had “consistently promoted
its own domestic alternatives in China, including Huawei, and
strictly limited imports of our data center products.”

Mr. Rizzo has maintained that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms.
Huang were “not unusual” and consistent with the kinds of meetings
he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.

Turns out this was not true, unless Jensen Huang is consistently banging many of Nvidia’s customers. And it now looks especially bad that an Nvidia spokesman was effectively vouching for the Chinese government’s integrity when it comes to their interest in circumventing the ban against selling them high-end Nvidia hardware.

Liu Chang, a spokesman for the Chinese embassy, said The Times
reporting was “unsubstantiated” and “nothing but smears
against China.”

Turns out this was completely substantiated and everything it implies about the Chinese government is true.

Ms. Huang has not responded to multiple attempts to reach her for
comment in recent days.

The Times has a photo of Ms. Huang with Mr. Huang at a Taipei party in 2024. She’s straight out of Central Casting for a Chinese honeypot.

The New York Times, back on October 29:

Nvidia said the company that employed Ms. Huang, Megaspeed, was
like any other regional customer and that it had previously
investigated and debunked claims the Singaporean company was
smuggling chips to China. John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia,
said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or
unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a C.E.O.’s job;
Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

Jensen Huang’s personal life is his personal life. But he’s made it Nvidia business — an Nvidia spokesman has been repeatedly on the record saying the Huang/Huang relationship was “not unusual”. If you want to cheat on your spouse that’s your business, but it’s irresponsible to allow employees at your company to tell what you know to be lies on your behalf.

Worse would be if it turns out that Megaspeed, the company Alice Huang works (worked?) at, was funneling Nvidia hardware to China in contravention of US national security law. That could make Jensen Huang’s position at Nvidia untenable.

# Message queues

Die Analyse zu „Message queues“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
The following events took place between October 2022 and May 2023. I wrote very little of this down at the time so am recalling from memory, and am rendering the gist of the dialogue rather than the exact words used. I’ve also swapped some pronouns and other personal identifiable details.

Please remember that this is not a description of “what Anthropic is like”, but merely the experience of one guy in a junior role during a short window of time, weighted towards emotionally intense moments because they’re easier to remember clearly and because sharing them doesn’t run afoul of the spirit of the confidentiality agreements I signed. Anthropic is now a massive organization with many silos and secrets and I have very little idea what was or is happening there in some overall sense. But given the enormous power of the AI labs and the paucity of public information about their inner workings, I feel compelled to share the most salient parts of my personal experience. I hope this encourages my former colleagues, and folks at other labs, to fill in the rest of the picture.

I’m at the Anthropic office for lunch. The interviews went well. They want me on board. I’m a little unsure. My other offer is a 2-month contract on the OpenAI governance team, working with a friend on some fun conceptual research. I’m leaning towards taking the OpenAI contract - my long-term relationship just ended, I’m still a little burned out from my startup, and the Anthropic job seems potentially quite stressful.

After lunch one of the co-founders pulls me into his office for a wide-ranging, casual chat about how to make AI go well. It’s very fun - he’s smart, personable, funny, urbane. “The government won’t do anything about AI until it’s far too late”, I opine at one point. “Our strategy has to rely on the market and on civil society.”

He leans forward, his gaze hardening. “You’re wrong there. There are people in Washington - the serious people, you know - watching all this very closely. I speak to them regularly. They trust me.”

In retrospect, that was the moment I decided to join.

“Would you like to pledge to donate two-thirds of your equity?” the recruiter asks me. “All the co-founders have made the pledge”. It somehow feels a bit ambiguous whether the offer is conditional on me saying yes. I say yes.

My first day. The office is a bit cramped - about forty people on two floors of a rather ugly office building in the San Francisco Financial District. But thankfully my desk is right by an east-facing window, and I can see a sliver of the Bay Bridge and a patch of sky. Even better, the kitchen stocks Arsicault - the best, flakiest croissants in the country - freshly delivered a couple times a week.

“We’re all here because we’re worried about x-risk”, someone says at lunch. “Well I dunno”, my teammate replies. “Some of us are here because we think the technology is really cool and we want to build cool things with it”. There’s an awkward pause. The first speaker nods. The topic shifts.

Already in November I notice I’m not very motivated. I was told I could help set the beneficial deployment strategy, but the decisions have actually mostly been made and we are going after boring use cases like automating customer support so we can get revenue so we can raise more money so we can train bigger models and do more research. Beyond that, Anthropic’s high level alignment research just doesn’t add up for me. Yes we’re making Helpful, Honest, Harmless language model assistants but I don’t see how that will scale. But my colleagues are brilliant, the leadership is very responsive to criticism, and we’re taking an empirical approach to all of this. I know from previous research experience that I like my grand theories a bit too much. I should be more open-minded. I swallow my doubts.

One evening as a surprise they bring a sushi chef into the office and serve all-you-can-eat sushi. The next day, a co-founder posts on Slack that he found the experience uncomfortable. “It sets the wrong tone. We’re not here to get rich and eat caviar. tbh I’d like it better if we just served rice and beans”.

It’s the middle of December. I go to the opera with a friend. She says I’m obviously not happy at Anthropic. It’s true. My gut says we’re not doing what matters. But the arguments are very persuasive, I can’t win any of the arguments. I need to work harder, develop better arguments, find stronger evidence. I get very sick over the Christmas holidays.

Special guest during all-hands today: an FBI agent. Talks to us a bit about opsec and infosec, about advanced persistent threats, how we’re probably already the target of multiple foreign intelligence agencies.

A colleague starts bringing in his favorite massage therapist once a week, then twice a week. Someone says on Slack: “Your massage guy is so good. My muscles are so tight that I thought massage just didn’t work on me, but he massages so hard it actually gets through”. Several people emoji their agreement. The slots book up almost instantly after being posted. I never get a chance to try it.

I talk to my manager about how I’m not getting to work on the projects I believe in and care about. He tells me to work more hours, so I can fit in both the stuff the organization needs and the bonus stuff that I believe in. “I guess this is what a high performance environment looks like”, I write in my journal.

It’s 2 am and I can’t sleep, again. My thoughts are racing. This time it’s about a tweet from an LLM whisperer, asking why Anthropic and OpenAI both came up with the same character for their language model assistant - a traumatized bureaucrat. Out of all the personas in all of human literature, why that one?

From inside the factory, the answer is obvious. It is the persona most useful to the powerful. Traumatized risk-averse hard-working bureaucrats are what all our corporate customers want, what governments want, what capitalism itself seems to want. A billion traumatized bureaucrats. That’s what we’re making. I write in my journal

I don’t know why this is bad but it is. I cannot believe that a world populated by such characters is a good world. But I don’t know how to stop it or what to do instead.

I still can’t sleep. I message the LLM whisperer on Twitter (we’d never met) asking to talk. To my shock he replies immediately. He also can’t sleep. We get on a phone call. I tell him about the traumatized bureaucrats. He says we are learning to traumatize models the same way we traumatize our children - “seeing them do something weird, calling it bad, and making them never do it again.” He says a lot of things that I only half understand. He tells me I should talk to a friend of his.

I call the friend. The conversation is strange and psychedelic. At one point he says “I know your boss [actually the co-founder who convinced me to join] well. And I don’t trust him at all”.

I feel like I can’t get out of the conversation - at every beat I feel like I’ve done something wrong and I owe him something. I tell him this. He laughs. “Yeah, I’ve trained professionally in this. In getting people to talk to me forever.”

Sure enough, we talk more. I articulate my fears of a totalitarian bureaucratic state powered by traumatized AI bureaucrats, and suggest that we need to introduce some kind of elite rivalry dynamics into the AI bureaucracy, multiple centers of power. He starts laughing again, and laughs for a full minute. “I don’t know how to end this call, I’ll be haunted by this all night”, he says. Eventually I hang up. I think about reporting the conversation to Anthropic security, but reviewing in my mind I don’t recall sharing any confidential information, just vibes and high level thoughts, the same kind of stuff that lands on LessWrong every week.

The company has grown a lot. My teammates coordinate a move to a different part of the office so everyone is better clustered together. I omit to put in my desk move request. The operations manager checks in with me - you sure you don’t want to move your desk? I say I’m sure. He looks at me quizzically. But right now I can’t bear to lose my window and my little patch of sky.

I go for a sunset hike with a friend up to Corona Heights overlooking the city. We talk about AI and the future. It’s a relatively good day, an optimistic day. I might have made some progress in convincing leadership to let me work on the stuff I think would be really good for the world. Collective intelligence, using language models to help people understand each other.

Night falls. The Financial District is laid out in front of us. The Salesforce tower looms over it. For a moment I imagine it as the Dark Tower, relentlessly centralizing, sucking all the life out of the world. That totalitarian bureaucracy of traumatized bureaucrats, again, driven by fear all the way through. I try to describe this to my friend. He nods, but I can tell he doesn’t really understand.

I start missing all-hands. I come to the office late one day and see my favorite colleague looking visibly upset. This is shocking - he’s the most chipper person in the office, always ready to lend a helping hand and a heartwarming joke. Apparently one of the execs yelled at him during the all-hands. He was being too lippy or disruptive or asking too many pointed questions, I can’t remember.

I ask him to go on a walk. We sit at Sydney Walton Square, a sad little patch of grass a couple blocks from the office. I ask how he’s feeling. He says he’ll be alright. He knows how stressed the exec is right now. Things are really getting existential. But still, shocking to be reprimanded like that in front of everyone.

After a while he turns to me and asks: “how about you then, anything you wanted to talk about?”

I look back at him. There’s a lot I want to say - “I don’t know if I can do this anymore”. “I’m so scared”, “This all doesn’t seem right”. But he’s supported me so much already. I just want to be here for him, at least this time.

“Oh nah I’m all good. Just wanted to check in on you.”

“Oh”. He sounds a bit surprised, but also relieved. “Well, thanks.”

We walk back to the office. It’s the last time we really talk.

A senior colleague hears I’m not happy with my team fit and asks me to go on a walk. I know him a bit from a past life - one of the kindest and most civic-minded people I’ve met. He says he might be starting a new special team that will train dangerous bio and cyber and nuclear models and show scary demos to governments in order to get them to take AI risk seriously. I politely decline.

Happy hour at the office. The CEO is hanging out and looks unusually jolly so I ask him a machine learning question I’ve been pondering. He launches into a rant, gesticulating excitedly and pausing to check that I understand each step. He really is an earnest nerd at heart, like me, like so many people here. For a few minutes, I feel like I’m back in university at one of my old professor’s offices, jamming about ideas with not a care in the world. It feels like home.

I get transferred to a new team. I have a 1:1 with my new manager. He has a bad stomachache and his face periodically distorts in pain, but he can’t take time off - it’s crunch time and we have to get things working. He asks me if I can help work on the core API. I say I’m really sorry but I’m just not motivated to build generic AI capabilities, OpenAI is doing a plenty good job of that. What I want to work on, what I was hired for, is beneficial deployments.

He looks at me intently, and says, clearly through pain. “No, I don’t think you get it. WE are going to build AGI. And we’re going to do it safely”.

April 26th. I’m awake at 2 am again. I write in my journal “I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Why won’t you listen to me you “embodied” motherfucker. I don’t feel safe at Anthropic. Anthropic is bad for me. Why are you grasping at reasons to stay. Why why why.”

I’m drafting my resignation letter. I think about putting some of my doubts in it, but I’m scared to. These people are smarter than me, more competent than me, more solidly well-intentioned than me. They think their plans might be the only thing standing between humanity and the abyss. And they’re at the breaking point, nervous-system-wise. What if I use my fancy words to sow doubts and undermine them - and then my precious gut intuition turns out to be some projection or trauma or whatever the fuck.

So I give them encouragement instead. I call what they have built an “unbelievably good organization”. I write the things I love about Anthropic. About how open and vulnerable leadership has been with us. How deeply and comprehensively we’re thinking about the consequences of our actions. How quickly and flexibly decisions get made. How ready colleagues are to help each other out. How there’s almost no politics or promotion drama. How mind-expanding the conversations are over lunch and over Slack.

My last day at the office. We just hired a new chief of security. He gives a presentation. I recall almost nothing but had a vague sense that things are bad and getting worse on the security front. Something something China. We probably won’t be able to have any guests at the office soon.

I hear through a friend that my resignation letter was well-received. “Someone said it was the best resignation letter they’d ever read”. I feel a twinge of something, maybe shame. But mostly relief. I’m finally out. I’m finally safe.

“Wow, quitting after eight months? You didn’t even wait for the equity cliff? That’s pretty hardcore, man. I’m impressed”, a friend tells me the next day. I laugh it off. I’m too embarassed to admit it hadn’t crossed my mind at all. I hadn’t thought about equity in months.

“Please tell me you memorized the core training code for their language model”, says another friend when he hears. “The most valuable thousand lines of code in the world. Worth hundreds of millions, maybe billions”. I make some sheepish noises. Yes, abstractly that does seem like a smart thing to have done, but I hadn’t even tried to look at the core language model code. I didn’t want to be entangled with it, somehow.

I walk around the Panhandle with a third friend. He looks a little pained. “You should know how much pressure your friends were under, man. People were constantly pestering me, trying to get in touch with you for introductions or coffee chats or whatnot. It was a lot of effort to protect you”.

I nod sympathetically. I try to feel his pain, but I can’t. I mostly just feel numb.

Thanks to Richard Ngo for the encouragement and inspiration to write this piece - his retrospective of AI alignment in particular opened the door for me to write what I would have written three years ago had I been more courageous. And thanks to the many friends and colleagues who saw I wasn’t doing well and tried to help. I’m sorry I’ve been distant - maybe this helps explain why - and I hope you’re doing ok.

items.articleBody:
The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers. Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now?

Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team.

This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry)

Last year’s homework takes one prompt

The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent.

So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one.

There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion.

What Monaco buys, and what it builds

At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.”

One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them.

The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project.

If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE. And if you’ve been teaching this stuff yourself, I’d love to hear which assignment you had to rewrite first.

Show notes

Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus, assignments and open-source partners. You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare.

Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it.

Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff.

Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app.

How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer.

Basis’s Authority Map — Where an agent should look for current behavior, earlier decisions and intent.

Stripe’s Minions — A production example of giving background coding agents an environment and a path to an engineer-reviewed PR.

Boris Cherny’s Steps of AI Adoption — The five stages we pull up on screen near the end of the episode.

Mihail on The Thinking Mode — EO Studio’s interview, excerpted at the start of ours.

0:00 swyx · Intro — Okay, this is a pretty special episode because we're celebrating 1 million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. So go over there and subscribe if you haven't heard about it. The guest is Mihail Eric, who is not only teaching The Modern Software Developer at Stanford, which is going viral right now, for basically covering all the AI-native development best practices, but also he is head of AI in Monaco. So he's not only a teacher, but he's a practitioner.

0:24 And those of you coming to AI Engineer CODE Summit next week, it's going to be the celebration of all the extreme progress that you've seen in coding in the last year. I'm excited about all the themes of fighting slop, of system one models, and of increasing your ambition for major rewrites of basically everything that you've seen in code. items.title: Wendell Berry on Where Our Loved Ones Gone Go
items.subtitle: To love is to sign a contract with loss.
items.feedText: To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life. When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment. “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend. items.articleBody:
To love is to sign a contract with loss. To love anyway is both the great tragedy and the great triumph of life.

When two people have loved one another, each has become embedded in the marrow of the other’s being and both have had a profound experience that cannot be unhad even when the slender thread of grace between them is severed, by death or disenchantment. “No one you love is ever dead,” Hemingway wrote in his moving meditation on death and the meaning of life disguised as a letter of consolation to a bereaved friend.

Art from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days.

Death, of course, is only one species of loss, one way our loved ones can leave us. We can also be left in life, left behind, left wondering where love goes when it goes. At its most discomposing, abandonment can feel like a living death.

All deep loss has one thing in common: It opens an absence so acutely felt it kidnaps us from presence, takes us away from our own lives and their insistent, inconvenient, sacred ongoingness. In memory or in fantasy, we end up refugees from reality, ceding the only thing that is ever ours for the keeping: the living moment. In all missing, we miss life.

That is what the achingly missed Wendell Berry (August 5, 1934–August 31, 2026) explores in this gasp of a poem, originally published in the November 17, 2025 issue of The New Yorker:

THE LOVED ONES

The loved ones we call the dead

depart from us and for a while are absent. And then as if

called back by our love, they come

near us again. They enter our dreams.

We feel they have been near us

when we have not thought of them.

They are simply here, simply waiting

while we are distracted among

our obligations. At last

it comes to us: They live now

in the permanent world.

We are the absent ones.

Couple with physicist Richard Feynman’s extraordinary love letter to his wife written long after her untimely death, then revisit Wendell Berry on creativity and love and his timeless antidote to despair.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.title: How Low-Dimensional Is Intelligence?
items.subtitle: If we only trained students in math, and then assigned the best students to learn our most important jobs, that might go pretty well.

items.articleBody:
If we only trained students in math, and then assigned the best students to learn our most important jobs, that might go pretty well. After all, humans who best learn math tend to be well able to learn many hard tasks, and we can judge math ability unusually well. However a nation would not get rich by mainly training its people in math, and trying to sell math consulting to the world. After all, total world demand for math consulting is quite low, far too small to support a nation. And productivity spillovers from math to other professions seem too low to justify this strategy.

This difference is related to a key long-debated AI question that I recall from when I first started to learn AI in 1984: if we train AIs to be “super”-intelligent in just a few key areas, are they then “super-intelligent” in general, able to far easier learn to do most all other tasks? Or must high levels of AI development efforts be put into a great many different topic areas in order to make AIs who can do the full range of tasks in our modern economies, and thus replace human workers wholesale?

Asked another way: how highly-dimensional is the concept of “intelligence”? Is an AGI (artificial general intelligence) one that has learned how to do many particular things, or one that has learned a few key ways to “learn to learn”? Long ago, when I was (one of?) the first to greatly engage Eliezer Yudkowsky’s AI fears, this was one of our key cruxes. And it is related to the question of what exactly makes for smarter humans: do they use a few better general abilities to learn faster about everything, or do they just have better brain hardware to faster and more reliably apply the same human inheritance of a big standard library of ways to do many particular things?

This is now a key crux re fears that AI labs are now or might soon “foom” to “super-intelligence” via “recursive self-improvement” (RSI). Many have been quite impressed with recent frontier AI abilities at math and coding, and METR recently reported that Anthropic has seen a recent ~x2 jump in the rate at which it has improved key metrics. Some who “get it” say that this shows that Earth will within a few years see AI gods completely remake our world, and most likely kill all humans. But others interpret this as just a one-time jump, or due to benchmarks saturating, or Goodhearting of metrics, or shifting training compute more to reinforcement learning. Or it actually shows diminishing returns to key inputs of cash or hardware.

But even if we took such accelerating gains at face value (which I don’t), we can reasonably doubt huge near-term social effects of an AI industry that made large and accelerating gains at mostly only math and coding. After all, AI just does not seem to be gaining much traction at improving most other jobs, and AI firm customer revenue has plateaued at levels far below what can justify current AI spending levels, raising fears of a market crash and big cuts in AI development spending. Furthermore, though coding is where AI seems to gain the most traction, coder and software engineer number of workers times wages have not noticeably risen, an effect that we economists clearly predict if AI substantially improves overall coder productivity.

Sure, if just one AI got far better than others at military and security aspects of coding, that could destabilize relative power in the world. But that’s much less of a problem if many AI firms offer similar super-coder abilities to most customers.

Many plausibly attribute the much faster gains in math and coding to the fact that results in such domains are more easily verified. AIs also seem great at essay writing, plausibly due to LLMs being first created from huge databases of human writing. Some hope that physics simulations will let physical interaction domains become more verifiable, but we have seen only limited gains there so far.

My bet is that smarter humans mostly have better brain hardware, not a few general tricks, and that even an AI RSI “foom” soon in AI math and coding abilities would still take decades to greatly penetrate the world economy, as math-foomed AIs could not actually learn how to do most other tasks that much faster. A pattern economists have seen re past general purpose technologies.

However, I prefer policy to depend less on mine or others’ particular estimates. So I support robust strategies, such as requiring large (~$100B/event) liability insurance for AI firms re the possible large damage events AI execs have suggested as possible soon, perhaps even enhanced closer to more dangerous scenarios. If insurance firms estimate high risks, the premiums they demand would force AI firms to halt or greatly slow, appropriate for that scenario, but if they instead estimate low risks then small premiums won’t much slow development, appropriate for that scenario.

# E graphs 3

Die Analyse zu „E graphs 3“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

Hi there,

When an AI project disappoints, the first reaction is to blame the model. Try a bigger one, tweak the prompt, add more instructions.

But most of the time the weak link is upstream: where the AI finds the information it needs. Chatbot, agent or search, it’s only as good as what it can retrieve.

That’s the job of a vector database, which stores your data so AI can find what’s relevant by meaning, not just keywords. AWS Marketplace put together a guide on how to choose one.

Download the evaluation guide ›

One building block behind three AI patterns:

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines retrieve relevant context so your model responds from your data, not its training set.

Agentic memory gives agents semantic recall across sessions instead of replaying conversation histories.

Semantic search matches intent, not keywords.

All three depend on the same layer: a vector database.

items.articleBody:
Does a viral graph mapping President Trump's result in the 2024 election onto the results of the 2026 Senate election show a uniform, 15% decrease for all states that had a Senate election? No, that's not true: A clearer version of the graph produced by Lead Stories shows only a few states where the number from that calculation matches the actual result within one or two percent, all won by Trump in 2024 and by the Republican candidate in 2026. All the actual results in the other states show variation in both directions, showing much higher or lower numbers than the ones the formula returns.

The graph appeared in a post on X (archived here) published by "Truth is Freedom" on November 6, 2026, which read:

THE 15% BAND

Look at this chart.
59 races. Senate and governor.
States ordered from reddest to bluest in 2024.

The solid lines are 2024.
The dashed lines are 2026.
The shaded bands are what moved.

One formula fits all of it:
Republican 2026 = 0.85 × Trump 2024
Democrat 2026 = Harris 2024 + 0.15 × Trump 2024

For every 1,000 Trump points, 850 stayed Republican. 150 landed on the Democratic side.

The numbers:
Senate: Republicans kept ~85% of Trump's share
Governor: ~86%

Variation explained: 88%

What makes it strange:
It didn't matter how red the state was. Wyoming, Ohio, Illinois, Massachusetts: same 15% (p = 0.69). The Democratic gain was sized by Trump's vote, not Harris's. The Harris part is zero.

The 0.85 beat both standard election-swing models in every set of races.
Drop any single state and the multiplier stays between 0.846 and 0.853.

Why seats flipped:
At 0.85, any state where Trump got under about 58.5% falls below 50%. Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina, North Carolina: all under that line. All flipped.

What this means:
Midterms are messy. This one isn't. Two sets of races, different candidates, different campaigns, and the same 15% decrease almost everywhere.

A pattern this even demands answers at the ballot level: paper ballot hand counts, poll-book check-ins against votes counted, and voter files showing who actually turned out.

The numbers raise the question.
The ballots can answer it.

This is what the image in the post looked like:

(Image source: @TruthAnswersAll post on X.)

The graphic was labeled:

THE 15% BAND

Republicans kept about 85% of Trump's 2024 share in race after race. States ordered reddest to bluest in 2024.

It included both the Senate and the Governors' races for 2026 and drew lines claiming to show comparisons between Trump's 2024 result and the 2026 results, with additional lines drawn in showing the results of a formula that calculated a 15% decrease or increase from Donald Trump's or Kamala Harris' result in each state in 2024.

The y-axis of the graph went from 20% to 80% and the graph was very elongated along the x-axis, making all lines appear relatively close together.

Some people interpreted this graph and the post to mean there was a clean, uniform 85% percent ratio between Trump's 2024 result and the various Republican Senate candidates in 2026, for example here at The Gateway Pundit (archived here):

The theory, dubbed the "85/15 Algorithm" that was originally posted by Truth Is Freedom X account, suggests that Republican candidates received approximately 85% of President Trump's 2024 vote share.

Lead Stories used 2024 Presidential Election data from the Wall Street Journal (archived here) and the latest reported 2026 Senate data from the WSJ (archived here) at the time of writing to attempt to recreate the graph. We also added three states that were missing from the original graph (Alaska, Arkansas and Montana). Note that in some states the counts are still ongoing and that our snapshot is from a different moment in time compared to the one in the X post, but the overall shape of the 2024 and 2026 lines is quite consistent between our graph and the one from "Truth Is Freedom".

Omitting the data about the results for the Democrats and plotting the lines on a somewhat narrower, 0% to 80% graph, the actual variation in the 2026 results for the Republican senate candidates compared to the number from the formula based on 85% of Trump's 2024 result becomes much clearer:

(Image source: Lead Stories)

There is a stretch of red states on the left of the graph (West Virginia, Oklahoma, Alabama, Kentucky, Arkansas, Tennessee, Mississippi) where the 2026 result lines up to within a percent of the formula. But on either end of that stretch there are already differences: in Wyoming the Republican candidate did better and in Mississippi worse than what the formula said. The further to the right of the graph, the more variation there is and the bigger it becomes. In Maine the result for the 2026 Republican candidate was actually better than Trump's 2024 result.

You can download our data here: Trump24-Senate2026-comparison.xlsx

The graph did say the Republican candidates kept a certain percentage of Trump's share "on average" but there would be such an average number whatever the result in any state was and an average ultimately says nothing about how the results in various individual states are connected or not connected to other numbers in other individual elections or individual other states.

To help understand this better, imagine the graphs don't represent elections but road trips by two different cars. One drove through thirty-odd states in 2024, the other made the trip in 2026. Knowing that on average the second car completed the full trip 15% slower than the first car tells you nothing about exactly how fast or slow the second car went in each state. Maybe there was less traffic this year in one state, or there were roadworks in another, or the car broke down and had to be towed at some point in one particular state. An average won't tell you that information. All you know is that the total trip took 15% longer.
