items.articleBody:
After some further experimentation with wavetables I came across an idea:

If you can use wavetables to construct evolving sounds would be possible to construct such wavetables that would create acoustic-like sounds like string plucks, bells or brass attack?

As far as I experimented this seems to be the case (and both bells and plucks are quite usable actually) but I did not find these wavetables (as default ones) in PPGs or similar synths nor in any software. Was this idea implemented somewhere or do I just reinvented slightly more complicated ROMpler? Do I miss something here?

Or maybe nobody bothered to do this as this can be easily done with sampling and wavetables were actually used to create new sounds not recreate existing ones.

(I started new thread as it seems there is no thread specifically for wavetables.)

items.articleBody:
Ein Signal aus dem All könnte weniger Angst auslösen als oft vermutet. In einer internationalen Online-Umfrage erwarteten 77,6 Prozent der ausgewerteten Teilnehmer einen künftigen Kontakt mit außerirdischer Intelligenz. Viele würden darüber begeistert sein, bei Fragen zu Sicherheit und Menschenrechten zeigen sich jedoch Widersprüche.

Durham (England). Die Suche nach außerirdischer Intelligenz richtet sich bislang vor allem auf mögliche technische Signale im Weltraum. Was eine bestätigte Entdeckung gesellschaftlich auslösen würde, lässt sich dagegen nur anhand hypothetischer Szenarien untersuchen.

Ein solcher Kontakt könnte von einem fernen Radiosignal bis zur Landung eines fremden Raumschiffs reichen. Dabei stellt sich nicht nur die Frage nach möglichen Ängsten, sondern auch nach angemessenen politischen Entscheidungen und den Grenzen menschlicher Werte.

Befragung in 88 Ländern

Forscher der Durham University um Prof. Michael Bohlander haben dazu gemeinsam mit Kollegen eine internationale Online-Umfrage ausgewertet. Von Juli bis Oktober 2024 gingen 7.441 Antworten ein, von denen nach dem Ausschluss nicht bestandener Bot-Kontrollen 6.492 aus 88 Ländern übrig blieben.

Die Teilnahme war freiwillig, der Fragebogen stand auf Deutsch, Englisch, Französisch und Spanisch zur Verfügung. Die Daten sind ausdrücklich nicht repräsentativ, weil 54,7 Prozent der berücksichtigten Antworten aus Deutschland stammten und 75,2 Prozent der Befragten Männer waren. Außerdem hatten sich 77,2 Prozent schon vor der Teilnahme eingehender mit außerirdischem Leben beschäftigt.

Die Untersuchung liegt als wissenschaftlicher Preprint vor und ist damit noch nicht als fachbegutachtete Buchveröffentlichung erschienen. Die Ergebnisse beschreiben Einstellungen dieser selbst ausgewählten Teilnehmer, nicht die Haltung der Weltbevölkerung.

Begeisterung trotz unbekanntem Signal

In der Stichprobe stimmten 77,6 Prozent der Aussage zu, dass die Menschheit eines Tages Kontakt mit außerirdischer Intelligenz haben werde. Bereits erfolgte Besuche der Erde hielten sogar 59,5 Prozent für wahrscheinlich beziehungsweise glaubten daran. Über die tatsächliche Existenz oder Anwesenheit Außerirdischer sagen solche Überzeugungen nichts aus.

Ein wissenschaftlich bestätigtes, aber unverständliches Signal aus dem All würde 74,5 Prozent der Befragten begeistern, während 23,9 Prozent besorgt wären. Bei einem eindeutig außerirdischen Artefakt auf dem Mond stieg die Zustimmung zur Aussage, begeistert zu sein, auf 78,3 Prozent. Da mehrere Reaktionen angegeben werden konnten, schließen sich Begeisterung und Sorge nicht aus.

Würde ein fremdes Raumschiff ohne Kontaktaufnahme die Erde umkreisen, wollten 63,3 Prozent ihren Alltag fortsetzen und lediglich die Nachrichten verfolgen. Zugleich würden 45,4 Prozent Lebensmittelvorräte anlegen. Bei einer Landung würden 82,2 Prozent zunächst beobachten und abwarten, während 81,3 Prozent eine Willkommensbotschaft senden wollten.

Wer soll über den Kontakt entscheiden?

Bei einer aktiven Botschaft der Menschheit ins All gingen die Ansichten stärker auseinander. 47,7 Prozent befürworteten solche Signale, 35,0 Prozent lehnten sie ab, obwohl die Erde dadurch möglicherweise ihren Standort preisgeben könnte.

Über das Senden einer ersten Botschaft sollten nach Ansicht von 71,1 Prozent wissenschaftliche Vereinigungen mitentscheiden, während 67,7 Prozent internationale Organisationen bevorzugten. Ein weltweites Referendum erhielt 60,1 Prozent Zustimmung, nationale Regierungen lediglich 13,8 Prozent. Die Befragten konnten mehrere Entscheidungsträger gleichzeitig befürworten, weshalb die Werte keine ausschließlichen Zuständigkeiten beschreiben.

Friedlich, aber nicht um jeden Preis

Die grundsätzliche Zurückhaltung gegenüber Gewalt zeigte sich auch in Sicherheitsfragen. Eine vorsorgliche Verstärkung der militärischen Weltraumverteidigung lehnten 54,2 Prozent ab, während 28,8 Prozent dafür waren. Ein gelandetes außerirdisches Raumschiff präventiv zu zerstören, unterstützten nur 13,4 Prozent.

Anders fiel die Antwort auf ein Szenario aus, in dem eine außerirdische Zivilisation die Menschheit mit Vernichtung oder Versklavung bedroht. Unter dieser ausdrücklich angenommenen Bedingung würden 66,4 Prozent die Verletzung der sonst im Krieg geltenden humanitären Regeln billigen. Die Bereitschaft zum friedlichen Kontakt bedeutet demnach nicht, dass die Befragten auch bei einer existenziellen Bedrohung an diesen Regeln festhalten würden.

Auch für technische Hilfe gegen Energiekrisen, Nahrungsmangel und Klimaprobleme wollten die meisten ihre Grundrechte nicht umfassend preisgeben. Dennoch befürwortete ungefähr ein Viertel Einschränkungen der Religionsfreiheit oder invasive Gedankenuntersuchungen Verdächtiger. 10,9 Prozent akzeptierten außerirdische Eingriffe in die menschliche Geburtenkontrolle, 6,2 Prozent sogar die Auslieferung von Menschen für Experimente gegen deren Willen.

Die Befragung beschreibt damit sowohl Offenheit als auch deutliche ethische Spannungen, ohne tatsächliches Verhalten vorhersagen zu können. Ob und wie Menschen auf einen wirklichen Erstkontakt reagieren würden, bleibt offen, zumal die Stichprobe besonders stark von bereits interessierten Personen geprägt ist.

items.body:
# Genz sozialismus revolte generation

Die Analyse zu „Genz sozialismus revolte generation“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.

items.articleBody:
Light is reflected from a rose in my garden. Focused by the lens in my eye, this forms an image on the retina, which in turn sets off a neural impulse along my optic nerve. This in turn travels to the visual cortex at the back of my brain, where a mental image is formed. I then see the rose. Activity arises in my pre-frontal cortex. Motor neurons in my spinal cord and arms activate the muscles needed to point the hose I am holding in the direction of the pot in which the rose is planted. The movements necessary to water the rose are coordinated by activity in the cerebellum which sits at the back of my skull just behind my brain stem. A swarm of bees approaches me. After my visual cortex registers this fact, the limbic system deep inside my brain activates the sympathetic branch of my autonomic nervous system, producing the ‘fight or flight’ response. My heart rate increases, I feel fear, drop the hose and run away.

Everything we do, experience, feel or think seems to either come from the brain or end up in the brain. Unsurprisingly, there is a strong temptation to claim that for all intents and purposes we are our brains, and this seems true to such an extent that philosophers have envisaged the possibility that for all I know I might be no more than ‘a brain in a vat’. They mean by this that a brain immersed in suitable nutrient fluid and connected up to a super computer feeding it appropriate neural stimulation could create all the ordinary experiences of everyday life: a world created within a brain. The story told above about the rose and the bees suggests that, provided I have the right inputs and they are coordinated with the outputs produced by the decision-making in my pre-frontal cortex, I could never know I was not simply a brain in a vat. (This of course is the basis for the film The Matrix)

Putting the brain in a vat hypothesis aside, it’s worth noting that neuroscientists and cognitive psychologists are quite happy to talk as if the brain produces ‘representations’ or ‘models’ of reality, suggesting that we come to know the world secondhand in the brain rather than in the world itself. To go back to the rose example, the account I gave indicates that I see the rose in my brain rather than in my garden, or at least that the only experience I can have of the rose is the representation produced in my visual cortex.

Something has gone seriously wrong here but it’s not immediately obvious exactly what it is. Two errors initially stand out. The first is the mistake of thinking that neural activity in the brain somehow is conscious experience; in my example, the conscious experience of an image of a rose.  However, although the brain is extraordinarily complex, it does not contain images. The brain is, after all, just a very complex biological entity composed of billions of cells. In what sense then could it contain an image? Certainly there is an image on the retina of the eye when I look at the rose – just as there are images on a camera sensor or, in the old days, on light sensitive film. But we kid ourselves if we think this somehow gets translated into a mental image, which although unobservable in the brain, exists there. It might be argued here that advanced scanners can show the activity in the visual cortex, and that this is the brain ‘seeing’ an image, and we might want to regard this as a kind of metaphorical ‘seeing’, but there is no image involved, mental or otherwise. Our eyes do the actual seeing and the objects seen are out there in the world around us. A fully operational visual cortex is absolutely necessary for us to see anything at all, but that is by no means the same as saying that the seeing goes on inside this part of the brain.

The second related error is to believe that our knowledge of the world around us can be reduced to sensory experiences. Once we accept this it’s an easy step to locate these experiences ‘inside’ our brains. The starting point for any understanding of the human condition has to be that we, along with others who are similarly self-aware, are self-aware human beings inhabiting a world of objects. Our relation to the world around us and to others is a crucial part of who we are. This cannot be reduced to brain biology.

Any attempt to regard this starting point as a shaky hypothesis, deducible only on the basis of sensory experience, ends up going round in circles. Remember that the brain itself is merely another object in the world. To talk about it at all is to have already accepted a level of objective existence which cannot be reduced to sensory experience. We should also recall that the ‘brain in a vat’ hypothesis mentioned early only makes sense if we already accept a world where vats and super-computers exist as objects in the world. Here’s a thought experiment: imagine seeing the neural activity in your own brain which corresponds to the image of this act of seeing. (This might occur while having brain surgery.) The seeing ‘would have to be both the experience and the experience of seeing itself from the outside: it would have to be at once subjective experience and an objective experience of the basis of the subjective experience’[1] This is hardly coherent to say the least!

One argument in favour of the view that perception must involve images in the brain is the fact that we can experience hallucinations. If I hallucinate a rose in my garden then I can’t be perceiving an actual rose. The rose I seem to be perceiving, it might be argued, must exist only in my brain. But hallucinations can involve subjective experiences that are indistinguishable from veridical experiences. So if we can claim the hallucinated rose is in my brain, why can’t we also claim the image of the actual rose I perceive is also in my brain? The first thing to say here is that although hallucinations might on some occasions be temporarily indistinguishable from veridical experience, they are very different in their nature and origin; the very fact that we can identify a class of experiences as ‘hallucinations’ tells us this. But in any case we don’t have to say that hallucination experiences are in our brains, other than in a metaphorical sense. Better to say that they arise from distorted perceptions or projections onto the world. And this only makes sense if we assume we are subjects existing in, and interacting with, an objective world. Brains play a crucial part in this process but they are not the whole story.

Memory is another area where we can easily be misled by a mistaken understanding of the role of the brain. Memory is a crucial part of our identity. Individuals with severe amnesia lose a sense of who they are, and so if memories are located in the brain then this seems to support the claim that we are brains. Psychologists claim that memories are ‘encoded’ in the brain. Let’s imagine I remember a rose in my garden from a couple of years ago and how it was bigger and more beautiful than the roses I presently have there. A neuroscientist might want to claim that the memory of this rose is ‘encoded’ within a series of synaptic connections in a particular part of my brain. But in what sense can a synaptic connection be of, or about, anything? Synaptic connections are simply physical structures which allow neurons to interact with each other. Unless we assign meaning to them, these structure cannot have a significance in themselves anymore than a series of marks on paper can have significance unless someone has assigned a meaning to them.

There is an even bigger problem with the idea that memories are encoded in brain structures. Let’s not forget that memories are about the past, and yet structures in the brain are simply what they are now. They do not have a tense. How can neurons or synaptic connections provide a sense of the past? One approach might be to argue that because memories, like old photographs, fade with the passage of time, so do synaptic connections weaken. This weakening, it might be argued, can provide us with a sense of the past. But of course this doesn’t work because a faded image – as with a weak synaptic connection – does not in itself signify the passage of time. The passage of time might cause the fading but that is a different matter. And of course some memories are extremely vivid, but that doesn’t mean they are not still about the past. The basic problem here is that physical structures of any sort cannot represent the passage of time without an observer. For a physical structure to have a ‘now’ or a ‘then’ or a ‘not yet’ requires a human subject. And yet encoded memories in the brain are suppose to give an account of how human subjects can grasp their ‘thens’ as opposed to their ‘nows’. So it seems that structures that are supposed to encode memories assume the very thing they are trying to explain. They assume a human subject who already has a grasp of the then/now distinction.

It might be claimed that the then/now distinction can be recorded in the brain through changes in the brain, or through a succession of brain events. Change or succession could perhaps represent the passage of time. But this doesn’t work either. Mere change or succession is not the same as grasping what has been as opposed to what exists now. William James makes a similar point about feelings when he says, ‘a succession of feelings is not a feeling of succession. And since to our succession of feelings, a feeling of their own succession is added, that must be treated as an additional fact requiring its own special elucidation’.[2] In other words, a mere succession of events (feelings or whatever) does not in itself provide a sense of the passage of those events through time.

An understanding of the human condition must include as a starting point not only self-aware subjects who inhabit an objective world with others, but also subjects who have an awareness of the passage of time. No amount of brain biology is going to somehow explain how that arises.

Of course none of this calls into question the importance of the brain. Having a brain is certainly a necessary condition for having memories, as it is for perception and the sense of self. But despite the amazing advances in neuro-science let’s not forget that there is much more to us than our brains.

[1] Tallis, R. 2011, Aping Mankind: Neuromania, Darwinitis, and the Misrepresentation of Humanity. Durham, acumen press, p97

[2] James W. 2007, The Principles of Psychology. New York, Cosimo, p628-9

The investigation into "Morpheral machines introduces the swarm a new approach to wavetable synthesis" examines the cognitive and psychological frameworks of mental resilience and intellectual focus. It analyzes grounded insights from cognitive science, practical strategies against digital distraction, and cultivating sustained focus in daily life. Further explorations and detailed perspectives remain available in the original source.

## Conceptual Framework & In-Depth Analysis

Engaging with these questions touches fundamental aspects of human judgment and cognitive autonomy. Through conscious examination of attention architectures, thinkers can cultivate deeper comprehension of complex systemic dynamics.

> "Critical discernment emerges through patient analysis of premises and empirical relationships."

items.articleBody:
On Thursday, the Atlantic staff writer George Packer delivered the Newark Public Library’s annual Philip Roth Lecture. This article is adapted from his remarks.

Philip Roth’s chosen vocation was the novel, and he practiced it almost nonstop for six decades with a monkish devotion. In his hands it became a thing of explosive invention, wildly comical and intensely serious. The critic Lionel Trilling wrote: “The most effective agent of the moral imagination has been the novel of the last two hundred years.” Roth’s readiness to experiment and provoke expanded his readers’ moral imagination—their ability to see beyond the appearances of their lives to the deeper reality.

The reign of the novel has coincided with the centuries of democracy. I don’t think this is a complete coincidence, because no other literary form has such plasticity and variety; no other genre is so concerned with the moral struggles of individuals amid the social forces that constrict or enlarge their humanity. If democracy is the political system that allows the fullest human flourishing, the novel is the literary form that most fully cultivates our understanding of human possibility and tragedy and endurance.

In 1959, 25-year-old Roth published a short story called “Defender of the Faith” in The New Yorker, just ahead of its inclusion in his first book, Goodbye, Columbus. Some Jewish readers strongly objected to the story’s caustic portrayal of a Jewish character. This was the start of Roth’s career-long embattlement with critics high and low. A certain Rabbi Emanuel Rackman, the president of the Rabbinical Council of America, complained to the Anti-Defamation League: “What is being done to silence this man? Medieval Jews would have known what to do with him.” Young Roth shot off a letter to Rackman: “He who criticizes must be silenced—that is a terrible tenet to have to live by, Rabbi, and I should imagine even more terrible to a spiritual leader.”

Writers work in the creative tension between freedom and attachment. They have to maintain an inner distance from external demands, including the demands of politics; at the same time, they aren’t excused from the responsibilities of being a human and a citizen. They need to be left alone, but they can’t escape the world. Much of Roth’s work conveys the tug of this social awareness, even or especially in revolt against the duties it imposes. He was also fierce on behalf of freedom, and not only his own. He edited Writers From the Other Europe so that work by Milan Kundera and other Eastern Europeans could bypass the Communist censors and be made widely available to English-speaking readers. When the Iranian regime sentenced Salman Rushdie to death, Roth had him to dinner at his London flat, accompanied by half a dozen security officers. Perhaps because Roth’s own need to write was an unstoppable, nearly biological drive, any attempt to silence a writer awakened his primal rage—and woe unto the Rabbi Rackmans of the world.

When it comes to threats to free expression, we usually think of government censorship. The current occupant of the White House, more than any president in my lifetime, is trying his best to be the grand inquisitor. He’s carried on a relentless campaign of legal actions and verbal attacks against journalists, broadcasters, comedians, immigrants with unpopular views, and just about anyone who criticizes him. His administration has allowed major media organizations to be bought up by his cronies and merged into near-monopolies. His executive orders have barred hundreds of words from official use. His Pentagon purged 381 books from the Naval Academy library, including Henry James and Sexuality (surprisingly popular with midshipmen).

We expect governments to try to restrict speech. It isn’t in the nature of power to let offending views go undisturbed. For the past decade, we in the West have been preoccupied with the divisive effects of the propaganda and lies that free people avidly consume on social media. But reporting in countries such as Ethiopia, Afghanistan, and Myanmar always reminds me that old-fashioned repression didn’t end with the 20th century. Publishing a poem or story can still bring the risk of jail or worse. The threat comes from police and vigilantes, and the red lines are kept dangerously unclear. Burmese poets invent an elaborately coded language of metaphors to get their social criticism past official censors who scrutinize every word. I’ve never heard the case for literary freedom so passionately made as in the rain-soaked streets of Rangoon.

[From the April 2021 issue: The relentless Philip Roth]

Fortunately, in our country we have a First Amendment, and not even this American president can throw us in prison for what we say and write and read. But free speech depends on more than the law. It needs a culture of free expression—a set of widely shared habits and expectations that guide daily life, an ability to tolerate disagreement, a willingness to listen even, or especially, when we don’t like what we hear. The First Amendment stands there like a block of stone against the efforts of would-be government censors, but a culture of free expression is a delicate thing that has to be trained and tended. It can bloom and fade. It lives or dies in the inner recesses of our minds, releasing or smothering thoughts and words regardless of the protections of the First Amendment. In a late essay, George Orwell wrote, “If large numbers of people are interested in freedom of speech, there will be freedom of speech, even if the law forbids it; if public opinion is sluggish, inconvenient minorities will be persecuted, even if laws exist to protect them.”

In other words, a culture of free expression is up to us. I want to explore why ours seems particularly weak. One of the reasons is coming from inside the house.

If Roth were still with us at 93, he would find that the censorious rabbis, commissars, and mullahs have become writers. This is a time of promiscuous boycotts, rampant deplatformings and depublishings—books removed from store shelves, canceled before publication, withdrawn from sale as if we had gone back to the age of medieval heresy-hunting. Except now, instead of being hoisted by the strappado or bound to the rack, heretics are disinvited from conferences and review-bombed on Goodreads.

I’ve had a front-row seat at this literary auto-da-fé—and I admit that my close-up vantage might distort my view a little. Shortly after October 7, 2023, I joined the board of the century-old free-speech writers’ organization PEN America. My timing was perfect: A pressure campaign by well-known writers had just begun against PEN and its leader for their insufficient zeal in condemning the war in Gaza. When, rightly or wrongly, PEN failed to say what its critics wanted to hear, they launched an aggressive boycott of the organization’s two premier events, its literary-awards ceremony and literary festival. Because I was new, it took me a little while to realize that the purpose of the boycott wasn’t to push PEN into a dialogue or allow writers to make their views known. The purpose was to flex enough cultural power to force the cancellation of the events; if possible, to destroy PEN America. The boycott achieved the first goal and nearly achieved the second.

I also learned that a successful campaign doesn’t depend on broad ideological agreement. A few true believers can build up a critical mass of support by applying heavy pressure through networks of friends and professional connections—convincing them that refusing to join would be morally wrong, or just not worth the trouble it would cause them—and recruiting enough joiners that the remaining holdouts are isolated and risk social censure. Under this pressure, a well-known writer called me to ask whether he should drop out of the PEN festival. He was worried about optics—because of the boycott, his panel might be down to a couple of white writers. Call me naive, but I still thought of writers as fairly independent-minded people who didn’t like to obey what D. H. Lawrence called their “mob self,” who were unwilling to be coerced by the crowd, ornery when it came down to the right to speak and hear, even a bit vain when given the chance to stand on their own. I urged my friend to stay on—but as we hung up, I could tell which way the wind would blow him.

Each big-name departure generated others, until the exodus became a stampede and the events were finally canceled because of lack of participants. This sad experience was a revelation: Writers turn out to be just as susceptible to peer pressure and social stigma as other people—maybe more so. PEN America survived, barely.

With new leadership, the organization went through another, related crisis. The trigger was again the Middle East. Last year, PEN published a long, detailed report on the cultural destruction of Gaza by Israel: the heritage sites, museums, libraries, and universities wiped out; the hundreds of journalists, writers, and artists killed. Then, this past summer, the organization published another document: This one dealt with the growing exclusion of Israeli, and even some Jewish American, writers from literary life. The piece didn’t try to prove a coordinated campaign of discrimination, but it described a hostile climate in which editors are reluctant to sign or even read work submitted by these writers and their agents, novelists are told to downplay Jewish characters and themes, and bookstores and festivals vet these writers for signs of “wrongthink.” The Pulitzer Prize–winning biographer Benjamin Moser exulted to The Wall Street Journal: “Zionism is out of fashion in the publishing world, and it’s not ever going to be in fashion again.”

None of this is surprising. After all, more than 7,000 literary professionals have signed on to a global boycott of Israeli cultural institutions, including of individual writers and publishers who don’t adequately affirm their support for the Palestinian cause. It would have to be a pretty incompetent boycott not to create a chill.

These two documents—one on cultural destruction in Gaza, the other on the exclusion of Israeli and Jewish writers—demonstrate why we need a group that’s committed to free expression regardless of political pressure. I don’t know of another organization that has done this work in showing the effects of this terrible war on culture across the lines of conflict. And yet, strangely enough, PEN America has become a pariah to many writers. The Gaza report didn’t get much attention; perhaps PEN’s boycotters already had what they wanted. But when the second piece appeared, it lit a small conflagration.

PEN’s new board president, a novelist, immediately resigned. Several board members followed him out. The now-ex-president began to denounce the organization, saying that it should never have published the piece and calling it “unethical.” His complaint was that the document would harm the Israel boycott by giving ammunition to its critics, including American politicians who have sought to ban it as discriminatory. I’m opposed to laws that criminalize boycotts, but I’m also against suppressing the truth just because it might hurt a cause I support. The ex-president argued that a cultural boycott is a form of protected speech—and it is. But let’s not kid ourselves: Its purpose is to ostracize and ultimately silence disfavored writers. It is incompatible with a culture of free expression.

[From the May 2020 issue: Philip Roth’s terrible gift of intimacy]

So this is where we are: The leader of a free-speech writers’ group quit because it defended the free speech of writers. A number of confused friends called to ask me what the hell was happening. I did my best to explain, but honestly, by now I wasn’t surprised. This was no longer a man-bites-dog story. To PEN’s ex-president and others like him, literary freedom was never the real concern. What mattered was whether PEN helped or harmed their political cause. I’ve learned the hard way that writers can’t always be counted on to support the freedom of other writers—that sometimes they’re the last people to count on. The principle that makes their life’s work even possible no longer seems to carry the force of belief. The question is: Why?

The answer has something to do with politics—with an idea about the role of the writer in politics, and the role of politics in writing. We live in an intensely political time, and unless you’re making a huge effort to ignore the world around you, your mind is saturated with existential elections, partisan hatreds, historic corruption, wars and war crimes, global apocalypses, and the poisonous nature of the very information you’re consuming. The future of democracy and maybe humanity is at stake every day. It’s natural for conscious people to speak out, and writers especially feel they have an important role to play. At least since Zola defended Dreyfus, in times of crisis, writers have given their names to political causes and tried to move others to do the same. They feel that their work is an expression of their moral values, and they want to put that status to more direct use than sitting all alone in the cloudy realm of truth and beauty.

Politics today seeps into everything, from pet-food choices to tampon brands. At the same time, literature is at risk of disappearing—or at least becoming the eccentric taste of a small elite, like opera. Philip Roth anticipated this back in 2004, when he said, “I don’t think in 20 or 25 years anyone will read these things at all. I think there are other things for people to do, other ways for them to be occupied, other ways for them to be imaginatively engaged, that are I think probably far more compelling than the novel, so I think the novel’s day has come and gone.” Right on time, we’re now told that we are becoming a “postliterate society,” we are entering “the new Dark Ages,” we have reached “the end of reading.” The percentage of Americans who still read at least one book annually has become as familiar an indicator of national decline as the Gini coefficient of economic inequality, or the life expectancy of non-college-educated white people.

So one reason some writers feel justified in silencing others for political reasons might be the declining value of writing itself. Politics has never seemed more urgent, while literature has never seemed more marginal. If I can strike a blow for human rights and justice by shutting down a writer whose country is waging a brutal war, why would I let an abstraction stop me? (And I won’t pause to ask what good I’m really doing, other than for my own moral hygiene.)

For example, the Pulitzer-winning New York Times columnist M. Gessen criticized the PEN piece on Facebook, essentially saying that its findings about Israeli and Jewish writers are exaggerated, irrelevant, or untrue—and if they are true, all the better. Gessen argued that no one would expect the writings of Heinrich Böll to have been published while he was a German soldier during World War II, or the work of a Russian writer who’s silent about the war in Ukraine to be made available in the West. Shouldn’t the same go for Israeli writers while Palestinians are being killed in Gaza and the West Bank?

I won’t get into the business of weighing the Holocaust, Ukraine, and Gaza on the scales of historic crimes. What interests me is the role of literature at such a moment. An Israeli writer named Mikhal Dekel, replying to Gessen, spoke about the need to make room for writing that doesn’t fall into clear ideological categories—that might use an indirect or ironic style. Dekel herself is writing a book about the complex lives of Arabs and Jews who reside in the same building in Haifa. She invoked the South African novelist J. M. Coetzee, who was criticized for not taking public positions on behalf of the anti-apartheid movement, but whose novels, both realistic and allegorical, brilliantly portray the psychology of oppression.

Gessen’s answer got to the point: “Now may not be the time for such literature. Not while the genocide is continuing and while the majority of people with those complex predicaments support it and tolerate it … Now, I think, is a time for laying down basic moral coordinates. The time when readers outside of Israel are ready to start filling in the many shades and colors of the grid will come later.”

When the time comes, presumably Gessen will let us know. But while we wait, it’s worth thinking about the phrase “laying down basic moral coordinates.” It seems to describe writing that takes a clear position and compels a simple response. I believe that there’s a place for such literature. We shouldn’t make a fetish of ambiguity and disinterestedness that would oblige us to cancel Hard Times and The Grapes of Wrath. When James Baldwin attacks Richard Wright for writing a protest novel that denies the humanity of its protagonist, I nod along—but I would much rather reread Native Son than Giovanni’s Room. The intensity of Wright’s vision of injustice makes the crudeness of his characterization less important. There’s value in a literature that compels its own time to see the truth about itself. No one can doubt where Darkness at Noon and 1984 stand on totalitarianism.

Yet Gessen’s “basic moral coordinates” make me uneasy—and not just because they’re offered as grounds for excluding certain writers. Something about the exhortation puts me on edge. It feels like the pressure of a hand on my back, gently but firmly pushing me toward foregone conclusions and absolute truths, when in fact the place where politics and literature meet is fraught with risk. Trilling called this place “the dark and bloody crossroads.” A lot of bad politics and bad books are buried there, or else emerged from the encounter damaged and diminished. At this intersection, politics often becomes what it rarely is or can be, a simple contest between right and wrong, while literature approaches a form of propaganda that makes artistic integrity impossible by requiring distortions and lies.

[From the April 2012 issue: Roth v. Roth v. Roth]

Entering the zone of politics seems to give writers a license to forget everything they ever knew about human complexity. Politics is the one place where life can be the morality tale that they’d never accept in a work of art. Social reality is reduced to an open letter with all of the right signatories, written in a tone of high righteousness—politics as an extension of personal conscience: “Here I stand. I can do no other.” The really dangerous temptation is to become a prophet—once writers let that happen, they stop being writers. Thomas Mann, who in his later years became a tireless public speaker for democracy and against fascism, was aware of the danger: “The political moralizings of an artist have undeniably something comic about them. Moreover his propaganda for humanitarian ideals must inevitably bring him closer than close to the platitudinous.”

And when politics enters a literary work, the result can be just as painful. Stendhal compared it to “a pistol shot in the middle of a concert, something loud and vulgar, and yet a thing to which it is not possible to refuse one’s attention.” Sometimes, a political agenda is slathered on top of an otherwise unrelated story like a coat of high-gloss paint. Or else characters are manipulated like ventriloquist dummies to dramatize a writer’s views, usually at the expense of their credibility. The critic Becca Rothfeld coined the term sanctimony literature to describe a wave of popular contemporary novels whose protagonists are represented as good people because they espouse the right progressive views in between couplings and breakups. The politics is already settled, with no conflicts in the quest for goodness, only a smooth convergence of opinion among authors, characters, and readers: frictionless fiction.

If the book world were predominantly conservative, sanctimony literature would present very different views. But that’s almost inconceivable. We’ve had groups called “Hispanics for Trump,” “Blacks for Trump,” and even “Arab Americans for Trump,” but I have serious trouble imagining “Poets, Essayists, and Novelists for Trump.” It’s even hard to think of a living American writer who could be a registered Republican—Cormac McCarthy might have been the last. It’s a sign of the saturation of culture by politics that the book world is so uniformly on the left.

Perhaps there’s a progressive bias to literature itself: an openness to new varieties of experience, an impulse to criticize the existing social order. Yet other times and places had their conservative and reactionary writers—critics of liberal democracy, skeptics of progress and equality: Dostoyevsky, Conrad, Eliot, Pound, Céline, Hurston, O’Connor. Maybe we should congratulate ourselves on having no prize-winning fascist poets. But in the 1940s, another period when literature came under the domination of politics, Trilling warned: “We have the books that point out the bad conditions, that praise us for taking progressive attitudes. We have no books that raise questions in our minds not only about conditions but about ourselves, that lead us to refine our motives and ask what might lie behind our good impulses.”

When literature applies no pressure to a general conformity, we read to be flattered and lose a crucial tool in understanding reality, including the murky nature of our deepest beliefs. Literary judgments merge with political ones until they’re indistinguishable. It ought to be possible to say: “This writer speaks for me—too bad he’s a terrible writer.” But readers, including professional critics, are more likely to assess the merits of a book before they’ve opened it. A judge for a prestigious prize once told me with evident pride that his committee had decided not to honor the book they thought was actually the best, but the one they thought was most politically relevant to the moment. Some literary prizes are so aligned with current orthodoxy that every few years, the winners reliably change with the political fashions.

I think this confusion of categories shows a waning faith in both politics and literature. Politics becomes a set of positions and slogans, not a public square where individuals encounter one another in a common enterprise, ideas and interests clash, and no one comes out completely clean. Literature becomes a demonstration of goodness, not the art form in which our humanity can be most fully explored.

The point is not to keep literature and politics separate. That would be not just impossible but undesirable—in fact, unthinkable. We would lose, among so much more, the Philip Roth of The Plot Against America. Politics is the business of everyone, including writers. Their work can be done only in an artistic freedom that needs political freedom to flourish. They have to balance the inner solitude of art with a nourishing connection to the outside world. Nothing about their vocation equips them any better than other people to answer the hardest questions confronting humanity—but neither are writers excused from the responsibility to face them. “A writer should not provide solutions,” Chekhov said, “but describe a situation so truthfully that the reader can no longer evade it.”

Sensitive readers know when the authorial thumb is on the scale—when they’re being recruited and flattered rather than enlightened and provoked. Filling in what Gessen calls “the many shades and colors of the grid” should be the aspiration of any literature worth the name. If Roth had written American Pastoral to lay down some basic moral coordinates, this tale of a decent, successful Jewish businessman whose precocious daughter becomes a 1960s revolutionary and blows up their lives would pander to the complacency of a conservative Jewish reader. In fact, Norman Podhoretz loved it, while missing the point. Roth’s masterpiece expresses all his ambivalence about assimilation and rebellion; in the end, there are no ideological winners, only the “massive historical pain” that the “indigenous American berserk” inflicts on the novel’s uncomprehending hero.

The novelist’s job is to bring abstract ideology into sustained contact with concrete experience. There, a mysterious transformation takes place; ideas never keep their pristine shape as they undergo the heat of human passions. Writers and readers are brought into a communion that’s higher than political opinion and, as Irving Howe wrote in his classic Politics and the Novel, “find some common recognition, some supervening human bond above and beyond ideas.”

Why should all of this matter to us now?

The world’s richest and most powerful men want to hustle us into a post-human age of history. They anticipate that our ability in relation to superintelligence will be about the same as that of chimpanzees is to us. Elon Musk recently predicted that in five years, “There really won’t be anything that AI can’t do better than humans, apart from being human perhaps.” The dismissive shrug of that perhaps! Musk makes being human sound like an afterthought, hardly worth mentioning. In the future, and soon, there will be something shameful and humiliating about it, stuck as we’ll be with our decaying bodies and primitive brains, struggling to put a few good sentences together, while machines fed with every human word ever written spit out perfect novels in a matter of seconds. We’ll have returned to the opening scene of 2001: A Space Odyssey, where shaggy hominids chatter moronically at the base of an inscrutable monolith.

[From the April 1969 issue: The journey of Philip Roth]

I haven’t read an AI novel and hope I never will, though it might happen without my knowing. After all, artificial novels have won major literary prizes, before researchers discovered the fraud through the detector Pangram, which is becoming a kind of literary Patriot-missile system, our only defense against the onslaught of machine literature. It’s also possible that 100 percent human-written texts will start to sound more like generative AI. Large language models are trained on our work, but the flow of instruction could be reversed, the way that algorithms dictate how we sound on social-media platforms where we think we’re free to sound like ourselves.

The more that our writing is done through AI, the more reductive and predictable and cloying it will become, like a robot lover in book form. It might not spell the end of literature, but it will probably mean the end of the kind of literature we’ve known throughout the democratic centuries—the work of a free individual mind. And if writing serves as the valet to a domineering politics that decides which ideas and writers are allowed into the house of literature—if writers lose faith in the principle that makes their work possible just when it stands to be swept aside by a trillion-dollar industry—then the whole thing might as well be done by machine, and probably will be. With the right prompts, AI will surely excel at laying down basic moral coordinates.

But if the creation of stories and the communication of ideas through language remain activities that differentiate us from computers and chimps, then literature will be one of the last barriers against surrendering our humanity to the million-headed god of superintelligence. If books written by human beings are to survive the hyper-politicization of this age and the artificiality of the next, it will be because this work does something special, something we want and need and can’t get anywhere else. On the verge of the singularity, we must cherish our words and the freedom to write them as flickers of that absurd and precious thing: human dignity.

items.articleBody:
Apples neuer Konzernchef John Ternus will die Entwicklung künstlicher Intelligenz deutlich beschleunigen. Während er die Fortschritte bei Siri AI öffentlich lobt, soll er intern zunehmend unzufrieden mit dem Tempo sein. In einem persönlichen Gespräch hat Ternus seinen Softwarechef Craig Federighi deshalb aufgefordert, ehrgeizigere Ziele zu verfolgen. Die bisherige Weiterentwicklung von Siri reicht ihm offenbar nicht aus.

John Ternus will in Sachen KI Gas geben

Der Führungswechsel an Apples Spitze sollte schnellere Entscheidungen und mehr Risikobereitschaft bringen. Nun zeichnet sich ab, dass Ternus diese Erwartungen auch gegenüber langjährigen Führungskräften durchsetzen möchte. Insbesondere bei KI sieht er Handlungsbedarf, da Wettbewerber wie OpenAI, Google und Anthropic ihre Systeme schneller um zusätzliche Fähigkeiten erweitern.

Federighis Zurückhaltung sorgt für Spannungen

Craig Federighi verantwortet seit dem vergangenen Jahr auch Apples KI-Strategie. Zuvor hatte John Giannandrea die Entwicklung geleitet, konnte die angekündigten Siri-Funktionen jedoch nicht rechtzeitig fertigstellen. Federighi übernahm das Projekt und brachte die überarbeitete Sprachassistenz schließlich mit iOS 27 auf den Markt.

Software-Chef Federighi im Sommer 2025

Nach einem Bericht von Bloomberg gilt Federighi intern allerdings weiterhin als KI-Skeptiker. Er beschäftigt sich intensiv mit Fragen des Datenschutzes, der Sicherheit und möglichen gesellschaftlichen Folgen. Zudem plant seine Softwareabteilung häufig nur 12 bis 18 Monate voraus, während Apples Hardwareteams über mehrere Jahre entwickeln.

Auch sein Führungsstil steht in der Kritik. Federighi soll technische Entscheidungen stark selbst beeinflussen und Gegenpositionen ausführlich hinterfragen. Mitarbeiter beklagen laut Bloomberg, dass dadurch alternative Vorschläge nur schwer vorankommen.

Siri soll künftig selbstständig Aufgaben erledigen

Ternus will Siri über die bisherige Sprachsteuerung hinausentwickeln. Der Assistent soll nicht nur einzelne Anweisungen ausführen, sondern künftig eigenständig Aufgaben verfolgen und mehrere Arbeitsschritte übernehmen können. Als Vorbilder dienen KI-Agenten, die Informationen dauerhaft beobachten und ohne ständige neue Aufforderungen tätig werden.

Siri soll zügig ausgebaut werden

Ein erster Schritt sind die erweiterten App-Aktionen, die Apple mit iOS 27.3 vorbereitet. Sie erlauben Siri unter anderem, Dateien zu organisieren, Nachrichten zurückzuholen oder Fotos in mehreren Schritten zu bearbeiten. Ein vollständig autonomer Assistent ist das allerdings noch nicht. Bereits bei seinem ersten großen Auftritt als Apple-Chef hatte Ternus das iPhone als Mittelpunkt für persönliche Daten, Apps und Apple Intelligence hervorgehoben.

Auch personell könnten Veränderungen bevorstehen. Der Siri-Verantwortliche Mike Rockwell erwägt laut Bloomberg, seine Position oder Apple im kommenden Jahr zu verlassen. Mehr Verantwortung könnte dann auf Amar Subramanya und Sebastien Marineau übergehen. Letzterer gilt intern als möglicher langfristiger Nachfolger Federighis, dessen eigener Abschied derzeit jedoch nicht absehbar ist. Ternus selbst hatte zuletzt wiederholt betont, dass KI vor allem konkrete Aufgaben erleichtern und persönliche Nutzerdaten geschützt bleiben sollen.

★ iPhone-Ticker bei Google bevorzugen ★

Der Beitrag Apple-Chef Ternus macht Druck: Federighi soll KI vorantreiben Wurde zuerst auf iphone-ticker.de veröffentlicht.

items.articleBody:
On 30 October 2026, Constitutional Tribunal judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, decided to suspend the President and Vice-President of the Constitutional Tribunal. In a recent post on Verfassungsblog, Kim-Lane Scheppele, Laurent Pech and Maciej Kisilowski praised this move as lawful and necessary to restore the rule of law. In this post I present a different view. I argue that the legality of the order is doubtful and that to truly heal the Tribunal something else is needed – a rebuilding of its legitimacy, credibility and authority. This cannot be achieved by legal tricks, but only through political compromise over the re-establishing the Tribunal based on new rules which would protect it from capturing by one political group.

A Doubtful Legal Basis

Judge Korwin-Piotrowska cited Article 130(2) of the Act on the Structure of Ordinary Courts as the legal basis for her order. This provision grants the Minister of Justice and the president of a competent court the right to order an immediate break in the exercise of professional duties by a judge. Such an order can be issued “if a judge has been apprehended in flagrante delicto in the commission of an intentional offense or if required by the gravity of the act committed by the judge, the dignity of the court, or important interests of the service.”

In 2009, the Constitutional Tribunal ruled that this provision does not violate the Constitution, so it remains in force. However, in my view, the constitutionality of this provision continuously raises doubts, given that the Constitution clearly stipulates that a judge may be suspended only by virtue of a court ruling. Moreover, when PiS was in power, this exact provision served as a legal basis for harassing independent judges.

The problem is, however, that judge Korwin-Piotrowska is not a Tribunal’s President. Therefore, to justify her action, she relied on provisions stipulating that when the Tribunal President is unable to authorize another judge to exercise certain powers, they are substituted by the judge with the longest judicial service. However, this provision is not applicable here as the seat of the Tribunal’s President is not vacant and the President was not unable to act – he became unable to act only after judge Korwin-Piotrowska issued her order.

Such an interpretation can be clearly abused in the future. Judge with the longest judicial service could suspend the Tribunal’s leaders to gain the control over it. Even if such a move had no substantive justification, that judge could always claim that a disciplinary court must decide whether the order is justified and that, until then, the order remains in force.

The order will have to be reviewed within 30 days by the Tribunal’s disciplinary court. However, one can expect that it will be difficult to assemble a panel of judges who satisfy the standard of impartiality in this case. Five judges who were prevented from adjudicating by Mr. Święczkowski are in a clear conflict of interest with him, while those elected before 2023 have already stated that Korwin-Piotrowska’s order was unlawful. Therefore, the disciplinary court’s ruling will most likely not resolve all doubts surrounding the legality of the order.

Scheppele, Pech and Kisilowski argue that, regardless of Korwin-Piotrowska’s explanation, the leadership positions in the Tribunal were vacant because neither the President nor the Vice-President “was lawfully appointed to his leadership office, because the assemblies nominating them included people who were not judges.” However, two important points must be made here. First, Korwin-Piotrowska clearly assumed that Bogdan Święczkowski and Bartłomiej Sochański are the President and Vice-President of the Tribunal. Nowhere in the order is there a statement to the contrary. Second, there has been no formal ruling by any domestic or international body declaring the appointments of both men null and void. Applying the conclusions of the CJEU judgment regarding the appointment of Julia Przyłębska to Święczkowski and Sochański would not be straightforward, as there were procedural differences between their cases. In any event, this issue requires more than a single sentence in a blog post.

I admit that there are many legal experts in Poland who do not share my interpretation of law and who defend Judge Korwin-Piotrowska’s order. However, my objections to this method of addressing the crisis around the Tribunal are not limited to legality.

What Is Going on in the Constitutional Tribunal?

Undoubtedly, the Constitutional Tribunal has been mired in a deep institutional crisis since late 2015. The crisis started with the unlawful election of three judges. Subsequent judges were elected formally lawfully, but some of them had clear links to the former ruling party. This also concerns the current Tribunal’s President, Judge Święczkowski, who in the past was an undersecretary of State in the Ministry of Justice in the PiS government and ran in parliamentary elections on PiS lists. All in all, PiS turned the Tribunal into a tool in its hands, used instrumentally to achieve political gains. Before 2023, it was used to legitimise various PiS moves that violated the rule of law and to question EU law and the ECHR; after the change of power, it tried to block the new ruling coalition’s attempts to reverse the PiS reforms and to hold PiS-appointed officials accountable.

The recent crisis around the oath-taking ceremony must be seen in this wider political and legal context. If judges elected by the current ruling majority were allowed to adjudicate, the Constitutional Tribunal’s character would inevitably change, given that they already constitute the majority of its composition. Therefore, by taking unlawful steps to prevent them from assuming office, the President of the Republic de facto protects his political group’s interests. The same conclusion applies to the motivations of the Tribunal President, who had clear political links with the former ruling party and, moreover, faces potential criminal liability, given that the prosecutor’s office is seeking to lift his immunity.

However, this catastrophic state of the current Tribunal and hypocrisy of many of its defenders do not mean that all actions taken by the new government are justified and truly contribute to rebuilding the Tribunal’s position.

Good Intentions?

Many Polish and some foreign commentators argue that a key difference between PiS’s actions and those of the current government is that the former aimed to destroy the rule of law, while the latter wants to fix it. I agree that we cannot equate the actions of PiS and those of the current ruling coalition. There is no doubt that the chaos in the judiciary was created mostly by PiS. However, what I find problematic is the very strong presumption that the intentions of Prime Minister Tusk’s government are pure.

How do we know that the current Government truly wants to build an independent Constitutional Tribunal? I do not think political declarations alone are sufficient. We have to consider the coalition’s actions, and some of them were problematic.

In 2024 the Government adopted two laws reforming the Constitutional Tribunal. The drafts of these laws were prepared by an NGO, the Stefan Batory Foundation. The first of them contained many important provisions aimed at strengthening the independence and impartiality of this body, such as those concerning an increase in the majority necessary to elect judges, or the introduction of a cooling-off period between holding political office and being able to be elected as a judge. However, the second law was much more controversial – it provided for, among other things, declaration of invalidity of all judgments of the Constitutional Tribunal issued with participation of so-called double-judges. Given sheer number of such rulings and various effects they produced over the years, the consequences of the entry into force of such a provision could be dangerous. Moreover, neither the Government nor the Sejm presented a comprehensive analysis of such possible consequences. It is therefore hard to assess if politicians were actually aware of the scale of possible problems.

Eventually the law was referred by the President to the Constitutional Tribunal which declared its unconstitutionality, preventing its entry into force. Subsequently, the ruling coalition adopted a strange strategy of boycotting Tribunal by not publishing its judgments and not electing new judges to vacant seats. Not only were these two actions criticised by the Venice Commission, but it was also hard to discern what the Government wanted to achieve.

It is worth noting that failure to adopt the laws reforming the Constitutional Tribunal did not have to lead to a complete resignation from attempts to change the law. Leaving aside the problem of constitutional compromise, which I will address below, the Sejm could have considered changing its own internal rules which regulate the details concerning election of the Constitutional Tribunal judges. In 2024 the Marshal of the Sejm asked several Polish NGOs and bar associations for their opinions about the desired changes in the regulation of the Sejm concerning the process of election of Tribunal judges. Many organisations responded that a key change would be to increase the transparency of the process and to introduce some form of pre-selection of candidates for judges with participation of non-political, expert bodies. Some suggested also the increase of the majority required for electing a judge. It must be underlined that changes in the Sejm’s Regulation could not be blocked by a President, who does not have a right of veto as regards this type of internal laws.

However, ultimately the Sejm ignored the suggestions and did not make any changes in its regulations.

In March 2026 the Sejm elected six new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal. Refraining from filling vacancies in the Tribunal for two years only to elect all judges on the same session violates the spirit of the Constitution and can be abused in the future to artificially “prolong” the terms of new judges. What was also problematic was that, while the election was legal, it was made in a hasty manner, without any meaningful consultations: there were only three days to nominate candidates, and the entire process took only three days.

The election of one judge in September 2026 raised even more controversies. A new judge, Maciej Berek, served as Minister in Donald Tusk Government just until August this year and the Prime Minister called him his right hand. It is hard not to see Berek’s election as a form of hypocrisy, given that just two years earlier the ruling coalition wanted to introduce provision which would block the election of politicians to the Tribunal. However, the coalition explained that this election was necessary to fix the Tribunal, with one of its politicians comparing Berek to a “MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter” and a sheriff.

Therefore, I argue that some of the actions discussed above contradict the declared goal of the rule of law restoration – rather than rebuilding the legitimacy and credibility of the Constitutional Tribunal, they strengthen its perception as a political tool. Unfortunately, this discrepancy between declared goals of the ruling coalition and its actions is not limited to the Constitutional Tribunal alone.

This leads me to an important point: the reality is far more complex than the simplistic narrative spread by the current government about good liberals doing their best to fix the crisis while being thwarted by “bad guys”.

What do we want to achieve?

Scheppele, Pech and Kisilowski argue that Korwin-Piotrowska’s order is “an important – and necessary – step towards restoring the rule of law.” I do not share this optimistic conclusion – not only because I have serious doubts about the legality of the order, but also because I do not believe that actions such as those can truly heal the Tribunal effectively and permanently. However, this issue is connected to another important problem, namely defining what is necessary to restore the rule of law.

The discussion about restoring the rule of law in Poland concentrates, in my opinion, excessively on whether it is permissible to break the law to restore the rule of law, and on how to use international and EU law creatively to reverse the negative effects of the harmful changes implemented by populists. In this regard, it is sometimes framed as a dispute between formalists who insist on compliance with a letter of law disregarding its spirit and non-formalists who advocate for a more creative interpretation of law. However, in my view, this distinction is based on an oversimplification.

The experience of the last three years in Poland proves that there are limits to what can be achieved through legal interpretation alone, even when leveraging EU and international law. While legal interpretation can help protect individual rights in specific cases, restoring entire institutions requires systemic action.

If we want to truly heal judicial institutions, our ultimate goal should not merely be their recapture, but rather rebuilding their legitimacy. This conclusion is valid also in the context of the Constitutional Tribunal, which, as an institution, can function properly only if its legitimacy is universally accepted. How can the Constitutional Tribunal safeguard the Constitution if only half of the society accepts its legality and believes in its independence and impartiality?

For this reason, I do not believe that Anna Korwin-Piotrowska can truly solve the crisis around the Constitutional Tribunal. Certainly, the Government will accept functioning of the “new” Tribunal, but the President, the opposition and large parts of the society will not. We cannot ignore the fact that both the order’s questionable legality and the context in which it was issued do not positively affect the perception of the Tribunal’s credibility. Moreover, following a future change of power, a new government would likely remove these judges and recapture the Tribunal – once again framing it as a necessary step to restore the rule of law.

The Value of the Compromise

Therefore, in my view, only a political compromise can create conditions in which the Constitutional Tribunal could finally be accepted by all actors in the domestic political scene and could start functioning normally. The state of internal war over judicial institutions in Poland must be stopped as soon as possible, because its continuation threatens the very foundations of the constitutional structure of the state.

I have to underline that by such a compromise I do not mean a political deal under which seats in the Tribunal will be divided between various political groups. A compromise solution, also known as “constitutional reset”, envisages termination of terms of the incumbent judges and electing their successors in a new procedure, as proposed recently by Stefan Batory Foundation. This would ensure more pluralistic composition of the Tribunal and protect it against another instance of political capture.

It is, therefore, surprising to me that Scheppele, Pech and Kisilowski completely neglect the value of such a compromise. They even claim that by advocating for a compromise-based solution, the Helsinki Foundation “fails to give sufficient weight to the European judgments requiring the restoration of a lawfully constituted and independent Tribunal, something that would not be fulfilled by a political compromise.” I cannot agree with this statement; quite the contrary – I believe that to implement European standards fully, we have to make necessary constitutional changes. In this regard, it is worth recalling that both the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers and the Venice Commission have emphasized the need to introduce measures “to prevent external undue influence on the appointment of judges”.

The current model of election of the Constitutional Tribunal judges is deeply flawed. All judges are elected by the Sejm by a majority of votes. Therefore, the election process is more prone to politicization than, for example, election of Ombudsperson, where two organs, the Sejm and the Senate, have to reach a consensus. The sub-constitutional norms do not improve the situation. The Regulation of the Sejm provides that candidates for judges are nominated by the Sejm’s Presidium or groups of 50 deputies. There is no transparent preselection process, no open competition, no involvement of the National Council of the Judiciary etc. Ultimately, the decision of who should be nominated and elected can be made by a party leader. Given that terms of judges are nine years, if one party stays in power for two terms, it can usually elect all judges and, if it is guided by bad faith, capture the whole institution.

Political Reality

It is often argued that the scenario of a “constitutional reset” is just an illusion, a fantasy for the naïve, given that there are no realistic chances of its implementation. While I admit that the chances are slim, I have certain problems with such an approach.

If we assume a priori that compromise is impossible, we make it so. The basic precondition of a compromise is to enter into a dialogue with the other side, and if we assume that there is no sense in engaging in a dialogue, there will be no compromise. I could accept the conclusion that there are truly no chances at all for any meaningful constitutional compromise regarding the Constitutional Tribunal if there were some attempts of reaching it and all of them would fail. However, there were none.

Admittedly, in 2024, a group of senators of the ruling coalition submitted to the Senate a draft constitutional amendment envisaging termination of mandates of the incumbent judges, but this proposal definitely required further refinement and, at the moment, the legislative works over it are stalled. The draft was also critically assessed by the Venice Commission, however, as I explained elsewhere, not every form of “constitutional reset” must be inconsistent with international standards.

Moreover, currently the idea of a constitutional compromise is accepted by many NGOs and by some political groups. Just recently, eighteen organisations, representing various sectors and worldviews, signed an appeal calling for a reset of the Constitutional Tribunal. Some politicians also expressed their support for the idea. I do not think that it is fair to say that all of them are naïve or delusional.

However, one may ask what would happen if the compromise proved impossible. In this situation, the war over the Constitutional Tribunal would likely continue. We can expect that under Anna Korwin-Piotrowska’s leadership the Tribunal will function better than under Bogdan Święczkowski. For instance, I believe cases will be allocated to judges more transparently, and the Tribunal will stop questioning EU law and the ECHR. Hopefully, it will also resist being used merely as a tool to bypass the President and focus on protecting human rights. However, as already mentioned, its legality and independence will remain to be questioned, and I do not believe that after the possible change of power it will be able to act as a check against the new government. The same tricks that were used to block its actions and recapture it from PiS-appointees could be used effectively to capture it again. In this situation, the Tribunal will become just a part of the system of spoils.

Concluding Remarks

The discussion of Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska’s order is part of a longer debate over the rule-of-law restoration process in Poland. In 2026, three years after the current government’s appointment and one year before the next parliamentary election, it is fair to conclude that this process has so far been largly unsuccessful, mainly because of political deadlock. In my view, this deadlock can be broken only through some form of political compromise, not through questionable actions that would contribute to a perpetual cycle of capturing and re-capturing state institutions.

items.articleBody:
As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance.

Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.”

Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust.

“Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers.

These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands.

Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.”

items.articleBody:
Of course as an economist I am always wondering what the equilibrium is.  And, in this case, what is the scarce factor?

It seems that in the case under current consideration, the returns to honeypotting are very high for somebody.  Maybe for China, maybe for the shorts, or maybe for parts of the Deep State that seek to shape domestic politics (and they possibly drove the timing of the leak?).

So why are not three potential honeypots sent every day to the most prominent men?  If the guy says no, you do not have to pay them for very long, right?  Or you can just have them try another, different guy.

I can think of a few hypotheses:

1. The number of attractive women with sufficient spy training is actually pretty low.  Furthermore the spy agency has to trust the woman to some degree.

2. The number of attractive women willing to do this is pretty low.  But at what wage?  And in some countries threats to the family, or benefits to the family, can be added to the transaction.

3. It is difficult to access the most prominent men, and that limits the number of honeypots that can be sent.  Furthermore, at some point the honeypot woman has to find time alone with the man, and that is not always easy.

4. In fact three potential honeypots are sent every day to the most prominent men.

5. Competition from the non-honeypot women is so strong the honeypots do not have such a great chance, thus limiting their supply.  The non-honeypot temptresses will sometimes have stronger vetting as well.

6. Some of the most prominent men “go the Epstein route” instead, hoping for delegated vetting and a kind of mutual “hostage-taking,” noting that proved extremely risky as well.

What else?

Shik S32: Features

Links

Shik S-32

Auf der Superbooth 26 wurde der Shik MIDI Controller vorgestellt. Nun kann das Gerät endlich vorbestellt werden. Leider ist derzeit nur der Controller erhältlich und nicht dazugehörige CV16 Eurorackmodul.

Was kann der S32?

Der S32 MIDI-Controller kann mehr als gewöhnliche MIDI-Controller. Er wurde mit einer individuell anpassbaren MIDI-Effekt-Engine und programmierbaren Makros ausgestattet. Mit einem extern erhältlichen Eurorack-Modul ist es möglich, MIDI des S32 in CV-Signale umzuwandeln. Laut Hersteller eignet er sich für Live-Performances und Studio-Sessions. Außerdem wurde er in ein Metallgehäuse verbaut und Werte und Befehle werden auf einem Display angezeigt.

Was können die Regler des S32?

Der MIDI-Controller wurde mit 32 Makro-Reglern ausgestattet. Jeder der Regler kann bis zu 4 MIDI-Nachrichten gleichzeitig senden. So ist es möglich, mehrere Parameter, Geräte und Ausgänge mit nur einem Regler zu steuern.

S32 Display (Bidquelle: Shik)

Welche MIDI-Befehle beherrscht der S32?

Kurz gesagt versteht der S32 alle bekannten MIDI-Befehle. Unterstützt werden CC, 14-Bit-CC, NRPN, Program Change, SysEx und mehr. Er unterstützt MIDI-Learn. Die Regler können Befehle „abholen“, wodurch lästiges Drehen bis zum korrekten Wert entfällt. Pro Regler können individuelle Werte bestimmt und an ausgewählte Empfänger gesendet werden.

S32 Anschlüsse (Bidquelle: Shik)

Die MIDI-Effekte des S32

Der S32 verfügt über eine MIDI-Effekt-Engine. Dazu gehören ein Harmonizer, Scale Remap, Arpeggiator, euklidischer Sequencer, Delay, Randomizer, MIDI-Routing-Tools und mehr. Mehrere MIDI-Effekte lassen sich gleichzeitig anweden. Die Nutzenden haben die Freiheit, die Effekte nach ihrem Geschmack miteinander zu kombinieren, sodass das System perfekt auf jedes Setup abgestimmt werden kann.

Warum gibt es ein CV16 Modul?

Shik bietet zusätzlich das CV16 Eurorack-Modul an, welches auf die Zusammenarbeit mit dem S32 abgestimmt ist. Leider ist das Modul noch nicht erhältlich. Es wandelt die MIDI-Befehle des S32 in CV-Steuersignale um und verteilt sie auf 16 Ausgänge. Die S32-Funktionen, Makros und Effekte können so mit der CV-Welt kommunizieren. Zusätzlich wurde das Modul mit einem LFO ausgestattet.

CV16 Modul (Bidquelle: Shik)

Preis und Verfügbarkeit

Der Shik S32 kann für 559,00 Euro vorbestellt werden. Das CV-16 Modul wird nach vor auf der Shik Website beworben, ist aber weder dort oder im Fachhandel erhältlich. Wir informieren euch, sobald das Modul auch erworben werden kann.

items.articleBody:
Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don't agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

The missing electrons

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there's these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.
