items.articleBody:
DESIGNBOOM X INDX|GLOBAL: ROOM FOR UTOPIAS

Challenging the impulse to package buildings into neat aesthetic categories, the Room for Utopias podcast series returns with Indian architects and designers interrogating the tension between enduring human rituals and the myth of signature style. Realized in partnership with INDX|GLOBAL during designboom.paris, this edition, themed A Future Without Formula, investigates what happens when practices step away from recognizable branding. Across two panel debates, hosted by designboom’s Managing Editor, Iñaki Laguardia, the series frames architectural identity not as a static visual stamp, but as an evolving narrative rooted in environmental responsibility and a fluid way of thinking.

BETWEEN DIGITAL HABITS AND UNCHANGING BIOLOGY

The fifth episode of Room for Utopias brings together Ankit Gupta of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects, Shalini Ganguli of Shalini Ganguli Interiors, and Kshitiz Manu of K Manu & Associates to examine how architecture can balance fast-evolving lifestyles with persistent biological instincts. The conversation moves past superficial trends to identify what built spaces must preserve and what they must urgently reinvent.

Kshitiz Manu of K Manu & Associates distinguishes between daily habits and human nature through a computational metaphor. ‘Ritual is a software and instinct is an operating system. Rituals can be changed… but our instinct stays the same. To maintain that balance is architecture,’ Manu explains. He critiques hermetic, high-tech interiors that disconnect occupants from nature, warning against what he terms ‘2:00 p.m. building’ where static artificial lighting and perpetual climate control freeze the perception of time. Instead, he advocates for spaces that let moving sunlight and lengthening shadows reveal the day’s progression, emphasizing that a building’s real life only begins once the designer departs and daily chaos takes over.

Shalini Ganguli of Shalini Ganguli Interiors addresses domestic fragmentation caused by private screens and self-contained bedrooms, urging designers to safeguard areas of unstructured shared presence. Ganguli argues that rooms must intuitively enable families to coexist without forced interaction. ‘In many rooms you have your own television, you can completely lock yourself out… but what happens is that your life goes unwitnessed. It is our moral responsibility to not ever get rid of areas in the house which enable the family to interact with each other,’ Ganguli states, calling for homes that accommodate human connection and layered memories over sterile, picture-perfect staging.

Ankit Gupta of Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects emphasizes the emotional power of spatial sequencing. Drawing on historic typologies, Gupta describes how traditional architecture moderated privacy through layered transitions, leading occupants progressively from public streets into verandas, central courtyards, and finally secluded quarters. He argues that contemporary luxury lies in this subtle, unhurried progression rather than loud visual statements, requiring an earthy, climate-responsive material palette sensitive to local topography, whether building for the dry heat or colder mountain regions.

1/3

Shalini Ganguli (Shalini Ganguli Interiors)
Kshitiz Manu (K Manu & Associates)
Ankit Gupta (Ankit Gupta & Ridhima Sogani Architects)

WHY STYLE IS JUST MARKETING FOR ARCHITECTS

The sixth conversation dismantles the commodification of architectural aesthetics. Moderator Iñaki Laguardia sits down with Sonali Bhagwati of Designplus Architects (DPA), Priyanka Mehra of PS Design, Manish Gulati of MOFA Studio, and Ajay Arya of A Square Designs to interrogate whether signature styles limit creative evolution and contextual responsiveness.

Sonali Bhagwati of Designplus Architects (DPA) differentiates between superficial packaging and genuine practice identity. ‘When you look at identity, you are actually looking at the core values that a firm or a practice wants to imbibe. You don’t have to try and superimpose a particular style which is trending onto everything,’ Bhagwati states. For her, design s anchored in a deep narrative rather than aesthetic imitation: ‘The moment your narrative is strong, your architecture will always have a place.’

Manish Gulati of MOFA Studio challenges the historical obsession with stylistic signatures, arguing that styles are retrospective constructs invented by critics to sell architecture. ‘Style is only useful for critics and journalists… It’s the packaging. If you have to sell something and you don’t package it well, it won’t sell,’ Gulati remarks. Describing his studio as’’optimistic non-conformists,’ Gulati asserts that architecture should respond to personal aspirations, user memory, and pressing planetary urgencies rather than dogmatic stylistic rules. ‘Future is not about style. Future is about what is important at the moment  — like climate change — that’s the most important factor when it comes to architecture,’ he notes.

Priyanka Mehra of PS Design defends contextual belonging, balancing client aspirations with geographic rootedness. ‘The house must sit where it belongs. A design has to be rooted in identity, in context where it is sitting,’ Mehra emphasizes. She argues that individual stories should drive spatial concepts. ‘No two individuals are alike. Why do the houses need to be the same?’

Ajay Arya of A Square Designs reflects on the evolving nature of urban living, noting that major cities are experiencing a transitional phase where rigid stylistic dogma is giving way to fluid expression. Arya argues that an architect’s identity should not be bound to reproducing the same look repeatedly, but should instead manifest in how materials are combined and softened to reflect the personality of the inhabitant. ‘I feel creativity should be fluid… and also they should have freedom of thought, and how new things would just come our way in the future,’ Arya shares, emphasizing that spaces must balance modern trends with enduring personal resonance.

1/4

Sonali Bhagwati (Designplus Architects)
Priyanka Mehra (PS Design)
Manish Gulati (MOFA Studio)
Ajay Arya (A Square Designs)

ARCHITECTURAL PRACTICE ROOTED IN VALUES, NOT LABELS

From domestic thresholds that allow natural light and time to mark the day, to studios actively unlearning signature aesthetics in pursuit of ecological and public responsibility, both conversations advocate for an architecture unburdened by dogma. These practitioners show that utopias in contemporary practice do not require inventing a novel aesthetic stamp. By prioritizing core values over trending formulas, they point toward an architecture that remains grounded, adaptable, and genuinely alive long after construction ends.

items.articleBody:
Who says TV rots your brain? These days, it delivers its fair share of great storytelling, whether original or adapted. But this is Literary Hub, after all, and so as the weather gets cooler, we’ll be hunkering down with some long form literary adaptations. The only question is: which ones?

Earlier this year, we asked for your help determining the best modern literary film adaptation, and now we’re back to consider the best literary adaptations* ever to grace the small screen, using what is obviously the most scientific and objective method of selection: a bracket.

We separated our favorite TV adaptations into four loose quadrants, as the format requires: Carnage, where you’ll find shows that trade in violence, brutality, and horror; Carnal, where we put the shows that foreground sensual, sumptuous pleasures of the body (like sex, but also food, and also gossip, and also sports); Cerebral, where you’ll find the shows you have to actually watch instead of looking at your phone; and Cozy, which is just what it says on the tin. (There is some overlap, as you might imagine; we’ve made judgement calls as necessary.)

As always, we offer a disclaimer: These initial draft picks are based on the tastes and interests of the Lit Hub staff. We’re very sorry if your favorite show isn’t here, but not really, because you’re probably wrong.

So what are you waiting for? Voting is open now, and will continue throughout the week as the field narrows. Yes, we’ll be here a while; might as well pop something in the microwave. But first, pick your favorites below.

*Anything adapted from a book, graphic novel, or short story counts here; the original text doesn’t have to be fiction, or “literary” in the generic sense.

[Click image to enlarge and zoom]

*

INSTRUCTIONS:

It’s simple: for every match-up, pick your favorite. We’re looking for the best show, not necessarily the most faithful adaptation—though that may factor into your thinking. Or not! In short, go with your gut. We’ll tabulate up the results using our best liberal arts major math, and bring you the results tomorrow.

*

Game of Thrones (1) vs. The Haunting of Hill House (16)

Game of Thrones (2011)

Emotional manipulation, with dragons

Based on: George R. R. Martin’s A Song of Ice and Fire series (1996–…)

Subgenres: Everyone Dies • The Last Stand of Monoculture • Water Cooler Fodder

David Benioff and D. B. Weiss changed the game with their adaptation of George R.R. (for Really Really Slow At Finishing the Next Book) Martin’s already popular books, bringing the swords, dragons, morally complex characters, and unrepentant violence to life with big budget visuals and great performances. The Haunting of Hill House (2018)

How to exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality (or not!)

Based on: Shirley Jackson’s The Haunting of Hill House (1959)

Subgenres: A Family Affair • Spooky Places • Get Me Out Of Here

This Mike Flanagan–helmed miniseries loosely adapts Shirley Jackson’s masterpiece of horror, alternating between the past and present as five adult siblings continue to be haunted by what they experienced as children while living at Hill House. The ten episodes are draped in shadow and mist, colored in muted blues and greys, but its cast stands out: This is the show that introduced viewers to now-iconic scream queen Victoria Pedretti. Fans include Stephen King, spooky kids, and anyone in between who appreciates the unsettling. Fun fact: Flanagan’s The Haunting of Hill House proved so popular it provoked a follow up, The Haunting of Bly Manor, which loosely adapts The Turn of the Screw.  –OS

The Terror (8) vs. Sharp Objects (9)

The Terror (2018)

When getting stuck in ice is the least of your worries

Based on: Dan Simmons’ The Terror (2007) and Victor LaValle’s The Devil In Silver (2012)

Subgenres: Stay On Land! • Beast Mode • Supernatural Spookys

This anthology series had a pretty good showing across all three seasons, though the first is the best by a good stretch. Each season is set in a compressed, atmospheric setting (a Royal Navy ship caught in the ice, a WWII Japanese interment camp, and a Queens NY mental hospital) where something evil lurks (a beast on the ice, a ghost from across the sea, and a monstrous possession). The first season (the ship) is dreadful and tense, full of cramped isolation. Desperate sailors start to mentally fray from fear, extreme weather, and the threat of a lurking monster. It’s a creature feature meets survival story with great acting (and make-up effects, as the men waste away) and genuinely frightening monster moments.

The second season drops off a bit, though the setting of FDR’s racist internment program adds an element of real world terror to the ghost story. And the third season is good but straight ahead, based on a spooky Victor LaValle book. –JF

Roots (4) vs. Dexter (13)

Roots (1977)

A very American family saga

Based on: Alex Haley’s Roots (1976)

Subgenres: Classroom Classics • It Did Happen Here • Generational Stories

One of the most watched miniseries in American TV history and a seminal dramatic portrayal of America through slavery and the Civil War. The show almost got pulled when ABC executives saw how unflinching Roots was about the brutality of slavers, especially when they were being portrayed by some of TV’s most recognizable white faces. The network insisted on adding a concerned white captain who isn’t in the book. Haley’s novel was known for being the first popular work of fiction to present the horrors of the Middle Passage, which the show maintains. Some of the novel’s nuance is lost in the translation to TV, but Roots is excellent and anchored in great performances, including an early performance by LeVar Burton. –JF

Dexter (2006)

Who kills the killers?

Based on: Jeff Lindsay’s Dexter series (2004-2015)

Subgenres: Sunny Bloody Neon Miami • Aging Actors Down With Wigs • Bad Police • Deeply Uncomfortable Sexual Tension

Sometimes, all TV needs is a great, repeatable premise. Dexter, a sort of Robin Hood of murderers, is an all-timer of a pitch. Set in sunny Florida, the show follows the exploits of Dexter Morgan, who works exactingly as both forensic analyst and vigilante killer who targets other (worse) serial killers, with very fun and complicated implications. I mostly remember Dexter for the main character’s carefully constructed, near-sterile murder rooms where he does his wet work. They’re like deadly spider webs made out of plastic drop cloths—every time I drape a towel over the sink before I shave, I think of Dexter and his obsessive cleanliness.

The secondary characters are hit or miss, as are his victims (though shout out to the great, evil John Lithgow), and Dexter’s backstory has always struck me as implausibly bizarre—his adoptive cop dad manipulates a PTSD riddled child into becoming a good guy murder machine? But a thrilling cat and mouse hunt combined with police procedural is kind of all you want from TV. –JF

Say Nothing (6) vs. You (11)

Say Nothing (2024)

Revolution retold

Based on: Patrick Radden Keefe’s Say Nothing (2018)

Subgenres: Based on a True Story • Fight for Your Rights • Party Politics

Patrick Radden Keefe’s excellent book was my first introduction to both the Troubles and its cast of determined revolutionaries. Keefe’s project, centering on the mysterious disappearance of civilian Jean McConville in 1972, explored a centuries-long occupation through the eyes of a few key players. Josh Zetumer’s adaptation also managed to render the political personal, but this viewer admired how the show’s structure left space for thematic exploration.

Drifting from the tight focus on I.R.A. icon Dolours Price gives the series air to float big questions. So on the one hand, we have Lola Petticrew eating up scenery as moxie incarnate, but on the other, we have meaty arguments on statecraft, paramilitary strategy, and political atonement.

I also felt, watching this show, how alive the conflict is. And how unsettled! Say Nothing framed every single one of its nine episodes with a winky chyron noting Gerry Adams’ denial that he was ever a member of the I.R.A. Maybe the revolution will not be televised because the past isn’t even past. –BKA

Justified (2010)

A years-long argument for practicing one’s quick draw

Based on: Elmore Leonard’s short story “Fire in the Hole” (2001)

Subgenres: Digging Coal Together • Big Hats • Shooty Show

You might think it would be difficult to hang six seasons of a television show on a single short story. And it is—in the sense that the story in question, which introduces US Marshal Raylan Given, who believes in justice over rules, and who comes back home to Harlan, Kentucky, where he finds himself squaring off against an old coal mining buddy, Boyd Crowder, now on the other side of the law, has little to do with the overall plot of the show beyond the first few episodes. But famously, showrunner Graham Yost gave all the writers bracelets with “WWED” on them, for “What Would Elmore Do?” And you can tell. The writing is great, the acting is great, the tone—a sort of Southern Gothic meets Western meets modern crime drama—is electric, and the whole thing is entertaining as hell from top to tail. –ET

Homicide: Life on the Street (7) vs. The Night Manager (10)

Homicide: Life on the Street (1993)

A police procedural with slightly less copaganda than usual

Based on: David Simon’s Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets (1991)

Subgenres: Copaganda Lite • It’s Kind Of Like Baltimore’s A Character In The Show • TV Unaccountably Shot on 16mm

Before he was the godfather of prestige TV as the creator and showrunner of The Wire, David Simon was a crime reporter for The Baltimore Sun. In the 80s and 90s, the pinnacle of a reporter’s career was landing a book deal based on their beat, which is how Simon came to publish Homicide: A Year on the Killing Streets in 1991. (This would not, it turns out, prove to be the pinnacle of Simon’s career.) The book was then adapted for television. Police procedurals weren’t anything new, but one where the cops were depicted as flawed, sometimes violent people who struggled with the brutal realities of their jobs, and where the bad guys sometimes got away with it—that was unusual. Our present culture is steeped in “gritty” versions of every kind of genre fare imaginable, and you can blame Homicide for being an early harbinger of this endless trend. –EF

Le Carré’s taut novel is his first set outside of the Cold War, and the BBC adaptation is propulsive and tense. Friday Night Lights has a ton of fans who don’t know (or care) a thing about football, a testament to the show’s quality and popularity. War & Peace (2016)

American (actors) in Russia (’s most celebrated novel)

Based on: Leo Tolstoy’s War and Peace (1869)

Subgenres: Napoleon’s Coming To Town • The Classics But Gorgeous • Cold In Gowns

War and Peace is one of the quintessential gigantic must-reads, and according to Wikipedia, there are at least 20 different ways people have tried to adapt Tolstoy’s chunky classic: films, TV, plays, musicals, operas, and at least one comic. And why not? There’s a lot that’s just crying out to be put on screen from the sweeping historical novel about aristocrats and Napoleon’s invasion of Russia: romance, high drama, battles. This miniseries version from the BBC went all out on the locations and costuming, so it looks great. And it’s got a pretty stacked cast—the leads are American, top of the call sheet types, but there are also a ton of great British stage stars like Callum Turner, Jessie Buckley, and Jack Lowden, who are all excellent. Paul Dano is great as the rich and awkward Pierre Bezukhov, and Gillian Anderson makes an appearance too. Always good. But I have to admit that Lily James as Countess Rostova is disappointing—she seems a little over her head in the role. Some reviews tagged this version as too soap opera-y (though I’d contend that Tolstoy’ original is pretty soap opera-y) and Russian viewers were especially down on this version: The Guardian quotes a St. Petersburg paper describing the show as a “classic with cleavage.” –JF

Our collective mental image of Hannibal Lector belongs, rightfully, to Anthony Hopkins, but Mads Mikkelson in Hannibal is a very near second. Hannibal reboots Harris’s novels as a case of the week police procedural, with the added wrinkle that the cops are unknowingly consulting a deranged cannibal who’s pulling all kinds of strings behind the scenes. Mikkelsen plays Lector passing as a non-sociopath—he’s an idiosyncratically classy guy, but he’s charmingly able to blend into the civilian world. This is a successful Lector, a knowledgeable and competent psychotherapist living opulently and cooking beautifully—the food in this show is unreal, and Hannibal’s kitchen set-up will make any home chef jealous. There’s a lot of visual delights in the show, from Lector’s dozen course meals to the murder scenes that are downright baroque.

But what really makes Hannibal tick is the insane chemistry between Mikkelsen’s cold yet caring Lector and Hugh Dancy’s dewy-eyed, traumatized Will Graham. The two highly dramatic actors keep us watching as they spend seasons in a deadly, very sexy dance. It’s like a frothier Michael Mann thing, where two workaholics fall in love over their shared competences. –JF

MATCHUP:

Sex and the City (4) vs. Interview with the Vampire (13)

******************************************

Sex and the City (1998)

The show that launched a thousand online quizzes

Based on: Candace Bushnell’s Sex and the City (1996)

Subgenres: Dating Dating Dating • Parade of Guest Stars • Iconic Post-Its

Much has been written about Darren Starr and Michael Patrick King’s take on Candace Bushnell’s column, but not enough discourse hinges on the way Sex and the City metabolized the acid baked into its source material. I will go to the ramparts screaming that the real hat trick of this maddening, magnificent series is in the tone.

Consider: for all their candor and wit, Bushnell’s columns were chilly to the bone. Her cynical avatar, bedeviled by modelizers and sociopathic financiers, could brook neither Charlotte York-ish optimism nor Carrie Bradshaw-esque delusion. Whereas I think the series shines brightest when it toggles between a glamorous New York fantasy (see: Patricia Field’s costumes) and its grimy cousin, New York reality (see: Carrie’s checking account). Based on: John E. Douglas and Mark Olshaker’s Mindhunter: Inside the FBI’s Elite Serial Crime Unit (2017)

Subgenres: Serialized Serial Killers Stories • Washed-Out Color Palettes • Grotesques and Their Wicked Ways • The Male Loneliness Epidemic

Ah, Mindhunter, the show that dared to ask the question: “What if Zodiac was 20 hours long and somehow even creepier?” David Fincher’s grimly compelling, uncommonly restrained murder show—based on the FBI profilers who pioneered the study of psychopathic killers in the 70s and 80s—was taken from us too soon, but it was fun (I use the term “fun” incredibly loosely) while it lasted. Holden Ford (Groff) is the hotshot loner savant who burrows into the heads of America’s most prolific murderers. Bill Tench (McCallany) is his gruff but bighearted family man partner. Wendy Carr (Torv) is the unflappable closeted lesbian psychologist who completes the basement-dwelling trio. Every Monster of the Week encounter is hold-your-breath stuff, with a particularly memorable performance by Cameron Brittan as the gargantuan “Co-ed Killer” Ed Kemper. –DS

Put it on when you wish your spouse would stop trying to initiate sex while you’re busy staring at your conspiracy board.

See also:

Meet the Forensic Expert Behind Mindhunter

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Alias Grace (2017)

The other big Margaret Atwood adaptation of Trump 1

Based on: Margaret Atwood’s Alias Grace (1997)

Subgenres: Peggy Atwood Tells Us About Misogyny • Sarah Polley Tells Us About Gender-Based Violence • Unreliable Narrator • Hysteria

Netflix’s Alias Grace came out the same year as Hulu’s take on The Handmaid’s Tale, and it swiftly found itself overshadowed by its sister show’s limelight. But for some viewers, the six-part Alias Grace, about a 19th-century servant girl caught up in a bloody crime, was the stronger Atwood adaptation. With sinewy, elliptical scripts from showrunner Sarah Polley and a hypnotic lead performance from Sarah Gadon, this true crime story revels in the ambiguity of its protagonist. Is Grace a remorseless killer or a traumatized witness? A liar or a hysteric? She’s whatever she needs to be to survive in a world where men hold all the power. –CG

Put it on when you want to relive the Peak TV glory years.

See also:

All of Our Good—and All of Our Evil—Lies in Wait in the Archives • On the Feminine Urge to Murder

*

MATCHUP:

Wolf Hall (2) vs. East of Eden (15)

******************************************

Wolf Hall (2015)

The King and I

Based on: Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall (2009)

Subgenres: Milord and Milady Drama • Ye Olde Case Law • Divorced Guy Problems • Stiff Upper Lip

Cards on the table: Hilary Mantel is one of my favorite writers of all time, so Wolf Hall occupies a weird space for me. On the one hand, there is no way a television show can exceed the experience of reading the books, and on the other hand, I’m thrilled any time I get to revisit Mantel’s stories.

Luckily, the first season of Wolf Hall is exquisite: patient, cinematic, and subtly acted. Mark Rylance, Damian Lewis, and Claire Foy are all different flavors of calculating, and the conniving dance they’re locked into is mesmerizing. So much is communicated in looks, many hard to discern in the low lighting or obscured by the distance of court and class. It’s an unsettled, quietly tense show that steadily heightens the arcs of each main character, who get what they want but at tremendous cost. Just incredible writing in the first season, which lands an emotionally satisfying ending even if you know where these real historical events are headed.

The second season, alas, loses its footing. The next two books in Mantel’s trilogy are excellent and I applaud the impulse to adapt them, but returning ten years later with the same cast is more than a little dissonant. Still, the first season is good enough to put this show almost at the top of the pack all by itself. –JF

Put it on when you are thinking of going back to school to get your law degree.

See also:

How My Friend Hilary Mantel Got Inside People’s Minds • Diplomacy Noir • How Much Actual History Do You Need for a Historical Novel?

••••••••••vs••••••••••

East of Eden (2026)

A retelling of a Biblical retelling

Based on: John Steinbeck’s East of Eden (1952)

Subgenres: California Dreaming • Timshel Time • Sibling Rivalry • Stanford Alums

This brand new Netflix adaptation is gorgeous, and unafraid to foreground Steinbeck’s thorny moral dilemmas. This is based on the Bible, after all. It helps that the cast can handle the nuance—Florence Pugh and Dong Hugh Lee’s performances are stellar. Cathy Ames is one of literature’s great villains and Pugh is genuinely frightening, though I’m inclined to agree with The New Yorker’s Alexandra Schwartz that the added traumatic backstory doesn’t quite work: let her be a monster, as Schwartz says. But it’s a small concession to the streaming sensibility. The show is an otherwise brilliant take on Steinbeck’s ambitious magnum opus. –JF

Put it on when you are dreading going home for Thanksgiving.

See also:

The Unconventional Morality of East of Eden

*

*

MATCHUP:

Brideshead Revisited (1) vs. Beauty and the Beast (16)

******************************************

Brideshead Revisited (1981)

We have always remembered when we lived in the castle

Based on: Evelyn Waugh’s Brideshead Revisited (1945)

Subgenres: Teddy Bears • Stiff Upper Lip • Everything Changed During the War • Drugs, Booze & Generational Privilege • Debating Catholicism

Evelyn Waugh’s observant humanism was always in interesting tension with his sublimated (then blatant) conservatism. His best book, Brideshead Revisited, is nostalgic for aristocracy but clear eyed about its sins, mining the tensions between class values and personal connection. So much to say, this eleven episode miniseries succeeds by faithfully and reverently adapting the novel to the screen—this is about as much of a one-to-one translation from the page as you can imagine, with most of the dialogue coming directly from Waugh. The friendship that unfolds over a few decades before WWII between Charles Ryder and the rich Lord Sebastian Flyte of Brideshead Castle is subtly acted by Jeremy Irons and Anthony Andrews. The rest of the cast is great too, and they’re allowed to mope and emote around beautiful location shoots. Laurence Olivier makes an appearance, as one might expect, and of course actor Peter Bull’s teddy bear named Delicatessen stuns as Aloysius. It’s a wonderful TV classic. –JF

Put it on when you are wondering if you should reach out to an old friend.

See also:

How Campus Novels Reveal the Power—and Danger—of Pure Ideas • Not Far From Brideshead: On the Sad Glitter of Oxford Between the Wars

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Beauty and the Beast (1987)

Sexy beast-men and the city

Based on: Jeanne-Marie Leprince De Beaumont’s La Belle et la Bête (1756)

Subgenres: Choices Were Made • Cult Classic • Your Furry Awakening

This is probably the most radical and ridiculous reimagining of a source text that we have on this bracket. Cult classic Beauty and the Beast turns the classic Bête from a cursed prince into “a noble man-beast” living in the Tunnel World, a secret community of outcasts below NYC (it’s a little like Nightbreed‘s Midian but makes less sense?). And the Belle is no longer the pure of heart merchant’s daughter, but instead a corporate attorney who becomes a city ADA after falling for the Beast. The plot oscillates insanely between romance, action, and gritty crime drama, which makes it beloved by some and hated by others. But you can’t argue with Ron Perlman in beast-face.

Fun fact: George R.R. Martin was a writer and a producer on this show—make of that what you will. –JF

Put it on when you wish old fairy tales had more cops.

See also:

10 Transgressive Fairy Tales for Grown-Ups • Umberto Eco on the Elusive Concept of Ugliness

*

MATCHUP:

My Brilliant Friend (8) vs. I, Claudius (9)

******************************************

My Brilliant Friend (2018)

Female friendship, the Italian way

Based on: Elena Ferrante’s The Neapolitan quartet (2012-15)

Subgenres: Gorgeously Shot • • Nino Sarratore Sucks In Every Medium • Do We Think Ferrante Had a Secret Cameo?

If you’re reading this, I probably don’t have to remind you of the phenomenon that was Ferrante Fever. There was a brief span when it seemed like everyone was reading them—I was simultaneously texting my mom and my guy friends about Lenù and Lila. So it was a bit surprising to me that this visually striking adaptation didn’t make a bigger splash. Maybe it was the subtitles. A lot of people seemed to feel like that the show was almost too beautiful—the colors and shots are frequently arresting, putting Naples front and center in the story—and worse, too slow. But like the source text, this is an adaptation that rewards patience. –JF

Put it on when you can’t afford a ticket to Europe.

See also:

My Brilliant Friend is the Kind of TV We Need Right Now: Slow • “Wade Into the Muck With Me.” On Reading and Re-Reading Elena Ferrante • Language is the True Protagonist of My Brilliant Friend’s Third Season • Before the Neapolitan Quartet, There Was Sula

••••••••••vs••••••••••

I, Claudius (1976)

Thinking about the Roman Empire…

Based on: Robert Graves’s Claudius novels (1934-35)

Subgenres: Latin Nerds Assemble • Now This is Acting!! • Curly Haired Patrick Stewart

This show is often cited as one of the best TV shows of all time, and while it’s a little dated by contemporary standards, it certainly lit the path for many of the prestige dramas that would follow. This miniseries seemed to understand that, like a novel, television has the advantage of time, which allows for a deep evolution of character that often isn’t possible in a film. The story of the Roman Empire’s early days, from Augustus’s search for a successor to the reign of Nero, is told through the eyes of Emperor Claudius, portrayed by Derek Jacobi, a generationally talented Shakespearean actor and one of the founders of the National Theatre. The writing pulls the best interpersonal dramas and agonizing decisions from Graves’s novels: these are scenes that actors dream about and boy do they make the most of their opportunities. –JF

Put it on when you need a grand drama with a past generation of thespians at the height of their powers and want to see a couple 70s haircuts with togas.

See also:

Eight Books to Read If You’re Still Thinking About the Roman Empire

*

MATCHUP:

Pachinko (5) vs. Agatha Christie’s Poirot (12)

******************************************

Pachinko (2022)

Nearly a century of family bonds

Based on: Min Jin Lee’s Pachinko (2017)

Subgenres: Big Historical Moments • The Immigrant Experience • Significant Business Trips

Sweeping novels can often feel smaller when adapted to the screen: the episodic storytelling, weaving of storylines, and time jumps can feel more dissonant in adaptation. Pachinko manages to avoid these pitfalls, mostly because the source material is so excellent and full of dramatic turns and reveals, but also through the excellent direction, writing and casting— I’m always impressed when multiple actors can convincingly portray the same person at different ages. There is high drama here—war, desperation, betrayal—but the broader social picture of Korean immigrants to Japan and their descendants, Zainichi Koreans, is particularly moving, and the textural details of each era the show traverses, from 1915 to the 1980s, bring us closer to each story. It’s a great show that succeeds through its specificity and warmth towards its characters and their struggles. –JF

Put it on when an arcade game gives you a Proustian flashback.

See also:

The Many Forms of Love in Pachinko • Read an Excerpt from Pachinko

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Agatha Christie’s Poirot (1989)

Belgian stereotyping with a side of murder

Based on: Agatha Christie’s “Poirot” novels (1920-75)

Subgenres: Murder Follows the Protagonist • Really Good Tea Sets • Mid-Series Genre Shift

Agatha Christie’s Poirot ran for almost 25 years, went through at least two major shifts in tone and format, and appears to have guest starred every notable actor in the UK at least once. But there was only ever one Poirot: David Suchet, in what remains the most iconic take yet on Christie’s Belgian investigator. In Suchet’s hands, Poirot’s fussy neuroses go from comic to pathetic from moment to moment, while Poirot’s intelligence becomes a warm, empathetic curiosity about the people around him. However much Suchet’s Poirot preens and waxes his elaborate mustache, we can always see his little gray cells working away. –CG

Put it on when you are prepared to Google at least one murder suspect per episode to confirm that the actor really did become a movie star ten years later.

See also:

Agatha Christie is the best-selling novelist in history.

*

MATCHUP:

Lonesome Dove (4) vs. Rivals (13)

******************************************

Lonesome Dove (1989)

A story as big as that Montana sky

Based on: Larry McMurtry’s Lonesome Dove (1985)

Subgenres: Horses • Someday I’ll Leave This Town • Yeehaw • Walking Off Into The Sunset • Tears Falling on a Dusty Trail

There have been a lot of think pieces over the last year about the Lonesome Dove-aissance. It’s a great book, the kind of lengthy classic that reads as fast as a beachy thriller, and has been a sensation since it was published—it only took four years after publication to make it to the screen. The four episode, made for TV miniseries was an instant hit too, breaking all kinds of viewership records and raking in the awards, thanks in part to its top-tier cast: Tommy Lee Jones, Diane Lane, Robert Duvall, Danny Glover, Anjelica Huston, and many more. The only person who didn’t like it was Larry McMurtry himself; after the adaptation aired, he famously began to regret how the book had landed as “a kind of Gone with the Wind of the West.”

“I thought I had written about a harsh time and some pretty harsh people,” he said, “but to the public at large, I had produced something nearer to an idealization.” That’s TV for you! –JF

Put it on when you think you’d look good in a cowboy hat.

See also:

The Book That Changed My Life • What If I’m Actually a Character in a Larry McMurtry Novel? • Orphans, Institutions, and Adventures Out West: Five Books Featuring Unconventional Families

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Rivals (2024)

80s fashion, 80s sex, 80s England

Based on: Dame Jilly Cooper’s Rivals (and the larger Rutshire Chronicles) (1985-2023)

Subgenres: Soaps! • Thatcherite England • Rich People Behaving Badly • Juuuuicy Stories • Class Warfare

They really don’t make ’em like this anymore, or they haven’t in a while. Jilly Cooper was always a bigger name in the UK than in the States, and the show is very British—but its unapologetic horniness (sexual and also capitalistic) is in many ways a perfect melding of cross-Atlantic passions. People behaving badly, people having raucous sex, people spending insane gobs of money, people wearing riding breeches and/or big-shouldered suits and/or wild dresses—the show is insane, the books are insane, but they’re also a cheeky delight, and its the 80s of it all that tips this adaptation into the Cozy corner. If the 80s were really like this, I’m glad I was born at the end of them and also I’ll never tire of watching people act out this kind of nonsense. –DB

Put it on when you’re teasing out your hair.

*

MATCHUP:

Little House on the Prairie (6) vs. Big Little Lies (11)

******************************************

Little House on the Prairie (1974)

Tradwife-core

Based on: Laura Ingalls Wilder’s Little House on the Prairie novels (1932-71)

Subgenres: The Good Old Days • So Many Episodes • They Had To Cover The Child Actors’s Braces With Clay

This is one of the longest running shows on our bracket, with hundreds of episodes, specials, and TV movies. This is quintessential cozy TV, a wholesome family show set in an idealized vision of an American farming community after the Civil War. There’s a pretty sharp divide among fans of the books, many of whom see the show—which is repeatably situational, and not serialized—as too unfaithful. TV Little House pulls from episodes in Wilder’s books, but quickly charts its own path with the characters.

As Little House on the Prairie has aged, it’s come to stand in for the revisionist tendency in our portrayals of America, the rose-colored and naively nostalgic take on a dark period of history (though you’d be hard pressed to find an American era that wasn’t dark). The show has been grabbed by all sides of the culture war debates, with predictable outcomes. And yes, Little House’s portrayal of late nineteenth-century America smooths many bloody edges, but to its credit did address larger societal issues fairly regularly in its long run. While it is more than a little cheesy, the Ingalls family’s struggles can be more resonant than its loopy pink title might lead you to assume. –JF

Put it on when you want to go to a place where seldom is heard a discouraging word.

See also:

Little House of Propaganda: Homesteading Myths and the Sentimentality of Self-Reliance • Why Americans can’t seem to quit Little House on the Prairie.

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Big Little Lies (2017)

The Witherspoon book-to-TV machine’s biggest hit

Based on: Liane Moriarty’s Big Little Lies (2014)

Subgenres: Murder-Mystery • Wealthy California Moms • Scary Men • Scarier Kids

Whether you’re the targeted consumer of a Liane Moriarty novel or not is irrelevant when it comes to Big Little Lies. The show was a sacred union of Reese Witherspoon, Nicole Kidman, Shailene Woodley, Zoe Kravitz, and Laura Dern, all in the roles they were destined to play. That is: over-the-top-wealthy helicopter mothers who intermittently spend their time having anguished conversations with their husbands, their children, each other, and then gazing off into the ocean while drinking chilled wine. Each actress is so compelling and addictive to watch, with their domestic and social lives in such complicated and realistic turmoil, we almost don’t need the show to also be a murder-mystery of the highest caliber, and yet it is that too. We watched with bated breath to find out each and every detail of the murder, for this mystery takes the medium one step further: not only do we not know who the murderer is, we don’t even know who was killed. Even once you know those details, the show begs for a rewatch. The actors, the music, the money, the minutia, the Monterey Bay setting: all of it adds up to a soothingly impeccable version of an hour long drama. –JH

Put it on when you need to remember wealth ≠ happiness.

See also:

Women Can Lead Lives of Quiet Desperation Too

*

MATCHUP:

M*A*S*H (3) vs. Bleak House (14)

******************************************

M*A*S*H (1972)

Antics among atrocities

Based on: Richard Hooker’s MASH: A Novel About Three Army Doctors (1968)

Subgenres: War is Bad • Wisecracking is Fun

Iconic anti-war sitcom *M*A*S*H* challenged what a television comedy was supposed to look like, layering drama and genuine commentary with its humor. A spinoff of the 1970 Robert Altman film, which was adapted from the Hooker novel, it ran for 11 seasons and its finale was, at the time of airing, the most watched television episode in American broadcast history. Set during the Korean War, it more obviously paralleled and criticized American involvement in Vietnam. Now considered classic TV, there’s a reason appreciation for *M*A*S*H* endures over 50 years after its premiere. –OS

Put it on when you need a history lesson with personality.

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Bleak House (2005)

A mini series with big Dickens energy

Based on: Charles Dickens’s Bleak House (1852–53)

Subgenres: Rather Dickensian • The Law But Thrilling

Bleak House is a sprawling and twisting adaptation that is about as exciting as a story about estate law can get. There are so many characters, plotlines, and wonderful details in the novel, and the show doesn’t skimp on putting them all on screen. The result is a beautifully composed ensemble piece, full of glittering performances. Anna Maxwell Martin’s Esther is excellent at the heart of the story, but Gillian Anderson as the conniving and tortured Lady Dedlock steals every scene she’s in.

The show was broadcast in half hour episodes, breaking with BBC tradition, but more reflective of how Dickens had serially published the story. The frequent, sometimes forced cliffhangers are something we’ve all gotten used to in the streaming era, but the pace works since the material was written with this same cadence in mind.

And it’s always a delight to remember how good Dickens was at names: Bleak House has Krook, Clamb, Snagsby, Caddy Jellyby, and Prince Turveydrop, to name just a few. It’s MAD Magazine stuff! He had a comedian’s ear for a funny name. –JF

Put it on when you feel the need to keep track of a lot of overlapping secrets.

See also:

The Many Bad Moms of Charles Dickens • On Charles Dickens’ Devious, Hypocritical “Nice Guy” Cop

*

MATCHUP:

The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (7) vs. Olive Kitteridge (10)

******************************************

The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (1984)

The definitive adaptation of the original detective

Based on: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes stories (1887-1927)

Subgenres: A Clue! • You Might Not Like It, But This is What Peak Male Friendship Looks Like • Workaholics on Screen

Many Doyle-heads and Baker Street wannabes consider this to be the best adaptation of the Sherlock stories and Jeremy Brett to be the best of the many actors who have portrayed the detective over the years. It’s certainly the most faithful—the ubiquity of the Holmes cycle seems to compel most writers to monkey with the source material. But this 80s series mostly stays true. There are a few cases that are mashed together into one, and this version does have Sherlock kick his cocaine habit, which is not canon but probably best for the kids watching who might think coke makes you a super detective. Still, the true heads know: this is the best Holmes to ever make it to a screen of any size. –JF

Put it on when you want to crack a case from the couch.

See also:

How Sherlock Holmes Got His Name • The 12 Best Sherlock Holmes Stories, According to Arthur Conan Doyle

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Olive Kitteridge (2014)

A family saga slowly told

Based on: Elizabeth Strout’s Olive Kitteridge (2008)

Subgenres: Fictional Maine • Family Sagas • Ann Dowd Can Do Anything

Olive Kitteridge does right by its Pulitzer-winning source material: the interlinked stories of the book become a coherent, patient miniseries. I imagine the simplest choice would have been to divide the narrative into distinct episodes, like the book does, but the adaptation cleverly weaves everything together. Though she’s not the main character per se, Olive is the most prominent and recurring resident of Crosby, Maine. She’s played expertly by Frances McDormand, who is able to sell the glimmers of love and hope behind Olive’s crabby exterior. There are some deeply tragic moments in this story but the humor sticks out most in my mind: I love the bizarre set piece of Olive and her husband fighting while they’re being held hostage. It takes talented actors to ground a scene like that. –JF

Put it on when you want to feel like you’re watching a novel.

See also:

Six of the Best Bad Women in Fiction • Writing “Women of a Certain Age.” A Roundtable on Crafting Older Female Characters in Fiction • Romance Finely Aged: On the Unique Dynamic of Older Couples

*

MATCHUP:

Pride and Prejudice (2) vs. Parade’s End (15)

******************************************

Pride and Prejudice (1995)

Thee Pride and Prejudice

Based on: Jane Austen’s Pride and Prejudice (1813)

Subgenres: Bonnets • Yearning • Water Cooler Fodder When There Were Still Water Coolers • Every Scene of the Novel

Has there ever been a TV mini series as beloved as this BBC charmer? Adapting one of Austen’s most beloved novels with scrupulous fidelity, Pride and Prejudice was an immediate sensation on both sides of the Atlantic when it premiered in 1995. Bright-eyed Jennifer Ehle rode her performance as Elizabeth Bennet straight into an acclaimed theater career, while Colin Firth’s turn as the saturnine Mr. Darcy was so magnetic it transformed him into a Hollywood leading man almost overnight. In the years since, there’s been more than one Pride and Prejudice on screens both big and little. But for purists, there’s never been anything to touch the classic. –CG

Put it on when you have a hankering for charged flirting in a drawing room.

See also:

Martin Amis on the Genius of Jane Austen (and What the Adaptations Get Wrong) • Every Mr. Darcy* Ranked • Why We Still Love Mr. Darcy, 200 Years Later

••••••••••vs••••••••••

Parade’s End (2012)

War is hell, and the home front’s no picnic

Based on: Ford Madox Ford’s Parade’s End tetralogy (1924–1928)

Subgenres: Yearning • Tom Stoppard on Screen • Stiff Upper Lip • Socialites in Disarray

A social drama of obligation, infidelity, and class is set in a changing world upset by war and new norms—a long way of saying Parade’s End is Very British. The novels excel because of their modernist distance—I’ve read Ford’s approach to war and romance described as bafflingly anticlimactic, “a tragedy without a denouement.” Stoppard streamlined Ford’s novels, clipping out nearly a whole book, but the edits work to bring the characters convincingly onto the screen. As a playwright, Stoppard builds the story around scenes that actors can live in, and the leads Rebecca Hall and Benedict Cumberbatch take full advantage. Both are excellent at portraying the inner turmoil of thwarted desires and tragic heartbreak, all while keeping a brave and decorous facade—again, Very British! –JF

Put it on when you need to wallow in someone else’s misery for once, or have a thought that one mustn’t have…

See also:

On Saintliness and Despair in Ford Madox Ford’s Parade’s End

*

******************************************

Thanks for voting! We’ll see you tomorrow with the results!

items.articleBody:
The Commonwealth War Graves Commission has unveiled a memorial to the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps in Freetown, Sierra Leone.

Officially opened this weekend, the memorial designed by Oshinówò Studio sits on top of a war memorial designed by British architect Edwin Lutyens in 1931.

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

Photographys

Previous

Next

Photographys

Close

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

While the original memorial honoured soldiers who died in the first world war, it did not include the names of the 946 members of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps – men enlisted to transport supplies and materials – who also died in the war.

Oshinówò Studio extended the Lutyens-designed, stone memorial by adding a structural glass pyramid etched with the names of the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps men.

Photo by CWGC / Lansana Mansaray

"The Freetown Memorial is conceived through a material symbolism that allows it to resonate across cultures and contexts," said Oshinówò Studio founder Tosin Oshinówò.

"The structure we designed is, in effect, an extension of Sir Edwin Lutyens' existing monument. By following its tapering geometry, the new monument rises higher, elevating the immense volume of names etched into glass. "

According to Oshinówò, placing the names of the carrier corps men higher than the soldiers was also a symbolic move.

"In this gesture, the Sierra Leone Carrier Corps are symbolically carried by their comrades, reversing the relationship between those who served and those who were served," she said.

"There is a profound irony in this act: it becomes a fitting expression of gratitude to men whose sacrifice was fundamental to shaping the world we inhabit today."

items.title: The Pressure on LA’s First Socialist Mayor
items.subtitle: On paper, the second-largest city in the country has its first democratic socialist mayor.
items.feedText: Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman declared victory on Thursday over the embattled incumbent Karen Bass, joining a list of socialist mayors who have risen to power in recent years, including Zohran Mamdani in New York; Seattle’s Katie Wilson; and most recently Janeese Lewis George in Washington, D.C., who won in a landslide this week. items.articleBody:
On paper, the second-largest city in the country has its first democratic socialist mayor.

Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman declared victory on Thursday over the embattled incumbent Karen Bass, joining a list of socialist mayors who have risen to power in recent years, including Zohran Mamdani in New York; Seattle’s Katie Wilson; and most recently Janeese Lewis George in Washington, D.C., who won in a landslide this week.

Raman, however, did not campaign unabashedly as a socialist. Though she ran as an endorsed member of the Democratic Socialists of America’s Los Angeles chapter, the national DSA threatened to override the local chapter and rescind the endorsement over concerns around her stances on Israel and Palestine.

Unlike her counterpart in New York, to whom she draws most comparisons, Raman did not make sweeping socialist promises, such as free public transit, universal childcare, or taxing the rich. Instead, she focused on what’s wrong with the city. Riding a wave of resentment for Bass’s alleged mismanagements of the Palisades fire and the Lineage Logistics warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, Raman talked about filling potholes, fixing street lights, and making roads safer for pedestrians and cyclists.

In addition to DSA-LA support, she earned the endorsements of popular anti-corruption City Controller Kenneth Mejia and Unite Here 11, a major local hospitality workers union, whose large membership canvassed for her in the general. But she lacked endorsements from most key labor groups and social justice nonprofits, and the organizing base they provide. Her fellow DSA members on the Los Angeles City Council all pulled for Bass, forcing Raman to battle back the perception that she struggles to build coalitions.

While Mamdani, 10 months into his term, now finds himself under pressure from New York’s left for refusing to fire NYPD’s police commissioner, his massive base of organizer support offers a buffer to criticism. Raman won over the city’s voters, but it’s not clear how much time that will buy her to tackle the city’s most vexing problems once she takes office.

“Folks in New York are willing to cut Mamdani more slack on the movement side, because he was one of them on a bunch of issues,” said David Levitus, executive director of LA Forward, a progressive nonprofit that endorsed Raman in the general election. ”I think Nithya” — who did not come from the ranks of DSA organizing like Mamdani — “has more skepticism from parts of the left because of that.”

Raman will face scrutiny from LA’s progressive left on a host of issues: bloated police department spending amounting to roughly a quarter of the city’s nearly $15 billion budget; fear of collaboration between ICE and law enforcement agencies; the 2028 Olympics prompting an expansion of surveillance; rising homelessness; and failing infrastructure.

Weeks before the November election, Raman seemed less concerned with movement-based allegiances or ideological labels, saying she is “a capitalist and I’m also a democratic socialist.” Before the primary in June, she said she was “one of the most independent voices in City Hall” when asked about her membership with DSA. The statements and her votes in city council have prompted intense debate among DSA-LA’s members over whether Raman holds up to democratic socialist ideals.

Related

The Los Angeles Left Is at War With Itself Over the Mayor’s Race

While most Angelenos do not care about such fine distinctions, Raman’s measured embrace of socialist mantle has created among some activists the perception of a more responsive audience in city hall compared to previous administrations. Yet to others on LA’s progressive left, Raman’s ideological elusiveness reads as political unreliability.

“I don’t think Nithya Raman is accountable to anyone in the movement,” said Kris Rehl, an activist who volunteered for Raman during her 2020 city council run and now runs the mutual aid group LA Street Care. “If you do not subscribe to any ideology, you can’t be held accountable to it.”

Rehl, who advocates for abolishing anti-camping bans that criminalize homeless encampments near schools and daycares, expressed dismay over Raman’s previous votes on expanding the police department despite running on defunding the police in 2020.

Others like Tal Levy, a member of DSA-LA’s electoral politics committee, remain more optimistic about what Raman can deliver as mayor. While DSA-LA is pushing for reallocating funds from the police budget into social services, Levy sees the value of Raman’s pledge to support LA Forward’s initiative of citywide expansion of unarmed crisis response teams, which divert certain 911 calls to teams of social workers and clinicians, rather than police.

“Even if Nithya were a fire-breathing abolitionist, it would still be a long fight to make those changes,” said Levy, who has been organizing with DSA-LA for nearly a decade. “But I believe there is plenty of room for us to make material wins in the short term.”

Room to Push

While there is debate over how much power DSA-LA has within LA’s political landscape, the group provided Raman additional attention and credibility among leftist voters, which was only bolstered by the successes of other DSA-endorsed candidates in New York and in congressional races across the nation.

The DSA’s National Political Committee, however, spurred one of the biggest public rifts during Raman’s campaign. The committee held a vote to un-endorse Raman over her perceived lack of support for the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement, which hadn’t been included by the DSA-LA on its endorsement questionnaire. After a week of debate and dueling resolutions, and an email from Raman, in which she wrote, “the best way for working Angelenos to stand in solidarity with Gaza is through non-violent protest, legislative action, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS,” the national committee decided against rescinding its endorsement of Raman by a narrow margin.

Frances Gill, one of three DSA-LA members on the DSA national political committee, voted against rescinding the group’s endorsement. She opposed the idea of alienating the organization’s second largest chapter as “bad organizing and bad leadership,” especially in a high-profile race when the stakes for the regional and national chapters were so closely intertwined.

“The public ties us to one another,” Gill said of the DSA and Raman, “and there’s not a lot of other key players who have also played such a critical role in her being able to win. So I think that gives us an outsized seat at the table.”

Related

Israeli Real Estate Expo Advertising West Bank Settlements Returns to NYC

She was a part of the faction among national leadership that instead called for a long-term pressure campaign on Raman on the issue of Israel and Palestine. The group is planning to push Raman on what she can do as mayor to halt the transportation of military hardware that makes its way through the Los Angeles International Airport to Israel. Organizers also plan to call for an end to real estate events in LA facilitating the sale of housing illegally built in the occupied West Bank. They will also examine whether the city itself is invested in companies that are profiting off Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid rule of Palestinians.

“I think there is room to push,” Gill said.

Another major public spat between progressives and Raman took place in January before she announced her candidacy for mayor.

Catching housing advocates by surprise, Raman introduced a motion to reform the city’s “mansion tax” to make exemptions for developers. Raman claimed that the tax, known as Measure ULA, was inadvertently preventing construction of new multi-family housing. Organizers opposed the idea, since the tax generates funds for services to support existing affordable housing and keep people housed, and that carveouts for developers would only fuel displacement of low-income renters, possibly pushing more people to the streets.

LA Forward was among those blindsided by the motion, which she eventually withdrew. Before endorsing Raman, Levitus and the group met with the candidate alongside organizers in an activist’s home.

“She talked about, ‘The times when I’ve succeeded, it’s because I built a coalition, the times when I failed, it’s because I didn’t, and I didn’t bring people along,’” Levitus recalled from the July meeting. “She really owned her mistake. I don’t know how much her mind has changed intellectually about the policy, but think clearly she recognizes that she needed to do something different — and that might lead to her pushing for a policy that is different from what she had pushed for before.”

Police Chief Dilemma

Among Raman’s early tests progressives will be watching for is how she fulfills her pledge to fire LAPD police chief Jim McDonnell. Raman was among the councilmembers who approved his appointment in 2024, despite concerns around his track record of collaborating with ICE as LA County sheriff. She has since said she would fire McDonnell over his response to the ICE raids and his refusal to enforce a state law that banned federal agents from wearing masks.

Yet the pledge to replace McDonnell may present a political quagmire for Raman, given that the mayor in LA cannot unilaterally force out a police chief. The city’s police commission, consisting of five civilians appointed by the mayor, must make that decision. Raman first will need to assemble her own commission, but that process also requires approval from a city council that remains largely supportive of the police department.

William Gude, a vocal police accountability advocate who supported Raman in the election, said he planned to push the mayor to circumvent the process by asking McDonnell to resign. “I’m putting pressure on her from day one,” he said. “There’s some promises that she made, and those promises need to be kept.”

In her first press conference as mayor-elect, Raman sidestepped a question about whether she still planned to fire McDonnell, amid public threats from the police union warning of “Armageddon.” “Public safety is the most important service the city is delivering to its people,” said Raman, noting the chief was one of her first phone calls after winning.

Activist pressure could be a burden for Raman — or a tool she could use to force legislation through a city council she knows well, according to Gude. “Does she want to have activists coming after her, also while battling 15 council members?” said Gude, who goes by @FilmthePoliceLA on social media. “Or would she rather have the activist base going after the council members that are coming after her, to create a buffer, to do a lot of her heavy lifting? It’s a choice she has to make.”

Hamid Khan, who heads the Stop Spying LAPD Coalition, is among those who is closely watching who Raman appoints to her police commission. But he sees Raman’s pledge of firing McDonnell as “a band-aid” for the more glaring structural issues of the department. While crediting Raman’s opposition to automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and Axon, Khan also pointed to Raman’s historic support for expanding the police department.

While in city council, Raman voted to expand LAPD’s budget three times: in 2021, 2022, and 2023. But she also voted against police raises in 2023, and this year, she opposed a plan by Bass to hire 170 more officers. She has said on the campaign trail she does not wish to expand the police budget, but also said she would not cut into it either.

Related

LAPD Deployed Drones to Spy on No Kings Protest

In the span of her time in city council, the LAPD has expanded its surveillance reach, Khan said. The department is slowly unrolling its Real-Time Crime Centers, which meld automated license plate reader technology, social media monitoring software, and CCTV cameras into a constant surveillance tool. He warned such a technology, while marketed to curb retail theft, will disproportionately harm Black and brown Angelenos.

“We have to situate the people’s expectations in Los Angeles that they’re not based upon the comment, ‘I’m gonna fire Jim McDonald,’” said Khan, who advocates for abolishing the budding police outposts. “What does that do? The fundamentals still remain the same.”

A True Outsider

There is a notion among some on the left that Raman is very much a part of the political machine that bred some of LA’s ongoing problems. She has served on city council for five years and was an ally to Bass, having endorsed Bass just weeks before jumping in the race herself. Yet Raman, a Harvard-educated urban planner and former entertainment director of Time’s Up, is in many respects an outsider to the political establishment.

Former City Councilmember Mike Bonin called Raman’s victory a “reordering of the governing class in Los Angeles.” For the past several decades, LA politics has been run by establishment Democrats, such as Bass or her predecessor, Eric Garcetti, son of a former LA County district attorney; the chambers of commerce; lobbyists; longtime city hall staffers; all riding the influence of homeowners.

Related

The Elon Musk Funder Trying to Sway the Race for LA’s Top Lawyer

For Lex Steppling, an organizer with Los Angeles Community Action Network and a critic of Raman’s time in city council, the “political recalibration” with her victory in city hall was a welcome sight.

Steppling grew up in a generation of LA political activists who got their start organizing with Community Coalition, which Bass founded in 1990 and for a long time was the only progressive organization in the city offering paid political work. He watched as his peers grew to leading campaigns on issues such as policing and mass incarceration, then began running for elected office. They brought with them their organizing chops, but also their relationships with the organizations that gave them their start. Steppling described this as a “relational ecosystem,” in which movements would be co-opted into electoral politics — in which scoring political points became more important than addressing the issues.

He blamed the lack of gains on policing and mass incarceration since the 2020 George Floyd uprising on such a relational ecosystem. A victory for Raman could mark a reset to such an establishment, and he hopes activists will capitalize on the opening.

“The right kind of openings to do the right kind of work will reemerge,” said Steppling, who helped lead a successful anti-incarceration measure in 2020. “It’s gonna once again start to be about the demands.”

Raman’s election evoked for Bonin memories of the last time an LA incumbent mayor was ousted. In 2005, then-state Assembly member Antonio Villaraigosa beat James Hahn, becoming the city’s first Latino mayor. Villaraigosa, previously director of Southern California ACLU, was seen as a progressive candidate at the time. That’s not how he governed. An early sign of his establishment politics was hiring a longtime political insider as his chief of staff.

Raman will also signal her governing priorities with the hires for her transition team and cabinet.

Some organizers were encouraged to see progressive figures added to her campaign, such as Faizah Malik, a civil rights attorney and former city council candidate also endorsed by DSA-LA, and Jamie York, an advocate for greater transparency in city politics whose high-profile rejection by the city council as an ethics commission appointee drew public scrutiny. It remains unclear what if any role they would play in city hall.

The LA Times reported that Rick Cole, former deputy mayor, is expected to supervise Raman’s transition team alongside Andrea Conant, Raman’s chief of staff in city council.

“How big is the table,” Bonin said, “and how much of the activist community is at the table?”

# Sunday thread mailbag 2bb

Die Analyse zu „Sunday thread mailbag 2bb“ untersucht die kognitiven und psychologischen Mechanismen mentaler Widerstandskraft und intellektueller Fokussierung. Im Fokus stehen fundierte Erkenntnisse der Kognitionswissenschaft, Strategien gegen digitale Reizüberflutung sowie die Kultivierung geistiger Klarheit im anspruchsvollen Alltag. Vertiefende Ausführungen und praktische Perspektiven sind im Primärbeitrag dokumentiert.

## Hintergrund & Vertiefung

Die Auseinandersetzung mit diesen Fragen berührt grundlegende Mechanismen menschlicher Urteilskraft und kognitiver Autonomie. Durch die bewusste Reflexion von Aufmerksamkeitsarchitekturen können Lernende und Lehrende ein vertieftes Verständnis komplexer Zusammenhänge entwickeln.

> „Kritische Urteilskraft entsteht durch die geduldige Analyse von Voraussetzungen und empirischen Zusammenhängen.“

## Perspektiven & Anwendung

Für Schule, Forschung und gesellschaftlichen Diskurs eröffnen sich konkrete Anknüpfungspunkte: Statt passiver Informationsaufnahme fördert die methodische Reflexion eine eigenständige und nachhaltige Urteilsbildung.
